entry.title: Review: The Gen 6 Santa Cruz Tallboy is VPP-Free and Thriving
entry.content:
Earlier this year, Santa Cruz completely overhauled the Tallboy, its popular short-travel trail bike. The redesign included a slightly slacker head tube angle, a lighter frame, and the addition of 10mm of travel at both ends. The biggest story, however, was the move away from Santa Cruz’s longstanding VPP suspension platform to a simpler 4-bar Horst-Link layout. This last design change led many to question why they would even buy a Santa Cruz without its brand-defining suspension platform.

When the Gen 6 Tallboy was announced, I was immediately interested in testing it. As someone who enjoys short- to mid-travel trail bikes, I got along pretty well with the past two generations of the Tallboy — they were nearly identical, after all. That said, I felt the previous Tallboys had some limitations, and the VPP suspension platform has never really been my favorite, which is why the Gen 6 redesign appealed to me so much.  

I got my hands on the latest Tallboy back in August and have been riding it off and on until just recently. I’ve pedaled it for hundreds of miles on the trails in and around Reno, NV, and the greater Lake Tahoe area. I can confidently say that the Tallboy is more capable and versatile than its predecessors, and is easily the best version yet. It’s a freaking blast to ride, and I sure wish I didn’t have to send it back.

What’s New?

We covered the Gen 6 updates to the Tallboy in our launch article several months back. You can check that out here if you want to revisit the details. Long story short, there were some major changes, most notably bumping travel to 130mm in the rear and 140mm up front, and the move to the aforementioned 4-bar Horst link suspension layout. With 120mm XC bikes, including the new Santa Cruz Blur, growing increasingly capable, the overlap in the lineup and the weight penalty of the previous Tallboy wasn’t making much sense anymore, and the increase in travel moves the Gen 6 more squarely into trail bike territory.

Of course, the move away from VPP means the frame’s silhouette has also changed a little bit with a less complex linkage and pivots on the chainstays. This also allowed for a straighter seat tube with increased insertion, making it easier to run longer travel droppers. Santa Cruz wisely carried over its well-executed in-frame storage, normal internal cable routing, threaded bottom bracket, and molded rubber protection on the downtube, bottom bracket, and chainstay. It has all the features we’ve grown accustomed to on modern mountain bikes.

The Gen 6 Tallboy frame is offered in Santa Cruz’s top-tier CC carbon fiber only, and it’s still a dedicated 29” bike, no mullet option here. While its travel has increased, Santa Cruz claims it reduced frame weight by ~300 grams. Geometry-wise, Santa Cruz made some tweaks but didn’t deviate too far from the existing formula. The biggest change is a slightly slacker head tube angle, at 65.1° in high and 64.8° in the low flip-chip setting. Adjusting the flip chip also changes the bottom bracket height by +/-3mm. 

First Impressions 

Right out of the box, the Tallboy started making a strong impression. I’d argue that the updated frame and 4-bar layout have a clean, modern look, and the Gen 6 is the best-looking version yet. The dark purple frame with reflective silver logos really did it for me, and proved to be attention-grabbing out on the trail, too. At just over 29 pounds in the XO AXS RSV build, it’s also respectably lightweight for a 130/140mm trail bike. On the first ride, the low weight was immediately apparent in its snappy handling and willingness to get up and go.

A Questionable Front Tire Spec 

The stock Maxxis Forekaster tire spec undoubtedly contributed to its spirited, fast-rolling nature, and this bike simply felt quick, responsive, and efficient up, down, and all around. Those tires are not only quick, but they’re surprisingly grippy in the right conditions, too. Grippy enough that they lulled me into a false sense of trust and confidence. I think the Forekaster is an excellent rear tire, but it quickly became apparent it was not the ideal front tire in the typically loose and loose-over-hard conditions in my area. 

I ran the stock tire setup for the first couple of weeks, but after washing out the front tire numerous times — one of which resulted in a very hard crash — I swapped the front tire out for a more aggressive Kenda Double Diamond Trail. I eventually swapped the rear tire out for the new Kenda Ripper Trail, and ran that setup for the remainder of my testing. This simple tire swap made an enormous difference in the Tallboy’s performance, and highlighted the importance of matching your tires to both your conditions and riding style. 

This tire swap took the Tallboy from fast, fun, and kinda squirrelly to fast, fun, and way more predictable. Being able to trust the grip of the front tire significantly boosted my confidence and allowed me to ride the Tallboy way harder. Of course, the dual Forekaster setup may be ideal for some riders and locations, but if I could do it again, I’d switch out the front tire for something more aggressive before the first ride, and I’d probably recommend that most riders do the same — unless you primarily ride mellower terrain and/or hero dirt.

Climbing

Right out of the gate, one of the first things I noticed about the Tallboy was its more relaxed seated pedaling position. The 475mm reach and 76.5° effective seat tube angle are almost exactly the same as the previous version, but the stack is a bit taller, and there’s no shortage of adjustability in the front end.

The XO build I was testing came with a 35mm rise OneUp Carbon V2 handlebar, Race Face Turbine SL stem (flippable for +/-6mm rise), and 40mm of stack height to play with. I tinkered around a bit, but landed roughly in the middle of the available adjustment range. The point being, it’s got a fairly trail-oriented pedaling position that I found to be quite comfortable for a bike with its (bordering on XC-bike-esque) climbing performance and efficiency. 

I always thought the pedaling performance of VPP was one of its best attributes, but it sacrificed sensitivity and generally felt a bit harsher for it. In my opinion, the Gen 6 Tallboy’s 4-bar suspension offers significantly more comfort over small bumps and trail chatter, great climbing traction, and it doesn’t sacrifice much, if any, pedaling support or efficiency — even with 10mm more travel. That’s hard to quantify, of course, but I was genuinely surprised to see my climb times on Strava pretty much neck and neck with the Pivot Mach 4 SL I was riding for much of the summer. 

Still, it’s not an XC bike, nor is it pretending to be. But I think Santa Cruz did an excellent job with the suspension to improve rider comfort while still delivering the efficient pedaling performance expected from a lighter trail bike. It was similar to the Allied FITZ in that I felt I could ride faster, farther, and for longer, while staying fresher than on some other bikes in the same travel bracket. 

I found its handling to be sharp, and it was easy to maneuver in tight spaces and technical sections of trail, and I was genuinely surprised by just how zippy and energetic it felt on single track, fire roads, even on the pavement. I had no issues navigating tight switchbacks and always found ample traction at the rear wheel when scrambling over rocks, steps, or loose, blown-out surfaces. That said, the bottom bracket is fairly low at sag, and I definitely encountered a few rock strikes when pedaling through techy spots. It’s 3mm higher in the high flip chip setting, but again, still relatively low.

Descending

Both of the previous Tallboy generations were very adept and capable on the descents, particularly in their short travel context. If you ever rode either of those bikes, then you’re probably aware their only real limitations were their suspension travel and what you were willing to ride them down. Not surprisingly, the Gen 6’s 4-bar suspension, increased travel, and slacker head tube angle all combine to enhance its downhill capability compared to the previous version. At the same time, the Tallboy doesn’t lose the lively, nimble, and downright playful character that helps define its downhill performance.

It’s easy enough to throw around the words “ more capable”, but what exactly does that mean? In the case of the Tallboy, it is undoubtedly a better descender than its predecessor for several reasons. First, and perhaps most obviously, it has more travel to soak up bigger hits, get you out of trouble, or, in my case, help offset my general lack of descending skill. I know 10mm may not sound like a lot, but it makes an outsized difference on a shorter travel bike like the Tallboy. At the same time, it doesn’t really add any weight or try to turn it into something it’s not.

Second, I believe the 4-bar platform provides a more well-rounded suspension performance. While I appreciated the mid-stroke support and big-hit performance of VPP, I always felt it lacked sensitivity off the top, and it transmitted a fair amount of feedback to the rider. With the 4-bar layout and revised kinematics on the Gen 6, Santa Cruz delivers a much better balance throughout the travel.

It’s more supple and responsive right off the top, mid-stroke is still supportive and poppy when you want it to be, and there’s enough progression at the end of travel to avoid bottom-outs unless you’re doing something stupid. Don’t get me wrong, the VPP Tallboy was good, but I think the 4-bar Tallboy is much better.

Third, the refreshed geometry brings it up to date without taking it too far. The head tube angle is marginally slacker, which undoubtedly helps enhance stability at speed and composure in steep terrain. The higher stack also contributes to a more confident descending position. Still, these are fairly subtle changes that don’t detract from its responsive handling feel, at least in my experience. Personally, I’m glad they didn’t make it much slacker or try to turn the Tallboy into some kind of wannabe mini-enduro bike, because I think it’s just right the way it is.

Overall, the Gen 6 Tallboy is smoother, calmer, and more confidence-inspiring on the descents than its predecessors. It’s far from a plow-machine, and it still rewards good line choices, but the margin for error is a bit greater. And thankfully, the Gen 6 update didn’t rob it of its spunky and playful attitude. I found myself pulling up to manual through all the dips and popping off just about every roll and side hit on the trail, no matter how small. It might not have inspired me to ride everything as fast as possible, but it certainly had me squeezing all the fun I could out of every ride.

The Build

The XO AXS RSV build I tested is second from the top of the line, and comes in under the $10K mark. As expected, it’s pretty much perfect right out of the box, and there are almost zero component changes I’d make out of the box. Hell, Santa Cruz even spec’d the AXS Rocker paddle shifter, so I don’t even have the AXS Pod ergonomics to complain about. The RockShox Ultimate level suspension and Reserve 30 SL wheels are top-notch and help contribute to the smooth and damp ride quality. The SRAM Motive 4-piston brakes paired with thicker HS2 rotors offered ample stopping power. My old wrists also appreciated the OneUp Carbon V2 handlebar. 

Other than the front tire spec, which is down to personal preference and easily changed, I only found one other thing to complain about, and that’s the OneUp V3 dropper. I’m a huge fan of OneUp’s affordable droppers, and I have been for years. Two of the three V3 droppers I’ve ridden this year have worked flawlessly. I couldn’t figure out what was going on with this one, but it made a subtle but pretty annoying knocking noise when descending over rough, chattery terrain. It was particularly notable given how silent the bike was otherwise. 

My Takeaway

Santa Cruz made the bold and somewhat divisive choice to ditch its VPP suspension design in favor of the simpler 4-bar layout, and I think the Tallboy is a better bike for it. In my opinion, it provides a more balanced, well-rounded suspension performance without detracting from its efficiency or muting its playful character. The bump in suspension travel and refined geometry are also welcome additions that enhance its composure and capability and position it more squarely as the true do-it-all trail bike it is. 

These days, there are lots of amazing mountain bikes on the market, and the Gen 6 Tallboy is one of the best I’ve ridden all year. Unless you’re riding aggressive enduro-style terrain all the time, this is a bike you can jump on for pretty much any ride and have a great time. Most importantly, it’s a heck of a lot of fun to ride, and that’s the whole point.

santacruzbicycles.com

entry.title: In the Drops: Clever Redshift pedal adapters, SunGod high-contrast glasses, handy Stubble & Co backpack and Cameron Winter
entry.content:
Cyclist
In the Drops: Clever Redshift pedal adapters, SunGod high-contrast glasses, handy Stubble & Co backpack and Cameron Winter

It’s the Blackest of Fridays and this year I am thankful for you, for reading this article focused around probably full price products (spoiler: there are deals here too) when half the internet is 30% off. You are the real MVPs.

If you are interested in deals, be sure to check out our Black Friday roundup though, which has been lovingly put together by the industry’s most prolific talent Paul Norman.

Elsewhere on the website this week, Paul has also updated our gravel bike tyres guide, and we’ve finished up our road bike mudguard reviews with this lovely buyer’s guide from Mildred Locke.

The latest episode of the Cyclist Magazine Podcast is available now too, featuring author Gareth Cartman talking about the 1926 Tour de France, the toughest of them all.

And finally, tech editor Sam Challis unleashed his latest Tech Talk newsletter onto cyclist.co.uk, and he thinks he’s found the one bike to do it all.

Let’s get in the drops, don’t forget your gloves it’s cold out.

Redshift Mousetrap pedal adapters

Sometimes you see a product and it’s an immediate ‘yes’, that was our reaction when Redshift revealed the Mousetrap SPD pedal adapters. We’ve finally got our hands on them a few months later, and yes keeps yessing.

These clever contraptions attach onto clipless pedals to make them grippy flat pedals – very handy if you use the same bike at the weekend and on your commute, for those who want system flexibility or for journalists who find themselves unexpectedly bringing a new bike home from work without the right shoes to hand.

They’re made from glass-reinforced nylon, attach and detach easily while staying secure when in use, and when not in use they’re lightweight and small enough to fit in a pocket and are conveniently magnetised to keep them together.

They can be used either two per pedal for a full flat setup or one per pedal for a hybrid system, and because they attach to the clipless pedal they should keep you at the right saddle height unless you’ve got platforms on.

After initially launching with the SPD model, Redshift has now launched SPD-SL and Look Keo versions. I’m particularly looking forward to getting a set on power meter pedals to prove how overrated clipless is.

  • Buy now from Redshift Sports (£37.49 – currently 25% off)

SunGod Vulcans Vent glasses with Plum lens

Tis the season for parking your sunglasses in their nice cloth bag and dusting off the clear and photochromic lenses. For the 2026 darkness, SunGod has launched two new lenses for low and changing light conditions: the 8KO Iris Gold photochromic lens and this, the 8KO Plum high-contrast fixed-tint lens.

Not only does it look fantastic, but the Plum lens helps to enhance contrast, making obstacles and hazards more visible in dull and dark conditions. They have a Fixed Category 2 Tint, meaning they let 31% of light through, and SunGod says they maintain the 100% UV protection needed to fully protect your eyes.

So far I’ve been using them on my commute, where their protection from the elements has been vital for my eyes and their high-contrast has helped me spot the immeasurable number of hazards riding through London.

  • Buy now from SunGod (£150)

Stubble & Co Hybrid backpack

I used to be happy with any old cheap backpack – surely spending money on a bag doesn’t make it that much better than the old reliable Amazon Basics? I was young and naive, I can only apologise. Great bags are great bags, and especially if you’re the kind of person to accumulate all sorts in a backpack that just gets lost in a disorganised system, a well thought-through design is one of the most underrated things you can invest in.

Stubble & Co’s Hybrid backpack is exactly that. It’s been designed to meet working, training and day-to-day needs with a split zone system that will make even the most disorganised among us feel like Marie Kondo.

Going back to front, features include: a padded sleeve for attaching to luggage; an Air-Flow back panel for breathability; adjustable chest straps; rear opening with padded laptop sleeve; main compartment – in this case 20 litres, which has a suitcase-like clamshell opening to make everything easy access; a smaller zip pocket inside the main compartment; compressions straps; an elasticated bottle pocket; a hidden front pocket; and TPU-coated water-resistant zips.

On top of that, it’s made with ergonomics in mind, with padded straps and all sorts of adjustability. It also has extra loops to attach extras such as lights or carabiners, has a handle both on top and on the side, and is made with durable waterproof materials and weather-proof bound seams.

Have that Bezos.

  • Buy now from Stubble & Co (£108 – currently 30% off)

What we’re into this week: Cameron Winter, ‘Live at Carnegie Hall’

I will keep breaking cups until my left hand looks wrong. Until my miracle drugs write the miracle song. I will keep rolling down until my best shirt rolls of. Until the conga line behind me is a thousand chickens long.

Imagine opening one of the great albums of the last few years with that and shortly after becoming one of the youngest artists ever to play a headline show at Carnegie Hall, which just so happens to be filmed by Oscar winner Paul Thomas Anderson.

It seems like every winter is a Cameron winter at this point, and in 2026 that means the release of his Live at Carnegie Hall album and the film of that show.

I loved the Heavy Metal studio album, and Winter’s live versions take the whole thing to another level. It is absolutely sublime and weird and very good. Highly recommend.

The post In the Drops: Clever Redshift pedal adapters, SunGod high-contrast glasses, handy Stubble & Co backpack and Cameron Winter appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Best aluminium bikes 2026 reviewed
entry.content:
Cyclist
Best aluminium bikes 2026 reviewed

The best aluminium bikes are better today than they’ve ever been, rivalling and in some cases beating similarly priced carbon bikes for overall performance and value.

Since carbon became the default material from which to make competitive road race and gravel racing bikes, steel has forged a second life for itself. However, if steel is vinyl – outmoded but charming – then aluminium has risked becoming an eight-track cassette tape – an unloved evolutionary stepping-stone doomed to the charity shop of history.

It wasn’t always so. For around a decade from the mid-90s to the early-2000s, aluminium was the material of choice, with Miguel Indurain being the first to win the Tour de France aboard an aluminium bike, a Pinarello, in 1995.

However, with Lance Armstrong ‘winning’ on a carbon Trek OCLV Madone only three years later, aluminium has often since found itself largely consigned to brands’ entry-level machines.

Don’t discount the metal option though. We’ve picked seven aluminium bikes that highlight the continuing appeal of aluminium.

Reviews of the best aluminium road bikes and gravel bikes

  1. Boardman SLR 8.8: RRP £875 – Read our full review
  2. Cannondale CAAD14 3: RRP: £2,500
  3. Canyon Endurace AllRoad: RRP £1,099
  4. Condor Italia RC Disc: RRP £1,299 (frameset) – Read our full review
  5. Specialized Allez: RRP £1,000 – Read our full review
  6. Specialized Allez Sprint: RRP £2,600 – Read our full review
  7. Sonder Camino AL gravel bike: RRP £1,818.99 – Read our full review

Should I buy an aluminium bike?

You certainly shouldn’t rule aluminium out, particularly if you’re spending less than £3,000 / $3,500.

Aluminium has been enjoying a revival, with new manufacturing methods once again making it a viable choice for race-winning bikes (or just plain fun ones). Aluminium bikes can be stiff, zippy and very light.

A note on nomenclature, by the way: aluminium is often referred to as ‘alloy’ which is strictly speaking quite vague, since all metal-framed bikes are made from alloys of one sort or another.

Are aluminium bikes harsh?

They can be, but they don’t have to be. The ultra-stiff aluminium race bikes of the nineties and 2000s gave the material a reputation for harsh ride quality, but how a bike rides depends on multiple factors including frame design, spec choices and tyre pressure.

The best aluminium frames build in some vertical flex for comfort, typically with skinny or dropped seatstays or flexible seatposts. The trend towards wider tyres has helped here too – many road bikes now come with 28mm tyres as standard and can accept wider ones still.

Aluminium can also handle the rough and tumble (we hope not too much of the latter) of gravel better than carbon too, tending to dent rather than break if it takes a hit.

How we test and why you should trust our advice

Our team of expert testers led by tech editor Sam Challis has an immense combined experience of riding everything from the very cheapest entry-level bikes, up to the latest and greatest flagship superbikes.

We’re riders just like you who love cycling for the joy, the excitement, and the physical challenge and we review bikes by putting in the miles in all weathers. We value bikes that are at once easy to live with and a pleasure to ride, and we admire brands that dare to be different or that offer a particularly compelling package for the money.

We will never recommend a bike we wouldn’t spend our own money on.

The best aluminium bikes reviewed

Boardman SLR 8.8

£875 | Buy here

  • Pros: Smoothly welded frame, tubeless ready wheels
  • Cons: External cables, some cheaper drivetrain components, relatively heavy

Boardman has long been a leader on value and the SLR 8.8 is a fantastic introduction to road cycling, with a nicely finished aluminium frame that looks remarkably carbon-esque.

Price well below a grand, there are some spec compromises in the form of cable disc brakes (as opposed to hydraulics) and a crankset that doesn’t match the Shimano Tiagra drivetrain, but nothing that stops this being a solid buy.

The SLR 8.8 is fun and engaging despite being at the heavier end of the road bike spectrum. The brakes may be basic but they offer plenty of confidence, while a generous range of gears will get you up most hills.

For a little more cash, the Shimano 105-equipped Boardman SLR 8.9 is also worth a look.

  • Read our full Boardman SLR 8.8 review

Cannondale CAAD14 3

£2,500 | Buy here

  • Pros: Looks good, lightweight, smooth riding
  • Cons: Pricey, aggressive ride position may not suit all riders

Cannondale was famous during the ’90s for its slinky-looking CAAD frames, which are still objects of lust for a particular breed of bike nerd. Having diverged from the older CAAD aesthetic with previous generations, the latest CAAD14 returns to a classic double diamond frame and oversized tubing.

It’s lovely-looking and lighter than many carbon competitors, while its chunky looking tubing should also provide a ride far smoother than you’d imagine possible. The CAAD14 1 halo bike is stunning and boasts a 7.9kg claimed weight.

Tyre clearance is now 32mm and the Delta steerer, ported over from the carbon SuperSix Evo offers full cable integration. There are just three specs on offer, with this Shimano 105 mechanical option the least expensive.

Canyon Endurace AllRoad

£1,099 | Buy here

  • Pros: Great spec for its price, 40mm tyre clearance
  • Cons: Single spec only

The Endurace is no longer just one bike, there are four Endurace platforms, with the Endurace AllRoad the sole alloy representative. It’s a brilliant value alloy road bike with 40mm tyre clearance and fitted with grippy 35mm tyres, so it can handle light off-road as well as on-road and commuting duties.

A carbon fork helps keep things smooth at the front, internal cables keep them neat, while mudguard and top tube bag mounts add versatility. Canyon fits a wide-range Shimano CUES 10-speed groupset, complete with hydraulic disc brakes, adding yet more versatility.

Condor Italia RC Disc

£1,399.99 (frame only) | Buy here

  • Pros: Great looks, spec built to order, now with disc brakes
  • Cons: Limited availability, racy geometry may not suit some riders

London cycling stalwart Condor produces its range in Italy. The race-oriented Italia RC is a legitimately fast bike with a moderate price tag, ideal for regular racing and fast training.

Featuring an asymmetric down tube with a flattened profile to resist twisting, it should be happy to get thrown about.

Having previous eschewed anything as crassly modern as disc brakes or bolt-thru axles, this latest version sports both. Thankfully the Italia is still gorgeous to look at in deep two-tone blue.

The Italia is sold frame-only, and Condor will help build the bike up to match your requirements. You can also call on the experience of its in-house fitters to get it spot on.

  • Read our Condor Italia RC review (rim brake version)

Specialized Allez Sport

£1,600 | Buy here

  • Pros: Disc brakes and wide tyre clearance
  • Cons: Significantly more expensive than its predecessor, wheels need upgrading

The Specialized Allez had a major update in 2023, its first since 2017. Gone are the rim brakes in favour of disc brakes, while tyre clearance has increased to 35mm, both putting the Allez in line with modern trends.

The base model Allez has a Shimano Claris 8-speed groupset and mechanical disc brakes, but you’ll need to pay almost 50% more for the higher spec Allez Sport, which we reviewed, and which has a 10-speed Shimano Tiagra groupset with hydraulic disc brakes.

It’s a durable bike with a weight just shy of 10kg. A good proportion of that heft is in the wheels and tyres though, which feel due for an upgrade to improve the Allez’s performance.

  • Read our full Specialized Allez review

Specialized Allez Sprint

£2,600 | Buy here

  • Pros: Aero alloy frame, stiff and responsive
  • Cons: Ride position is quite aggressive, expensive for alloy

The standard Allez is Specialized’s entry-level, do-it-all road bike while the Sprint is a hardcore racer created to showcase the brand’s aluminium construction technology, and provide a real alternative to carbon.

The Allez Sprint is very sculpted for an aluminium frame, employing SmartWeld technology to produce an aero-tested frame that’s effectively a metal version of the Specialized Tarmac.

In fact, many features are nicked from the Tarmac including the geometry, and while the Allez’s frame is a good bit heavier its 1.5kg weight is still respectable enough.

The Allez Sprint is a stiff and lively bike, and we found a lot to like when we reviewed it.

Sonder Camino AL

£1,818.99 | Buy here

  • Pros: Wide tyre clearance, stable over rough ground, great value, broad spec choices
  • Cons: Stock bars are a little too flared, sedate on tarmac

Sonder’s Camino AL has room for 50mm gravel tyres and, as standard, is fitted with 45mm rubber, which ensures plenty of grip off-road, as well as a degree of cushioning from uneven surfaces, so that you’re not likely to be slowed down by roots and rocks. The Camino’s geometry offers stability on slippery tracks and when descending, although this does lead to a sedate ride when you need to link in tarmac sections.

All specs are now 1x, with either a SRAM or Shimano groupset, including electronic shifting options. The low base price leaves plenty for room for the extensive range of upgrades available, including Sonder’s own carbon wheels, a dropper seatpost and even a RockShox suspension fork. Sonder’s build-to-order approach allows you to choose crank and stem lengths and a range of saddles too.

The only change we’d make to the reviewed spec is a swap to the less flared Hurricane bars, as the Bomber bars’ very angled drops leave you resting on the edge of the levers, rather than the tops, which are broader.

  • Read our full Sonder Camino AL gravel bike review

The post Best aluminium bikes 2026 reviewed appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Save up to 70% in Scott’s Black Friday sale
entry.content:
Cyclist
Save up to 70% in Scott’s Black Friday sale

Black Friday month 2026 is well underway, with more and more cycling brands introducing big discounts across bikes, tech and clothing.

That includes Scott, which has Black Friday deals on its framesets and clothing as well as Syncros components.

Here’s what’s on offer:

Scott Black Friday cycling deals 2026

  • Scott Addict RC Ultimate HMX SL frameset – Was £4,899, now £4,409.10, save 10%
  • Scott Scale Gravel RC frameset – Was £2,299, now £2,069.10, save 10%
  • Scott Shield Light Sensitive sunglasses – Was £110, now £77, save 30%
  • Syncros Capital 1.0s 40 wheels – Was £1,649.99, now £1,154.99, save 30%
  • Syncros Capital 1.0s 60 wheels – Was £1,729.99, now £1,210.99, save 30%
  • Scott RC Weather Ultralight WB women’s jacket – Was £130.99, now £65.50, save 50%
  • Scott RC Weather Ultralight WB gilet – Was £89.99, now £45, save 50% (men’s / women’s)
  • Scott Commuter WB jacket – Was £134.99, now £67.50, save 50% (men’s / women’s)
  • Scott Explorair Light Dryo 2.5 Layer jacket – Was £165, now £82.50, save 50% (men’s / women’s)
  • Syncros Nanaimo 1200 front light – Was £94.99, now £28.50, save 70%
  • Syncros Pannier bag – Was £129.99, now £90.99, save 30%

Scott Addict RC Ultimate HMX SL frameset

£4,409.10 | Buy here

Starting at the highest end of Scott’s range, a pair of framesets have 10% off for Black Friday. The first of those is this Addict RC Ultimate HMX SL, the super-lightweight road frame that’s part of its ground-breaking Addict RC Ultimate Bike, which is the brand’s lightest ever production race bike.

Made with an HMX SL carbon frame and fork with ultra-thin tube walls, the frame weighs just 640g and the fork just 275g, making climbing a walk in the park. The frameset also includes the Syncros SP-R100-SL Carbon seatpost.

Scott Scale Gravel RC frameset

£2,069.10 | Buy here

If it’s a gravel bike frame you’re after. Scott has also discounted the Scale Gravel RC frameset. The Scale is an adventure-focused design, usually specced with flat handlebars for easier navigation of extreme terrain, but that doesn’t mean it’s slow.

The frame and fork weigh a combined 1.69kg, which includes Scott’s Advanced Shock & Standing Damping System for soaking up impact – something it shares with the brand’s hardtail mountain bikes. And there are also plenty of mounting points for loading up bikepacking bags.

Scott Shield Light Sensitive sunglasses

£77 | Buy here

Moving on from frames the savings increase, with 30% off the Scott Shield Light Sensitive sunglasses. The racing-oriented design of the Shield glasses is paired with photochromic lenses to adapt to changing light conditions, whether that be riding into the night, in tunnels or in low-light.

The curved shape of the big lens alongside the frameless design offers a huge field of vision, and they only weigh around 32g.

Syncros Capital 1.0s wheels

40mm: £1,154.99 | Buy here / 60mm: £1,210.99 | Buy here

Scott’s components brand Syncros is part of its Black Friday sale too, with 30% off the Capital 1.0s in both 40mm and 60mm. They feature the same carbon rim as the Capital SL monocoque wheels, but swap the integrated carbon spokes for DT Swiss stainless steel Aerolite spokes and also use DT Swiss 240 hubs.

With a 25mm internal width on both front and rear, they’re compatible with tyres ranging from 29mm to 50mm, so can be used for either road or gravel riding. Scott says the 40mm deep wheels weigh 1,335g and the 60s weigh 1,470g.

Scott RC Weather Ultralight WB women’s jacket

£65.50 | Buy here

Scott has also knocked 50% off a range of jackets, ideal for riding outside over the colder and wetter months. The first is the women’s RC Weather Ultralight WB jacket, which, as the name suggests, is lightweight as well as packable, for rides where it’s always wise to have a spare layer.

It’s made with Pertex Quantum Air fabric to be windproof and breathable, and has been designed to best fit in riding position, so flapping is kept to a minimum – the silicone bottom hem grip helps with that too.

Scott RC Weather Ultralight WB gilet

£45 | Buy men’s here | Buy women’s here

The exact same fabric and design has been used for the Scott RC Weather Ultralight WB gilet, which is half price in both men’s and women’s versions.

It offers the same weather protection as the jacket including water-repellency, but keeps the arms free for when you don’t need full coverage.

Scott Commuter WB jacket

£67.50 | Buy men’s here | Buy women’s here

For commuters or those looking for a looser fit cycling jacket, there is also 50% off the Scott Commuter WB jacket, which is still wind-resistant and packable, but has a more casual fit, plus reflective details and more pockets.

It’s made with PFC-free DURObreeze, DUROxpand and DUROzone materials for weather protection, breathability and stretch, and both men’s and women’s models are on offer for just under £68.

Scott Explorair Light Dryo 2.5 Layer jacket

£82.50 | Buy men’s here | Buy women’s here

For more serious weather protection, the Scott Explorair Light Dryo 2.5 Layer jacket is half price too. Made for all sorts of outdoor adventures, it has a loose fit and a hood, a two-way front zip, and it all packs down into the pocket.

The real winner is its weather-proof qualities though. It uses PFAS-free DRYOsphere 1.5L and DRYOzone technologies to provide waterproofing to 20,000mm and breathability to 20,000g/m2, giving you protection from the wind and rain without compromising sweat levels.

Syncros Nanaimo 1200 front light

£28.50 | Buy here

The biggest discount in the whole of Scott’s Black Friday 2026 sale is on the Syncros Nanaimo 1200 front light at a whopping 70% off.

That means for just £28.50 you can get your hands on a 1,200 lumen front light, which has two LEDs and five modes, including a light-sensitive mode that can switch between the most efficient see and be-seen lights depending on the conditions. Running time is up to 16 hours in the most efficient settings, and it’s ideal for use with Scott’s integrated cockpits but there are also a range of other mounts available.

Syncros Pannier bag

£90.99 | Buy here

Finally, for the adventurers and commuters, there’s a 30% saving to be had on the Syncros pannier bag. It’s a fully waterproof rear pannier with a roll-top closure to keep your stuff clean and dry.

It has a 30-litre volume, weighs 700g, has a Racktime hook top fixation system for extra security and is compatible with 9mm, 11mm and 14mm rack tubes.

entry.title: UCI CX World Cup Debuts in Czechia with Ostrava’s Snow & Industrial Night Racing
entry.content:
UCI World Cup cross racing kicks off this weekend with a Czech double-header – beginning in Ostrava.

But this is a story more about the unique start the UCI Cyclo-Cross World Cup takes this season in Ostrava, CZ. Beacuse not only is this an all-new venue for the World Cup – itself pretty wild as it’s an old industrial site inside the city, but it’s also taking place at night… under a ton of flood lights. Oh, and a snowstorm dropped in yesterday, covering the racetrack in a blanket of snow, and creating near white-out conditions for the Junior Women & Men racing last night!

CX World Cup kicks off in Ostrava, CZ winter wasteland

Yeah, this is more a tale of iconic cyclocross vibes, rather than a new bike story, or even much about the first racing results of the opener. So, instead of my typical bike tech style of covering cross racing, I’m kicking it off with more of a gallery about racing in this old industrial Moravian wasteland, in the snow, and at night under the lights.

The first World Cup of the season is always a test of the mechanics and team logistics. It’s often the first real global challenge. Adding a bunch of snow, made that all the more complex. Lucky for the mechanics, the course hasn’t gotten too muddy – the Ostrava course has a lot of paved surfaces hiding under that snow.

So there weren’t a ton of bikes to constantly pressure wash. Instead, I spotted more action with mini electric air blasters blowing snow & sand out of bike drivetrains, making sure melt water didn’t freeze up on the bikes.

USA Cycling was just one of many digging through snow to keep their athletes going. And today ahead of the Elite races you were as likely to see mechanics shoveling snow-free places to work as you were to see them fixing bikes.

Junior Women’s & Junior Men’s first wins of the World Cup weekend

Officially, last night’s preview of Junior Women & Junior Men wasn’t the World Cup. Save that for the U23 & Elites racing tonight. But the racing was top-level, and the conditions were ideal for cross racers to show who was the strongest!

One the women’s front, young American racer and Pan-Am champ Lilliana O’Donnell took the first win in a dominant fashion as the snow started to pick up.

Then, you Czech rider Ondřej Bukovský did the same in the Junior Men’s field, riding out early and stayoing away in the heavy blowing snow.

CX World Cup in the old Vítkovice ironworks in Ostrava, Czechia

The backdrop of the Ostrava Cross World Cup is the old Vítkovice ironworks. So, while about 1/3 of the track looks like a classic Euro cyclocross course, winding up and down short, steep grassy hills and off-cambers, the rest is set in between a bunch of dark, decaying old industrial buildings.

But the ironworks is also a historically protected site, so it’s still quite a popular spot for visitors as well. There are a number of reinovated building turned into museums, restaurants, cafes, and hotels on-site. And there’s a big outdoor LED light art exhibit that the racers meander through, making the industrial wasteland somehow look like a festive winter wonderland under the falling snow!

It’s a pretty wild juxtaposition.

Back to the racing…

With a strange backdrop, the athletes are tackling something completely new to most. Then, throw a bunch of fresh snow and ever-changing ruts into the mix and it’s anyone’s guess how the Elite racing will turn out.

One thing is for sure – chaos.

A big sandy descent covered with snow, but not quite frozen should keep things interesting on Friday night.

As far as I can remember, I don’t think the Cyclo-Cross World Cup has ever had a night race. And a few Elite racers have noted that alone will shake up the bunch.

There’s still forecast to be a few flurries coming down for the Elite Women & Men, but at least they won’t have to deal with the heavy snow the Juniors saw.

That should make it a bit easier for fans to follow along at home. You know, being able to see the riders when the cameras zoom down the long straights.

When I popped out the zoom lens to follow the Junior Men’s leader late in the race, pretty much all I could see were snowflakes, backlit by the flood lights.

We’ll see if visibility is higher tonight!

UCICyclo-CrossWorldCup.com

entry.title: Best Black Friday cycling deals 2026
entry.content:
Cyclist
Best Black Friday cycling deals 2026

Now Black Friday is upon us, there’s a host of deals available on all things bike, so this is a great time to refresh your cycling inventory and replace items that have seen better days after another summer of riding. It’s also an opportunity to upgrade your setup so that you’re ready for a great year of cycling in 2027.

Finding the best Black Friday deals can be a chore, but here at Cyclist we’ve done the hard work for you, searching out the bargains that we’d choose ourselves in the pre-Christmas sales.

Read on for our pick of the 2026 Black Friday deals.

Giant Defy SL 1

Was £8,499, now £4,999 at Giant

Giant has a hefty discount on a range of its top-rated road bikes, so you can pick up the SRAM Force AXS-equipped Defy Advanced SL 1 with £3,500 off the standard price. The spec also includes Giant SLR 1 36mm carbon wheels with Cadex 32mm tyres.

If you want to get flashy, the pro-level TCR Advanced SL 0 with either Dura-Ace or Red AXS is priced down from £11,999 to £5,999 and there are also discounts on the last-generation Propel Advanced SL 0 aero bike. When tech editor Sam Challis reviewed the Defy, he gave it it an Editor’s Choice award, concluding it was “perhaps not the bike you want, but almost certainly the bike you need”, helping you to make up your mind.

Le Col Pro Jersey

Was £145, now £75 at Le Col

Le Col has its entire range discounted for Black Friday, so you can pick up the Pro jersey for just £75. It’s available in a full range of sizes in two of the four colours. The Pro Bib Shorts are even more of a bargain, with all sizes available in three colour combinations and all priced down to £130 from £220.

When we reviewed the Pro kit, we reckoned it was comfortable, with a straightforward design. It’s less pro than most pro kit, so it’s better suited to amateurs riding on UK summer days than WorldTour racers cresting the Ventoux in July.

Zefal Sense waterbottle

Was £11, now £5.99 at Cyclestore

If your water bottles are a little tired, having been slurped from through the summer heatwave, now might be time for a bottle refresh. Cyclestore has a range of bottles discounted for Black Friday, including the ever-popular Elite Fly Tex and Camelbak Podium, both in a range of sizes.

We’d opt for Zefal’s Sense bottle though, not just because it has a larger discount, but because it’s available with a No Mud cap (as are Elite’s bottles), so you can avoid drinking road grot from damp, muddy roads this winter.

Scicon Aerocomfort 3.0 travel bag

Was £999, now £459.54 at Scicon (bike not included)

Get ready to fly/drive/train to the spring training camp with a 50%-plus discount on Scicon’s Aerocomfort 3.0 soft case bike bag. Its internal stand holds your bike in place, without needing to take a wrench to your bars and seatpost, so you’ll get riding much more quickly when you arrive. There’s plenty of padding to baggage handler-proof your Pinarello (other bike brands are available) and it’s easy to wheel around thanks to quality rollers.

Scicon has Black Friday price drops on its gravel and tri bike bags too, as well as its Pog-alike sunnies. There are two-for-one offers on some styles and an extra 10% off at checkout and free shipping on orders over £190.

SunGod sunglasses

Buy one, get one free

SunGod has a buy one, get one free offer across a wide range of its sunglasses for Black Friday, including popular cycling styles such as the frameless Airas and half-frame Vulcans and Velans 2. We’ve been impressed by SunGod’s lens quality and low weight when we’ve reviewed the brand’s sunnies, plus there are loads of customisation options and lens tints, including its Iris photochromics and team edition choices.

Browse SunGod’s Black Friday page for more options, including styles for running and ski goggles, as well as its cycling glasses.

Zwift Ride with Kickr Core 2

Was £1,099.99, now £899 at Zwift

Zwift has over £200 off the price of the Zwift Ride smart frame with a Kickr Core 2 turbo, offering a turnkey entry into the world of indoor cycling, with a free 14-day trial of its Zwift Plus premium tier included.

There’s a discount too on the Wahoo Kickr Core 2, which is priced down to £399.99 from £499.99, while the Zwift Cog and Click upgrade kit, allowing you to install virtual shifting on your trainer has a huge markdown. It’s usually £49.99, but you can pick it up for just £12.50, with all Zwift Black Friday offers ending at midnight on Monday 30 November.

Wahoo Elemnt Roam 3

Was £399.99, now £349.99 at Wahoo

Wahoo has a Black Friday discount on its cycling computers, including the Roam, its mid-format touchscreen device. Wahoo has updated its internals, added connectivity to a range of biosensors and switched from button-only to a touchscreen interface, so it’s a full-featured GPS that won’t swamp your handlebars.

You can also buy the Elemnt Ace, which includes Wahoo’s innovative wind speed sensor, for just £10 more or scale down to the Elemnt Bolt 3, saving £100. There are sale prices for Black Friday across a range of Wahoo’s other hardware, including £132.50 off the Kickr Climb gradient simulator and the Kickr Bike Pro, with £700 off.

Hunt 44_46 Aerodynamicist wheelset

Was £899, now £539.40 at Hunt Wheels

The Aerodynamicist range is Hunt’s mid-priced wheelset and available in a range of depths, all with 25% off this Black Friday, with Hunt applying an extra 10% on top of its already discounted prices for Black Friday.

The Hunt 44_46 Aerodynamicist is the middle depth option and carries over tech from the pricier Limitless wheelsets. With hooked beads, there’s wide tyre compatibility, while Hunt points out that the 22mm internal width allows owners to fit tyres from 25mm up. At under 1,350g for the steel spoked wheels, it helps keep the weight down too.

Cyclist staff writer Laurence Kilpatrick was impressed by the carbon spoked version of the wheels when he reviewed them earlier this year, rating them great value.

We have a whole range of Hunt deals on our dedicated Hunt Black Friday sale page. Hunt says that its most popular deals are already selling out though, so if you have your eye on a wheel upgrade, you might want to act fast.

Scott Shield Light Sensitive Sunglasses

Were £110, now £77 at Scott Sports

Scott’s Black Friday deals include these large lens Shield photochromic sunglasses, available either with a black or white frame. They feature Scott’s gold chrome mirrored lens, which darkens from Cat 1 to Cat 3, so they’ll handle the typical range of light conditions across different seasons. Single tint Shields are discounted as well.

There’s a whole range of other discounts in Scott’s Black Friday sale, from clothing to Syncros Capital wheels. With the brand’s broad range of sports, there are discounts on trail running and ski kit too.

Specialized S-Works Aethos 2

Was £11,499, now £8,999 at Sigma Sports

Sigma Sports has discounts on a wide range of road and gravel bikes including the Cervelo S5 and this top spec S-Works Aethos 2 in a range of sizes. Lower Aethos 2 specs are discounted too, although in a more limited range of sizes.

Laurence Kilpatrick rated the S-Works Aethos 2 when he reviewed the bike, not least its 6kg weight in size 56.

Sigma Sports has Black Friday deals on a wide range of clothing, components and accessories too, so chances are that if you’re looking for something specific, Sigma will be offering a Black Friday discount.

Ribble Ultra-Grit Force XPLR AXS

Was £4,449, now £3,999 at Ribble Cycles

Ribble’s Black Friday deals change each week, so if you’re looking for a new gravel race bike, now’s your chance. The Ultra-Grit is ridden by the Ribble Outliers pro race team and features aero tube profiles, a one-piece cockpit and in-frame storage. In this spec, it’s kitted out with SRAM’s 13-speed Force XPLR AXS groupset and Vision SC45 wheels. The frame is suspension fork-compatible and you can upgrade to a RockShox Rudy Ultimate XPLR fork, as well as Zipp 303 XPLR SW wheels in Ribble’s bike builder.

Ribble’s Black Friday deals extend to a wide range of its other road and gravel bikes too. It’s now added its titanium models including the Allroad Ti and Ribble guarantees that, should the price drop later in the Black Friday sale, it will refund the difference.

Garmin Rally XC200 SPD dual-sided power meter

Was £959.99, now £599.99 at Tredz

The Garmin Rally power meter pedals are discounted at Tredz, offering you dual-sided power measurement for Shimano SPD gravel cleats for not much more than the list price of the single sided power meter. They have swappable bodies, so you can change to an SPD-SL or Look Keo power meter for the price of the upgrade kit.

Tredz has over 1,000 products discounted for Black Friday, including Garmin smartwatches and cycling computers and Garmin Tacx smart trainers, so it’s a great place to browse for your replacements and upgrades.

Castelli Sorpasso Pro Bibtights

Were £220, now £176 at Castelli

Not technically a Black Friday sale, as it finishes on 16th November, but Castelli has discounts on its cold weather essentials, so you can gear up with its jackets, base layers, socks and other cold weather gear for both men and women riders.

The Sorpasso Pro bib tights are Castelli’s top spec winter legwear, with its Progetto X2 Air seat pad, zipperless ankles and lay-flat bibs, as well as the reflectives to keep you safer on your winter rides.

Tacx Neo 2T smart trainer

Was £860, now £689 at Balfe’s Bikes

Tacx’s high tech Neo 2T trainer is discounted at Balfe’s Bikes for Black Friday and is available with either a conventional 11-speed cassette or Zwift Cog and Click for the same price. With 2200 watts resistance, it’s plenty powerful enough, it folds away neatly and can mimic a 25% incline. It’s quiet too, that is unless you want to simulate riding cobbles in preparation for an early season Belgian sportive.

It’s one of a wide range of cycling equipment and bikes discounted in Balfe’s Bikes’ Black Friday sale, including turbo trainers and indoor bikes from Elite, Wahoo and Wattbike.

Muc-Off Pressure Washer Starter Kit

Was £120, now £84.99 at Decathlon

If washing down your bike after a winter ride feels a chore, Muc-Off’s pressure washer can speed things up. It comes with a range of lances, including one that allows you to attach a bottle of Muc-Off’s bike cleaner and spray your bike with grime-busting foam, making bike cleaning much more fun.

Decathlon has a tasty discount on the Muc-Off Pressure Washer Starter Kit, which comes with all the lances you could need and is housed in a Muc-Off branded dry bag, making it easy to carry around. There’s a range of other cycling equipment and bikes in Decathlon’s Black Friday sale too.

The post Best Black Friday cycling deals 2026 appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Pas Normal Studios Introduces T.K.O. AW26: Everything In Its Right Place
entry.content:
As the days grow shorter and temperatures fall, the memory of summer takes on a different significance. The warmth of the sun, the colours of the landscape and the feeling of riding on those sunlit days become something to hold onto. For Autumn/Winter 2026, Pas Normal Studios translates these impressions into its latest T.K.O. collection.

T.K.O. is the brand’s signature outlet for artistic expression, offering a more experimental approach to cycling apparel under the creative direction of co-founder Karl-Oskar Olsen. For AW26, a dark red backdrop sets the tone, with graphics recalling the warmth of summer and bringing a sense of nostalgia into the colder riding season.

The collection brings this creative vision to both lightweight and cold-weather cycling apparel, built around the Essential Light and newly introduced Mechanism Thermal programmes. A selection of accessories completes the release, carrying the same visual identity throughout.

Product Highlights

T.K.O. Mechanism Thermal Long Sleeve Jersey 2.0

Designed for high-intensity riding in cold and wet conditions, the jersey combines Polartec® Power Shield Pro Knit for wind and water resistance with Polartec® Power Grid for enhanced breathability and moisture management. Its hybrid construction delivers weather protection and aerodynamic performance, with a 20,000mm water column rating and 20,000 g/m²/24h breathability.

T.K.O. Mechanism Thermal Long Bibs

Crafted in Italy from high-stretch, fleeced fabric, the bibs provide insulation and freedom of movement for cold-weather riding. A C0 DWR treatment offers protection against light rain and road spray, while ergonomically shaped legs, fleeced shoulder straps and silicone grid grippers ensure a secure, comfortable fit over long distances.

T.K.O. Essential Light Jersey

Defined by a balance of structure and expression, the T.K.O. Essential Light Jersey brings a distinct graphic approach to everyday riding. Lightweight materials support breathability and comfort across changing conditions. Cut in an updated Essential fit with a slightly closer silhouette, the jersey is designed for layering and extended use.

T.K.O. Essential Light Cargo Bibs

The T.K.O. Essential Light Cargo Bibs are a lightweight summer bib built for long days in warm conditions. Constructed in a breathable stretch-woven fabric with the signature Essential Light structure, they balance durability and comfort. Laser-cut hems and the signature strap material ensure a secure fit, while a cargo pocket on the right leg provides practical storage without
disrupting the clean silhouette.

Availability

The T.K.O. AW26 collection will be available from 27 November at Pas Normal Studios stores, selected retailers and online.

entry.title: Every Black Friday Sports Tech Deal – The Big List!
entry.content:
It’s that time of year again. Most brands have already put out their best deals of the year!

Virtually everything is now announced, and really the only wildcard here is if Uncle Amazon decides to randomly discount something for a few hours without authorization from the company (great for us consumers!). That tends to happen for slightly older things, but sometimes even newer things. Either way, if you see a deal you like, grab it now in case it disappears. You can always return/swap/whatever later (all the way till January in Amazon’s case).

As always, I’m constantly updating these deals hourly over the Black Friday weekend. Note: If you want a more simplified view of just the Garmin deals, there’s this page that filters that (still giant) list down a bit.

Update – Friday, Nov 27th Mid-Day: Here are the most popular deals (in terms of what you’ve bought thus far). Here’s the Top 10 ranking:

  1. 1. Garmin Fenix 9 for $100 off (and $150 for 43mm!): Technically, you’re buying slightly more Fenix 9 Pro units than Fenix 9 base units, but either way, with the new sale started a few days ago, that easily took the lead on what y’all are buying the most. And I’d agree, given it’s brand and the best sports watch on the market, $100 makes it an easier choice (bringing the base down to $899, and the Pro at $999). The 43mm base Fenix 9 is down to $849 ($150 off!)
  2. 2. DJI NEO 1 drone for $139: No surprise here, and this has moved into the 2nd place spot. This is a fantastic deal if you want a simple follow-me drone that’s virtually impossible to kill no matter the number of crashes. Trust me, I’ve tried. It’s perfect for sports, or kids.
  3. 3. Garmin Fenix 8 at $749: With flashlight, ECG, diving features, and then virtually all the new software features coming from the Fenix 9, it’s pretty much impossible to beat this. It was in the #1 spot above, before the new Fenix 9 sale started.
  4. 4. Garmin Varia RearView 820 at $249: This is $50 off, and I didn’t exactly think it’d make the Top 5 list, but here we are. It’s a solid new unit, and easily the best/most accurate radar on the market, especially with some of the firmware/Edge tweaks since release making it a bit less noisy.
  5. 5. Garmin Fenix 8 Pro at $849: This is $150 off the regular price, and also $150 cheaper than the base Fenix 9 unit, but with the ‘Pro’ name here, you get LTE & Satellite messaging. Plus virtually all those new Fenix 9 software features. It’s a good compromise between Fenix 8 and Fenix 9.
  6. 6. Wahoo KICKR CORE 2 at $399: This is a fantastic deal for a smart trainer, and I’d strongly recommend this if you’re in the market for one. It doesn’t really get any better than this price-wise. Note: Amazon has gone out of stock here, but REI still has it!
  7. 7. Amazfit Active Max for $119: At that price, it’s such a bargain. It’s got offline maps, a big beautiful display, a million sport modes and more. Sure, it doesn’t have the polish of Garmin or other brands…but it’s a great place to start.
  8. 8. Garmin Varia RTL-515 Radar for $149: This thing’s been around the block a lot, but it’s also the 2nd best radar on the market after the 820 up above. And it’s $100 cheaper. It still beats every other 3rd party radar on the market.
  9. 9. Apple Airpod Pro 3 at $149: These are my go-to headphones for both sport and non-sport usage. This is the lowest price they’ve ever been, and the optical HR in these units is really darn good (as is the audio). These are also my wife’s go-to headphones as well.
  10. 10. Apple AirTags 4-Pack for $79 (2nd Gen): I can’t even begin to count how many AirTags I have these days. Every bag that I travel with for sure, plus most city/etc bikes, sometimes a kid.

Personally, I think the Wahoo BOLT 3 ($227), Wahoo ROAM 3, and KICKR CORE 2 deals are also incredibly strong, but…above are what people are buying the last few days. I’ll update this as the sales progress.
