entry.title: Three Weeks in Japan: On Travel and the In Between – John Watson
entry.content:
Photos don’t magically appear, and text doesn’t write itself. Not over here at The Radavist, at least. In the era of AI content slop, we pride ourselves on doing things the human way. This includes late nights, sore bodies, and in-depth, world-famous Reportage. During our whirlwind trip in Japan with Sim Works, we managed to stay sane through camaraderie and by absorbing the wonderful culture of the regions we traveled through. Read on for a short but sweet homage to travel and the in-between time that makes these trips so fulfilling, written and documented by John, with fun BTS by Sim Works brand director Masashi Kimura…

Photo Masashi Kimura

Settling into the end-of-year recaps over here at The Radavist, and still coming off a post-travel high from our time in Japan, I couldn’t help but write a reflective post from our three weeks on the road in the land of the rising sun.

I’ve been thinking a lot about the differences between tourism and travel. As someone who has been to Japan a number of times over the past twenty years, I’m very conscious about being a gaijin, or outsider. During our time in Osaka for Bespoked, Cari and I couldn’t help but notice how clueless so many English-speaking foreigners were. Talking loudly on cellphones on the subway, being drunk in public in the middle of the day, ignoring respectful customs at temples, and being disruptive in restaurants. It felt jarring at times.

Photos Masashi Kimura

Tourism like that feels extractive. Travel, however, where you learn customs ahead of time and adapt your behavior to attempt assimilation, can be a wholly immersive experience. A tourist is egocentric, framing their view through self-interest, resulting in placelessness. They attempt to assimilate their surroundings to themselves. Meanwhile, a traveler hopes to gain a deeper understanding of a culture through respectful observation, deepening their understanding of place.

Cari, working early one morning: photo by John; John and Paul working late photo Masashi Kimura

This is why I absolutely adore what we do over here at The Radavist. Traveling to various factories, riding in bike events, and visiting bike shops give you a truly insider’s perspective on a country or locale and its traditions. Sure, my Japanese could always be better, and at 6’2″, I was constantly bumping my head. My physical stature was out of place in a country like Japan, but I tried my hardest to respect the culture as we visited various historical sites, and I will be forever grateful for this trip.

A brief architectural aside: After Bespoked, Cari and I spent a day visiting Tadao Ando’s Nakanoshima Children’s Book Forest, a children’s library perched on the Tosahori River. In an era where books are banned, it felt ceremonial to visit a space by one of the world’s most accomplished architects that celebrated them. Ando gave back to his home city of Osaka by investing in future generations with this project. A 45º circulation ramp intersects the space, bringing you close to books you can touch and away from those meant for display only. The scale was smaller, more intimate, and details were designed for children. 

Road trips with acquaintances often forge lifelong friendships. For over a week, Masashi Kimura drove Cari, Paul from Slow Spin Society, and me around in his wagon, through confusing traffic patterns in Tokyo and navigating streets so tight they required a spotter to squeeze through. On the road, plentiful highway-side konbini stops were made for snacks including onigiri, salty corn chips, Shigekix sour snacks, and the most intense sparkling water I’ve ever had. Each evening for dinner, we sampled local delicacies ranging from world-famous udon to sashimi, tempura, and more.

We all fell into a rhythm that matched our busy itinerary. Every morning began at 6:00 with a loud alarm, meeting at 7:30 in the lobby of whatever cheap hotel we could find, on site at 8 AM. Our shoots were long, with the iPhone Notepad and Google Translate always at the front of our app folder. Each night, returning to our new home for the night, photos were dumped, edited, and cataloged. Backed up on Dropbox and notes culled. I jotted down how I was feeling in that moment, or takeaways and “aha” moments, in hopes of returning to the mindset once we returned home in the States. Rinse. Repeat.

We had a single day of respite in the coastal city of Zushi, where we stopped for coffee multiple times (returning to the same shop), meandered streets off the beaten path, visited temples built by the Samurai, and rubbed the Buddha statue to cure our aching backs. Cari swam, a soothing refresh for a Cancerian living in a dry and arid place who longs for water.

Come the end of our time together with Masashi and Paul, Cari and I couldn’t help but feel like we’d made friends for life. Separated by a 14-hour flight, our newfound family would be reunited at trade shows, and connections maintained through video calls. As important as our newly formed friendship is, there was an even deeper reverence for the Japanese cycling industry. From the factory workers to the bike shop employees at Circles and Blue Lug, and the landscapes we traversed and the kilometers we covered by bicycle.

Blue Lug Kamiuma, photo Masashi Kimura

Being a traveler through this wonderful country is something I’ll never take for granted. These memories will always live on the website, but more importantly, they’re stored in my heart.

To everyone we met along the way on this trip, to MKS, Nitto, and Honjo, arigato gozaimasu, and to the Sim Works fam, thank you so much for the trip of a lifetime.

Follow along in the captions for more!

The post Three Weeks in Japan: On Travel and the In Between appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Roll Models: Bristol-Based Bikepacking Mentorship for WTNB Riders – Hailey Moore
entry.content:
“In an ideal world, Roll Models would be redundant, we wouldn’t need to create these safe spaces,” says founder Athlyn Cathcart as the Bristol-based bikepacking mentorship group approaches its third year providing community and skills-learning to women, trans, and non-binary identifying cyclists.

For many, commuting serves as the gateway drug into the sport of cycling. It is not uncommon for the workingman’s discipline to awaken in new riders a desire for more, an itch to go further. That oft-cited sense of freedom that even the utilitarian practice of pedaling to and fro—between work, school, and home—gives a sweet taste of is enough to draw novices down a lifelong rabbit hole. This was indeed the case for Athlyn Cathcart, who credits her time commuting during her university years as the portal through which she discovered a much wider world of cycling. A world that she is now actively inviting others to join.

Photo credit: Aphra Evans (left), Abbie Merritt (right)

“I discovered the bike as a way to avoid being underground,” Cathcart said on a recent Zoom call, referring to London’s sprawling Tube system. Born in Toronto, Cathcart spent most of her childhood in the Midlands of England before moving to study Sociology and Politics at Goldsmiths, University of London. You can trace the long-tailed ripple effects of her community-focused studies to the off-the-clock work that she does today with Roll Models, a bikepacking and adventure-riding mentorship organization for WTNB riders.

Cathcart founded the Roll Models bikepacking mentorship in 2024, in Bristol where she now lives, after she’d amassed more than a dozen years of riding experience. The seed planted by her time commuting germinated in chasing bigger, more adventurous rides, and becoming a seasoned bikepacker. Still, it took her a long time to warm up to the notion of solo touring. At some point, Cathcart said she realized, “I’ve been doing this for ten years, but I’ve never solo camped.” Maybe, in a proverbial sense, she was still figuring out how to avoid being underground, how to come up for air. How to be seen, or how to see herself in an industry where she is among the underrepresented. The roots were there, but she realized that cultivating a stronger sense of independence, and maybe sticking her neck out a bit, would allow her to truly flourish.

Photo credit: @Twoevstops

This kind of reticence is exactly what Roll Models aims to help its members overcome. On her hesitation about traveling as a solo woman, Cathcart said that this is broadly a “systemic issue, not a cycling issue,” and that “not seeing yourself reflected in [social] media or whatever it is” can inhibit one’s sense of agency, especially in the vulnerable context of bikepacking.

Once she finally rallied her resolve for a solo tour, Cathcart said she was surprised by the paradox she experienced. The fear that had been curbing her own ambitions gave way to an unmatched sense of escape.

“The way I feel when I’m on a solo trip, I get a sense of freedom that I don’t feel in many other aspects of life,” said Cathcart. “Completely care-free, completely at my own pace and rhythm.”

Photo credit: Abbie Merritt (left); @Twoevstops (right)

This is the feeling that Cathcart wants to impart to members of Roll Models. As a Community Interest Company (a business entity specific to the UK for social enterprises with profits reinvested back in for community benefit), Roll Models operates on the calendar’s cycle, opening its application window in late winter to prospective members interested in participating in its two annual community campouts, workshops, group rides, and other meet-ups that take place throughout the remainder of the year. Roll Models offers a sliding pay scale to members to cover the cost of insurance, reservations, food and other expenses associated with its events.

In its first season, in 2025, Roll Models received 70 applicants for its—at the time—1:1 mentorship cohort. Of those, they accepted 34. This year, they shifted the model from a 1:1 mentor-mentee ratio to a breakdown that favors collective encouragement over a more direct teacher-student dynamic. For every three members, there are two mentors. This lessens the burden on mentors and allows more applicants to participate. Of this year’s 100 applicants, Roll Models had room for 55. Cathcart also says that by placing less emphasis on an experience hierarchy, she hopes to show members that “everyone has something to learn, everyone has something to share.”

Photo credit: Abbie Merritt

Experience among members does span a wide range. Some have never bike camped before, and newcomers often ask what bike and kit they need. Cathcart likes to use her own first “bikepacking” bike—a Bianchi singlespeed road bike—as an example that you don’t need to go out and buy new gear; “I just walked the hills,” she says. For members who have more experience, Cathcart says that she often sees parallels between their confidence levels and those of her earlier self, citing how a member might say that even though they have “cycled across Cuba or Mongolia with my male partner, I don’t think I know enough to be a mentor.”

To accommodate such a broad swath of knowledge levels and abilities, Roll Models sorts members into small groups at the beginning of the year to talk about their past experience and future ambitions. During the organization’s two annual campouts, members can self-select into different pace groups to facilitate an experience that feels accessible and enjoyable to all. The first 2026 campout took place in June and included a 50-kilometer ride from Bristol, following flat bike paths and paved roads (with public transit as an alternate option for part of the route). Once at camp, the group set up tents before an evening of on-bike egg-and-spoon races (a Roll Models staple activity) while Cathcart cooked for everyone.

Photo credit: Aphra Evans (left); Cat Giovanetti (right)

In September, the group spent a weekend in South Wales, setting up shop at a basecamp destination and offering different day-ride options for folks to choose from. Post-ride activities included crafts (tie-dyeing and lino-cut stamp-making), sauna sessions, egg-and-spoon races (of course), and group dinners around a fire.

Photo credit: Aphra Evans

As proof of the demand that Roll Models is feeling from its members, this will be the first year the organization doesn’t take an off-season. Although their campouts are paused until next summer—with applications for 2027 opening in February or March—Cathcart says that they have a calendar of workshops on topics such as safety, bike maintenance, and making your own gear planned to keep the group together through the colder months.

Photo credit: Abbie Merritt

When members for the new year’s cohort are chosen, Cathcart says she often gets asked: “Where do I start with bikepacking?” To which she says, “That has so many different answers… there is no right way of doing this.” Instead of giving a prescriptive response, she prefers to meet question with question, challenging new members to foreground their own goals and emboldening them to consider the unceilinged possibilities: “What do you want to get out of this?”

The post Roll Models: Bristol-Based Bikepacking Mentorship for WTNB Riders appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Best Action Cam & Drones (2026 Recommendations Guide)
entry.content:
I use action cams and drones virtually every single day, and I’ve used virtually every mainstream consumer action camera and drone on the market today. Though, in reality, we’ve basically just got three main action camera companies: GoPro, DJI, and Insta360. And in many ways, they make relatively similar cameras. In fact, some of them are using the exact same image sensors and processors in certain models. That said, as you’ll see, it’s far more than just an image sensor that makes a good action camera. The app is just as important, especially for 360 cameras.

Meanwhile, on the drone front, we’ve got two and a half consumer drone companies. There’s DJI, of course, the giant that makes drones in almost every category. Then there’s HoverAir, which makes a ton of small follow-me drones. Beyond that, we’ve got a slate of pretend DJI shell companies trying to do business in the US, but mostly getting whack-a-mole banned on a weekly basis. Things like SkyRover, Specta, and Xtra. We’ll ignore these copycats for our purposes here. After all, nobody buys those outside the US because you might as well just buy the real thing (the DJI-branded one).

Then there’s the ‘half a drone’ company I mentioned, which is Insta360’s Antigravity spin-off. Currently, they have just one model, which is showing promise. But at its current price point, it’s pretty tough to recommend, given the competition. That said, I’m super excited to see where the company goes, and I think they could really stick the landing on a second model at some point (no pun intended).

With that, a quick note about my recommendations:

1) None of these are sponsored: I’ve bought all of these drones/action cameras myself. Yes, I spend too much on drones and action cameras. Inversely, the drone and action cam market is absolutely smothered with sponsored garbage/videos, almost everything, in fact.

2) My recommendations are based on real-world usage: And more importantly, not trying to sell you any specific model. I don’t really care what you buy, as long as you’re happy with it. Ultimately, these are also largely what I use daily as well, despite having every single model of every drone and action cam available to me.

3) DJI is challenging for US buyers: There’s no two ways about it. DJI got double-whacked over the past 18 months. First, there’s the FCC ban impacting *all wireless devices* that DJI wants to certify, which includes action cameras, drones, e-bikes, and anything else they make that has a Bluetooth or WiFi chipset in it (which is everything). Then, on top of that, there’s the overall no-foreign-drone ban that occurred last December 2025. Collectively, those two things mean that buying new DJI products in the US made after those certification/import bans doesn’t come with any support, and is basically bought in the grey market of random imported companies. Note that the drone portion of the ban affects all non-US companies going forward, not just DJI.

So let’s get right into it!

Action Cam Recommendations:

When it comes to action cams, I’d argue there are essentially just two main categories: full-featured, slightly bigger ones, and then tiny little action cams that sacrifice some features for the ability to stick it somewhere really small. That said, one thing to keep in mind is that the size difference between these two categories is actually really small if you’re using it within the case. Meaning, the size of an Insta360 Ultra Go in the case is basically the same as the main cameras. Except none of the small camera cases from DJI or Insta360 are waterproof (meaning you can’t take the larger case portion in the water, only the pod).

The reason I mention that first is that if you’re trying to decide between the two sizes, I’d almost always go with the large size one, as it’s fully waterproof (and thus really hard to kill accidentally), and the features-to-price ratio tends to be better. As does the quality. In all cases, the larger cameras have notably better quality/resolutions/frame rates.

Main Action Camera – GoPro Mission 1 Pro:

This is a beast of an action camera, easily the best on the market today. There’s not really any objective way you could say otherwise. It beats every other camera on specs, image quality, run times in most categories, and just about every other thing out there. Of course, that unfortunately extends to price too – it’s the most expensive action camera in the market today. Still, it’s pretty rock-solid, produces incredible shots, and syncs cleanly into the GoPro Cloud where I back up all my action camera footage. Insta360 has a similar cloud offering, though GoPro’s is unlimited GoPro footage at full/native resolution, while Insta360’s is capped at 2 TB, and you pay nearly double. You can blow through storage pretty quickly when shooting in 8K at high bitrates, which the GoPro Mission 1 Pro does. Ultimately, I’ve now bought a small fleet of Mission 1 Pro cameras that I use for most of my larger action cam needs.

My Backup Camera – Insta360 Ace Pro 2:

Prior to the GoPro Mission 1 Pro, I basically flipped a coin on whether I was taking the GoPro Hero 13 Black or the Insta360 Ace Pro 2. Both gave good performance, though the Insta360 Ace Pro 2 beat the Hero 13 for low light/night footage, while the GoPro beat it for daytime footage. Insta360’s benefit, though, was that it had/has better integration with the sports devices I use from Garmin, Apple, COROS, and more. Those metrics sync right into the Insta360 app, and I can instantly overlay them right onto the videos I make, showing stats like speed, distance, pace, power, and so on. DJI also has a similar feature, but I find Insta360’s a bit more flexible. The other reason I tend to prefer the GoPros is the dual-front/back screen, whereas the Ace Pro 2 has a back flip-up screen. That’s super cool for vlogging, but a little less practical for flipping up during quick selfie-style shots while holding a camera on a bike or other sport thing at high speed. Still, the Ace Pro 2 is a strong buy at the right price.

Honorable Mention – GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS:

This is a quirky one to me, not because it’s not good – as it’s really good. But it’s also just not something that most people looking for an action cam on a regular basis would want. The Mission 1 Pro ILS has an interchangeable lens system, like a mirrorless/DSLR. That’s awesome, and crazy unique. You can put any micro-4/3rds lens on it that you want. The only catch? No autofocus.

Now, for people who want to put tiny cameras in small places (like mounted in cars and such) that run for many hours without issue and have all the power of the new Mission 1 Pro series, this is a massive deal. But if you’re not used to manual focus, let alone manual focus on an action camera with a tiny screen…these can be hard to handle. I’ve got some amazing shots from this camera (and seen people do even crazier things), but equally, it’s definitely not going to be your primary action camera. This is a camera for someone who already has a fleet of them and wants some super creative angles/shots. It’s awesome for that.

ProductBuy
On Sale!GoPro Mission 1 Pro
Amazon $599
On Sale!Insta360 Ace Pro 2
Amazon $309

The Mini Action Cams:

I’ve done a stupid amount of testing of these three action cameras above, though I only managed to get the Insta360 Go Ultra reviews across the line. Sigh. If only my hard drives full of terabytes of footage could edit themselves. Still, I tend to use these cameras sparingly, since both the DJI & Insta360 tiny cams aren’t fully waterproof. Only the small pod portion is waterproof, not the full-sized case. And because the small removable pod is…well…small, it means you’re almost certainly going to attach it to a larger stick when in the water (so you don’t lose it). And once you do that, you kinda defeat the purpose of a small action camera.

Instead, the core/main scenario I use tiny action cameras for is actually clipping it to the magnetic necklace pendant, through my cycling jersey. So it looks like the camera is just hovering there on my chest. I usually do this when I don’t want to deal with a full chest mount/strap setup for the bigger cameras. This works well if you get the angle right, but admittedly a chunk of the time, if down in the drops (lower portion of handlebars), then this mount ends up mostly just filming the ground.

In any case, when it comes to these two, they’re honestly kinda a wash. There are very few differences between them. DJI includes internal storage, whereas Insta360 doesn’t (both take/allow MicroSD cards). Insta360 ties into their Insta360 cloud storage, whereas DJI doesn’t. These are very similar spec’d cameras. I personally tend to grab the Insta360 Go Ultra a bit more, merely because I find the Insta360 app better than the DJI Mimo one, but that’s really the only reason.

Now, you may be wondering about the GoPro Hero 4K/Hero 4K Lit seen up there in the combo picture. Well, I don’t recommend that one. This camera was super promising. Incredibly promising. Unlike Insta360 & DJI, it’s actually fully waterproof, which I find super important in an action camera. But then I looked at the footage. Unfortunately, it’s just not awesome at all, and nowhere in the same league as the DJI OSMO Nano or Insta360 Go Ultra cameras. Of course, it’s a notably less expensive camera, especially in the US. So perhaps that justifies it. But equally, you can pick up a DJI OSMO Action 6 for basically the same price, and that’s got great image quality, albeit it is a touch bit bigger.

I really hope GoPro takes another crack at the smaller form factor camera. Give me the same size as this little Hero 4K, but ditch the light, and then give me something with the new GoPro chipset in there. Please

ProductBuy
On Sale!DJI OSMO Nano
Amazon $349
On Sale!Insta360 Go Ultra
Amazon $359

The 360° Action Cams:

Next, there are the 360° action cams. These capture video 360° at usually 8K, allowing you to play it back either as a 360° video, or more commonly, as a ‘flat’ video at any angle you choose in 4K. This is the most common scenario where people (including myself) tend to use 360° action cameras. I never watch the footage back with VR headsets or such, I just rotate the view to the bit I want, and then export it as a normal video file in 4K.  This includes panning/zooming/etc. to follow action within the frame.

The thing to understand about 360° action cameras is that, in general, they take more effort. While capturing everything around you at once sounds like it’s less effort, in reality it means that every video requires at least some basic video editing to get the views/angles you want. Sometimes that’s just a few seconds’ worth, and sometimes it’s more complicated/messy.

My rule of thumb here is that if you’ve only got one action camera, just get a regular action camera first. It’ll make your life much easier. But if you’re looking to add a second camera to the mix, and enjoy video editing, then a 360° action camera can make sense.

My Main Pick: Insta360 X6:

The Insta360 X6 came out this past summer, bringing upgraded internals, better low-light processing, and much better footage. A number of the changes seemed small, but in total it was a ton of meaningful changes. I use 360 cameras mainly in three core scenarios: Footage of me running where the camera appears out front (and the selfie stick erased), footage of me and my wife cycling with that same perspective, and underwater footage. I also sometimes use it for boat and efoiling footage, again, to get that ‘off to the side’ perspective without a selfie stick.

However, it’s really the underwater footage where Insta360 and the X6 absolutely dominate. I’ve stopped bothering to take a regular action cam/GoPro down underwater for scuba or free diving. It’s purely the X6 now. The shots just come out so damn good, every time. And the ability to reframe when scuba diving is awesome in particular. But more than underwater footage, the main ‘winner’ for me on the X6 over the GoPro Max 2 is simply Insta360’s software app. It’s just got all these little useful features that make it faster and better than GoPro’s app. It’s not like GoPro’s app is bad, but it’s just not really in the same league as Insta360’s, which is constantly getting new features. So while it’s more expensive, I personally find it worth it.

The Honorable Mention: GoPro Max 2:

This is a classic example of why software is so darn important in the 360° action camera space. On paper, the GoPro Max 2 has slightly higher resolution and video-focused details than the Insta360 X6 does in daylight footage (for most people, though, it’s a wash). Heck, the GoPro Max 2 is even a fair bit shorter/smaller than the Insta360 X6 as well.

But that software gap I mentioned above is the singular reason I’d recommend the X6 over the Max 2 if the price is equal. But the thing is, these days the price isn’t actually equal. The GoPro Max 2 is $299, basically half the price of the Insta360 X6. And while the software isn’t as good as the Insta360 X6, it’s also not horrible either. It’s perfectly fine in most cases. It’s just that Insta360 has lots of small/little features that give it the edge when everything else is equal. Still, to be really clear – the GoPro Max 2 has phenomenal image quality and great color science. It’s why so many professional users use GoPro, and that carries into this camera. You certainly won’t be unhappy here.

ProductBuy
On Sale!GoPro Max 2
Amazon $274
On Sale!Insta360 X6
Amazon $629

The Best Drones:

When it comes to drones, I heavily use two main drones constantly, and then two others on a lighter basis. From an athletic standpoint, I’m constantly using the DJI NEO 2 in follow-me mode. It follows you around and is nearly impossible to kill. I’ve crashed it probably hundreds of times by now. Meanwhile, for ‘pretty’ shots that require some big-boy lenses, I use the DJI Mavic 4 Pro.

After that, I have the DJI Mini 5 Pro, which is a great drone, but I only tend to use it on vacations (or hikes) where I’m taking just one drone. And even then, I’d almost always defer to the DJI NEO 2 first, simply due to the better follow-me options.

Which leaves us with the last drone, the HoverAir Aqua above. This is a fully waterproof drone that can take-off/land/flip-over in the water. The design here is to follow you doing aquatic things, from stand-up paddleboarding, to surfing, to foiling, to swimming, and even on a boat. I’ve done most of those things (just not the surfing; I lack those skills). So let’s get into the details a bit more.

Follow-me drone – DJI NEO 2:

I use the DJI NEO 2 as my main follow-me drone. It’s basically indestructible for running, cycling, hiking, etc. Sure, it’s not super great above about 30KPH (it’ll slowly fall behind), but it’s still pretty solid for everything else. It has obstacle avoidance that’ll let it miss the big/obvious things, but there’s plenty (most) times it’ll whack right into the smaller things if you’re going fast. Still, despite me crashing it more times than I could possibly count (likely 100-200 times) since I bought it last year, it’s still going strong. Absolutely recommend this unit. Also, you can pair it up to a DJI remote and use it like a normal drone as well (or even just use your phone for the same, but the remote gets longer range).

As for why not a HoverAir drone here? Well, simply put, the DJI NEO 2 is both cheaper and more dependable. Sure, you can get marginally better footage out of a HoverAir Pro/Pro Max, but I find the HoverAir drones to be not reliable. Sure, they work like 9 out of 10 times, and then you get to the random 1 out of 10 times where you’re standing on the side of a mountain, and the unit gives you some unknown error message that can’t be troubleshot for whatever reason.  And if you use your drone enough, that 1 out of 10 times happens a lot with HoverAir, whereas it never happens with the DJI NEO 2. Frankly, I’m just tired of it.

The all-arounder – DJI Mini 5 Pro:

I use this one sparingly, basically in cases where I want a drone that goes a bit higher/farther, but don’t want to take the DJI Mavic 4 Pro due to size/weight limitations. Yes, this drone also does follow-me, but it requires using the controller (whereas the DJI NEO 2 doesn’t). It’s got better quality than the DJI NEO 2, though not actually a massive step-up in most normal lighting conditions. Instead, it’s in lower light conditions or tricky lighting that it does better. Also, it can rotate its gimbal 90°, for proper vertical filming. This is a great all-arounder drone, though if you’re into sports I highly recommend picking up a DJI NEO 2 first, and then this second.

Best Prosumer Drone – DJI Mavic 4 Pro:

I use this when I want stunning shots of something, and don’t mind lugging around the beefcake that is the Mavic 4 Pro. This drone has three cameras, essentially a wide-angle, a medium telephoto, and a full telephoto. It can fly upwards of 70KPH, and can track subjects across those lenses. All while putting forth incredible imagery. Of course, it’s not quiet, not cheap, and not lightweight. Living in the Mediterranean, I get a lot of use out of this with tons of stunning things to film in the ocean/mountains/beaches/boats, etc. Whereas if you’re living somewhere without a ton of scenic stuff, then…yeah, you might want to distribute your funds elsewhere.

The Waterproof Drone – HoverAir Aqua:

This is a fun drone if you spend time in the water. Or on the water. Either way, in places where you don’t normally want your drone to be in the water, this one is fully waterproof. You can throw it into the water upside-down, and it’ll flip itself over and then start following you. It’s super impressive. They’ve really done a lot of good work refining it over the past year since launch, but still, it’s a HoverAir product. Which means it’s still buggy. I went out last week for two separate swim days, and for reasons that are unclear to me, on both swims it tracked me just fine, but only recorded the last 75-90 seconds of some swims, while others recorded the full 5-8 minute track section. That’s just the way HoverAir drones have always been: They’re great when they work, but their software quality is just such a pain in the butt. Still, if you want a waterproof drone as I do, you’ve got no other real choice.

ProductBuy
On Sale!DJI Mavic 4 Pro Combo
Amazon $2,609
DJI Mini 5 Pro (with RC2 Remote) Fly More Combo
Amazon
DJI NEO 2 Fly More Combo (Extra Batteries)
Amazon
HoverAir Aqua
Amazon

Wrap-Up:

There ya go – all my top picks for drones and action cameras as of today. As always, if you’ve got any questions or more specific scenario recommendations, feel free to drop them down below, and I’m happy to try to answer them.

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: The Best GPS Sport Watches (2026 Recommendations Guide)
entry.content:
Here’s my full GPS watch recommendation guide for winter 2026-2027. This accounts for every model released to date, including ones that just came out two days ago. But more critically, it takes into account hundreds of comparison tests/workouts I’ve done this year alone with all these watches, as well as more than 17 years of experience testing GPS sports watches. Every single day I’m testing and comparing GPS watches, even when not working on a specific review. No run or ride goes without at least 3-4 GPS units, sometimes more.

The good news here is that there’s arguably never been a better time to be a consumer of a GPS sports watch. While the bigger brands (e.g., Apple & Garmin) have gotten bigger in recent years, the smaller brands (e.g., COROS & Amazfit) have found ways to offer incredible value in between the product roadmap cracks of the big companies. And all of these companies are effectively pushing each other to compete for your money, by delivering frequent and deep firmware updates – even for older watches.

While I know many of you will skip right to the recommendations, I’d really encourage you to read the next two sections, especially my ‘Rules of Thumb’ one, as there are lots of products to consider, but this might help quickly narrow it down a bit.

The Problem with Most Recommendation Guides:

Most sports watch recommendation guides suck, because they have two core problems:

1) They never used the watches: They’re either written by AI, or written by people who have never touched the watches. They simply read specs, combined with picking the most popular watches, to drive clicks. If you don’t see any real-world non-marketing photos in a recommendation guide, that’s a near-guarantee it’s slop (AI or human). That’s not me. Every device here I’ve tested, written reviews/posts on, and know what’s good and bad about it.

2) They try to appease manufacturers: I’m not here to try and make every manufacturer happy, or every single person happy by ensuring I recommend their watch. You can come here to see my recommendations from someone who has actually used all these things, and likewise, I don’t care if I upset a company because their watch didn’t get included. I’m going to give you recommendations the same as I would for all my friends and family who’ve been texting me over the last few weeks trying to decide on holiday gifts. That won’t include a lot of watches, or a lot of companies. Not everyone is a winner. I will, however, include some honorable mentions in each category.

There’s also one more factor that isn’t so much a problem with all guides, but just a fact of life that I feel like is worth mentioning to address the elephant in the room:

3) Yes, Garmin & Apple are in every category: Look, when you manufacture the most smartwatches in the world (Apple), or you make the most models (Garmin) and are basically the 2nd most popular smartwatch brand out there, you’re going to be in more categories. Especially because these companies make models targeted at the three basic price tiers. In Apple’s case, they have three models. In Garmin’s case, they have 2,328 models. Other companies also have models for each price tier, but tend to do best in one or two price buckets. Nobody beats Garmin’s feature depth at the top end. But equally, Garmin struggles to compete on ‘value’ in the ultra-budget range. Just like Apple struggles to compete on pure sports features across all price buckets, but dominates on integration with the iPhone. Nonetheless, there’s a reason these two companies sell tens of millions of units each year: People genuinely find their products the best/most dependable/compelling. If they sucked, people wouldn’t buy them for long.

If you find these recommendations useful from a real human, and all the time I put into testing things, then please share out this post to your friends and family. It’s as simple as that.

My Rules of Thumb:

When it comes to how I recommend watches to friends and family, there are kinda a few overarching questions to ask yourself first. It’s not a perfect flow chart per se, nor does it cover every edge case, but it gets you to the right overall group of watches to look at. This somewhat sets aside the budget question, and instead focuses on what you want out of a watch.

1) How much battery do you want? Are you looking for a watch that lasts 4+ days on your wrist (in smartwatch mode), or 20+ hours in GPS mode? If so, you’ll basically be skipping Apple/Google/Samsung watches, and focusing more on the Garmin/Suunto/Amazfit/COROS/etc. watches.

2) Do you want a smart watch, or a smarter watch? The definition of a ‘smart watch’ is imperfect and constantly evolving. Both Garmin & Apple make ‘smartwatches’, but I think we’d agree that for daily ‘smarts’ the Apple Watch can do more (whereas inversely, Garmin does more for sports areas). For most people, the biggest definition of a smartwatch is whether you can take phone calls on it. In the case of Apple/Google/Samsung, you can easily make and take phone calls from anyone. Whereas with Garmin’s LTE-based units, you can make phone calls to friends/family, but if your dentist randomly calls, it won’t route to your watch. And then for the rest of Garmin’s watches and Suunto/COROS/Amazfit/etc., you’ll need your phone with you to take that call. There are lots of other smart features beyond that, but that tends to be the biggest one.

3) Keep in the Ecosystem: Next, if you already have one or more devices in the ecosystem of a given company, then generally it works best to keep them in that ecosystem. For example, if you already have a Garmin Edge bike computer, then unless you want a smarter smartwatch, get a Garmin watch. Likewise, if you’re on Android and want the smartest smartwatch available with the best Android integration, then your choices are basically Google & Samsung. For Apple Watches, you need an iPhone, and for Samsung/Google watches, you need an Android phone. For all the other companies, it doesn’t matter, and they support both ecosystems.

4) All these watches do virtually all sport modes: Years ago, I had to write a separate guide for triathletes, a separate one for cyclists, hikers, and so on. But these days, all of these watches have virtually all sport modes. Most companies keep that list nearly identical across all watches. The edge case exceptions tend to be that high-impact watersports (e.g., waterskiing and surfing) tend to be reserved for watches with higher waterproof ratings (due to impact pressures). And likewise, Garmin gatekeeps their triathlon/multisport modes to mid-tier and above watches.

5) If Maps Matter: Specifically, offline maps while doing a sport mode. There’s a bit of a divide here. The default offline maps/navigation on Apple/Google watches aren’t really great for navigation in many cases, as they have limited/no ability to import hiking/etc. routes easily. There are 3rd-party apps that make this much better, though. Meanwhile, Garmin/Suunto/Amazfit/COROS have great offline map options that can easily import in routes from Strava/Komoot/etc. That said, Garmin gatekeeps these to devices that cost $500-$600+ usually (the exception being any Fenix unit on sale has full maps, as does any Forerunner 965/970 unit). Garmin units below that price have no offline maps, but can still do breadcrumb-style routing.

Ok, hopefully that helps a bit, and cleans up the recommendations down below trying to explain all that stuff for each model. So, let’s get into it!

I’ve divided things up into three basic price groupings:

Budget Category: These are watches under $250

Mid-Range Category: These are watches from $250 to $750

Top-End Models: These are watches from $750+

I know, you can probably subdivide that mid-tier more, or you can pretend the budget goes to $300 (it won’t change anything here), but as you’ll see, things all kinda work out. Ultimately, price brackets are simply a way for any recommendation guide to put things in certain buckets. You know your own budget best, and might have a different price ceiling/bracket.

Budget Category (under $250):

It’s amazing to see how freaking good the watches in this category have become. And it’s funny, these four watches all do the basics really well, but each has their own ‘strengths’ in surprisingly different ways. To decide which one is right, I’d defer again to the ‘Rules of Thumb’ section to help narrow it down.

Garmin Forerunner 70:

When Garmin launched the Forerunner 70 this spring, I argued it was one of the best watches they’ve released in many years. Not because it has the most features (it doesn’t), nor because it has the fanciest materials (it doesn’t), but because it was the rare Garmin model where Garmin was clearly going for blood on packing as much as they could into a sub-$250 watch (now $199 on sale). They took almost all their top-end training metrics from their $1,000 watches, and stuffed them in here, price be damned. If you don’t care about offline maps, but want the polish and connectivity of the Garmin ecosystem (including apps), this is probably the best watch for sports folks in this category. The downside is simply that it doesn’t have the offline maps of the COROS Pace 4 or Amazfit (it still has routing/navigation, though), nor does it have the triathlon mode of the COROS Pace 4. And then when it comes to fancier smart features, it doesn’t have those like the Apple Watch.

COROS Pace 4:

COROS made the Pace 4 even better just a few months ago when they surprise-announced they were adding free offline mapping (a year after release!), which is a crazy move for a company to make. This watch does everything you want a GPS running watch to do – from accurate tracking to navigation to daily activity/health tracking, and of course good battery life. But of course, it’s more than just a running watch, as it has modes for hiking, triathlon, cycling, and plenty more sports modes. You won’t ever find sales on COROS products, so the prices are what they are. The main ‘downside’ is that you don’t have apps on the watch like you do on the Garmin/Apple Watch, nor as many integration partners as Garmin/Apple do. Also, the running training metrics here seem to lack any scientific basis, though total training load is fine. Still, if you’re following some other plan and ignore what the watch is telling you to do, this is a great option.

Apple Watch SE 3:

The Apple Watch SE 3 is a great option if you want more of a ‘smarter’ watch than the others, especially if you want to get cellular on it to ditch your phone. Though, if you don’t care about taking calls/texts away from your phone, then the price plummets down to well under sub-$200 on sale. The main benefit of an Apple Watch (for iPhone users) is really the integration with your phone for calls and text messages, especially the ability to answer anyone anywhere. You also get a lot of the wider health tracking features found within the Apple Ecosystem. That said, the downside is you don’t get any of the new ‘Readiness’ features found on the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, because this unit lacks the newer optical HR sensor found on those units. Further, if you’re looking to do navigation/routing, you’ll want to get some 3rd-party app, because the stock one is mostly hot mess territory.

Amazfit Active Max:

If there’s one area that Amazfit dominates in options, it’s the sub-$300 category, but even more so, the sub-$200 category where this and the Active 2/Active 3 live. Those watches are all very similar, and mostly just have slight hardware differences around buttons and screens. But at $120 on sale, the Amazfit Active Max is just insane value. It’s even got full offline mapping (navigation), plus things like structured workout support, as well as a gazillion sport modes (the list is both hilarious and hilariously long, over 170 sports). And of course it does health tracking like everyone else. The main downside to Amazfit isn’t hardware build quality, but software build quality. The company tends to just release model after model, and many of the software features feel a bit unpolished/half-baked. Not usually bad or anything, but clearly rushed. Still, if you can deal with an occasional quirk, the value here is insane.

ProductBuy
On Sale!Amazfit Active Max
Amazon $118
On Sale!Apple Watch SE3
Amazon $179
COROS Pace 4
Amazon REI
On Sale!Garmin Forerunner 70
Amazon $199

There are also some honorable mentions here:

Garmin Vivoactive 6: This is a great all-arounder watch, which simply lacks the buttons of the Forerunner 70. But also lacks some of the new training features the Forerunner 70 got, hence why I prefer the Forerunner 70.

 

Garmin Forerunner 170 on sale: The watch is priced just a touch bit higher than the Forerunner 70, but essentially adds some extra hardware bits including offline payments (NFC), as well as offline music (Spotify/etc) in the Music models. I have an entire comparison post here going through all the differences.

 

Amazfit T-Rex 3: This is an awesome watch, which is much more rugged than the Amazfit Active Max. Likewise, the Active 2 and Active 3 are also great options. Seriously, this is a price bucket that Amazfit really delivers on.

 

Suunto Run 1: This unit did really well in my review when it launched, and I think if you view it through the lens of ‘buy it for what it has’ rather than any promise of new features that it won’t get, it can be a really good deal. Suunto just launched their Run 2 watch, but spiked the price well above the COROS Pace 4, making it kinda silly.

Again, there are a lot of good options that can also sneak into this category on sale, but that quickly makes it hard to keep up with.

Mid-Range Watches:

Look, this is a vast price range of $350 to $750. Sure, I could subdivide it up again, or I could shift it from say $400 to $750, but realistically that won’t change anything in the lower tier bucket. Or I could cut the ceiling off at $600, forcing the FR970 into the upper-tier bucket just for the heck of it. There’s no perfect option here. The problem is, in many ways these watches are actually really darn similar in terms of core capabilities; instead, you’re basically paying differences for what you value most. If you value Apple integration, you pay Apple for that. If you value deep sports features, you pay Garmin for that. If you value a little bit of everything while still having money in your wallet, you pay COROS for that.

Apple Watch Series 12:

There’s a reason the Apple Watch is basically the most popular watch in the world – the just-works factor is super high. And the Apple Watch Series 12 continues that tradition, but adds in a bunch of new software features this year focused on trending your daily metrics. That includes heart rate variability tracking, which rolls into a new ‘Readiness’ score (similar to what others already have). But beyond that, it’s the overall smartwatch integration into the Apple ecosystem and health/medical tracking that drives most adoption here. The main downside to the Apple Watch Series 12 continues to be it’s basically 1-1.5 day battery life of course, and then it’s sport profiles are rather simplistic compared to most other companies. It’s great for tracking a run (or doing a structured workout), but if you want to navigate a trail route, it’s a bit messy and will ultimately require a 3rd party app to do well.

Garmin Forerunner 970

The Garmin Forerunner series is legendary among runners, but the thing is, this watch is just as capable a triathlon watch as anything else. In fact, it has virtually all the sport modes of a high-end Fenix 9 series device (save things like diving), and most of the hardware internals – such as the LED flashlight. In many ways, the Garmin Forerunner 970 is referred to as the ‘plastic Fenix’ (much to the chagrin of the Forerunner team…but hey, sometimes the truth hurts). You’re basically trading the fancier materials/case design of the Fenix for nearly identical software on a Forerunner-branded model. But that’s ideal if you want a thinner and lighter model than the Fenix series; plus, it’s less expensive. So why buy this over the COROS Pace 4, which is $300 cheaper? In short, you’re buying a far more polished device/platform with wider integration, better maps, a flashlight, medically certified ECG, and a bunch of other things that don’t fit into a single paragraph. The downside? Really just one thing: The price.

COROS Pace 4 Pro

This is probably one of the best all-arounders in this vast price bucket. The COROS Pace 4 Pro has full offline mapping/navigation, has all the sport modes you might need, it has a big beautiful and brilliant 1.5” AMOLED screen at 3,500 nits, it’s thin and lightweight, and you can even pretend you want to talk to your wrist with its microphone and speaker. This model just came out last month, so it’s going to get updates for quite some time. Not just because it’s new, but because COROS is really good about providing new software feature updates for a really really really long time. More so than anyone else out there, albeit some of those updates are just catching up with what Garmin offers. But hey, it’s updates nonetheless! The main ‘downside’ to the COROS Pace 4 Pro would simply be that the mapping isn’t as deep as Garmin here, and there are no on-device apps like Garmin/Apple.

ProductBuy
On Sale!Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm)
Amazon $329
COROS Pace 4 Pro
Amazon REI
On Sale!Garmin Forerunner 970
Amazon $649 REI $649

There are so many honorable mentions here in this category that it could probably deserve its own post:

Google Pixel Watch 5: This one is tricky. If you don’t have an iPhone, but still want smarts, the Pixel Watch 5 is a great option. Seriously, it’s your next best option that’s not Garmin/COROS. And Google did some amazing stuff with software here for GPS accuracy that’s astonishing. And likewise, their Google Health app is doing incredible stuff around AI training recommendations that doesn’t suck (when every other sports AI thing I’ve tried sucks). But when it comes to actually using it for sports, there are still some weird gaps, like the lack of a lap button or the ability to pair a heart rate or other sensors. Further, it lacks sports route/navigation at all.

 

Suunto Race 2: This one is also tricky, as it probably would have made this list a month ago. With the COROS Pace 4 Pro coming along, it sorta sideswipes Suunto out of a win in this category, despite being very similar and priced the same. But this is mainly because the Suunto Race 2 is now a year older, and with Suunto’s new Race 3S being announced, I worry what will happen next year with software updates for the older Race 2 series. Whereas with COROS, they have a very dependable record of software updates for older units. Plus, the display and such is better on the COROS Pace 4 Pro anyway.

 

Garmin Forerunner 570: If you don’t care about mapping, but want Garmin’s other premium running/sports features and a larger display than the Forerunner 70/170, you can grab the Forerunner 570 instead. Or, if you do care about mapping, just get the older Forerunner 965, which people are pretty darn happy with. You just won’t get meaningful new software features on the FR965 like you would with the Forerunner x70 series (e.g., 70/170/570/970) because it’s considered a previous software platform.

 

Garmin Fenix 8 on sale: Right now the Garmin Fenix 8 is at $749 (and occasionally dipping lower). The Fenix 8 series gets virtually all the new Fenix 9 software features, and basically wipes away everyone else in this category from a features standpoint. It’s got certified dive support, the most feature-rich maps of anything here, medically certified ECG, an LED flashlight, and tons more. It’s hard to beat at prices this low.

Top-End Models:

At over $750, there are really only a few options in this realm. You’ve got the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and then you have 28 different Fenix models and variants. There are no other models in this pricing realm that are worth buying.

Garmin Fenix 9 Series:

The Garmin Fenix 9 series is the watch you buy when you want the absolute best option in the market for sports. There’s simply no competition anywhere remotely close to this. Of course, the Fenix 9 has many tiers/pricing available. Right now they start at $899 on sale, but normally $999, and then go up a few hundred dollars more into the $1,100+ range. The three tiers are Base/Pro/Pro inReach. Essentially, Pro adds a brighter display and some other hardware tweaks, whereas Pro inReach adds LTE capability and satellite messaging. Personally, I love the Pro inReach because I know I’ve got a way to get messages to someone outside of cellular range (either for general updates or emergencies). My wife runs all the time for hours by herself at night, and hates carrying a phone, so this works perfectly because I get an LTE LiveTrack link to follow along. Like with the Forerunner 970, the main downside here is price. It’s expensive; there’s no getting around that. The secondary downside of the Pro inReach models is that while they have LTE calling/texts, it’s really focused on keeping your immediate friends/family updated. It doesn’t share a phone number/line with your existing device. So it works well within the limited focus area, but is really about being a super-deep sports watch.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: 

As I noted earlier, Apple makes products in all these categories that are incredibly popular. The reality though, is that you’re purchasing the Apple Watch Ultra 4 not for deep sports features, but for the Apple ecosystem and the longer battery life. I wear the Apple Watch Ultra 4 daily on my wrist (the other wrist has a Garmin Fenix 9 Pro inReach 47mm). What I appreciate about the Apple Watch Ultra 4 isn’t so much the core sports features that it has, nor the diving support it has, nor even the emergency siren I’ll hopefully never use. Instead, I appreciate the iMessage integration and how good it is, as well as other smartphone notification-type features getting full photos and such on my wrist. Certainly, that’s also a function of Apple gatekeeping those features that way within iOS, but until that changes, that’s what I value most from the Apple Watch Ultra 4. The downsides to the Ultra 4 honestly depend a bit on why you’re buying it. If you’re buying it for deep athletic adventures, you might be a bit disappointed with the sports features and mapping/etc. But if you’re buying it to track/run a marathon, it’s awesome.

ProductBuy
On Sale!Apple Watch Ultra 4 (Trail Loop)
Amazon $649
On Sale!Garmin Fenix 9 AMOLED
Amazon $849

A few honorable mentions here:

Garmin Enduro 3 or Enduro 4: I just want to briefly mention that if you don’t want to spend the money for a Fenix 9, but want ultra-long battery life, the Enduro 3/Enduro 4 are basically Fenix 8/Fenix 9 models, except without the AMOLED screen and without the diving/speaker/mic features. And in doing so, the price ends up being a heck of a lot cheaper. Likewise, if you don’t want/need the Fenix 9, then check out both the Fenix 8 and Fenix 8 Pro, which share the same software, but just cost less and have slightly less bright displays.

Wrap-Up

Ok, I know there’s a lot to take in above, and frankly, you could sit here and subdivide categories all day long, or tweak recommendations to an individual’s priorities as well. One person might prefer mapping; the other doesn’t care one bit. One person wants a week of battery, the other is fine with one day. One person wants dive support, while another wants climbing support, and so on.

Thus, if you’ve got questions, I’ll try my best in the comments section. Again, my goal above is to provide recommendations as I would to my friends/family, not to try and cover every watch in the market for every possible scenario. But equally, I’m happy to try and answer questions down below to thread the needle in between all the gaps out there!

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Best road bike mudguards 2026 reviewed
entry.content:
Cyclist
Best road bike mudguards 2026 reviewed

The best road bike mudguards will protect you from road spray and not make a lot of noise in the process. Fitting mudguards to your road bike is a surefire way to stay dry, comfy and infinitely more presentable, plus they’ll also protect your bike’s components from wear, and even keep riders behind you from getting a face full of road grime.

Whether you prefer to have mudguards fitted all year round, or only opt for them in winter when the weather turns, they’re without a doubt one of the best upgrades you can make to your bike. There are also a lot of different types on offer, from full-length fenders secured permanently with metal stays, to plastic clip-ons that you can put on and take off as and when you need them. There are also gravel bike mudguards available that handle the extra width of gravel bike tyres.

To help you decide which type of mudguard is best for your road bike, we’ve rounded up our favourites below. And if you still need some more guidance, keep scrolling for our guide on the different mudguard styles and what’s needed to fit them.

Reviews of the best road bike mudguards

  1. Portland Design Works Full Metal Fenders: RRP £139.99 – Read our full review
  2. Velo Orange: RRP £75 – Read our full review
  3. SKS Chromoplastic: RRP £49.99 – Read our full review
  4. SKS Raceblade Pro XL: RRP £54.99 – Read our full review
  5. Kinesis Fend Off: RRP £60 – Read our full review
  6. Crud Roadracer Mk3: RRP £49.99 – Read our full review
  7. Zefal Shield R35: RRP £40 – Read our full review
  8. Ass Savers Win Wing 2 Road: RRP £24 – Read our full review

Why you can trust Cyclist’s advice

As riders ourselves, we’re always out reviewing and testing bikes, whatever the weather. So when it comes to the essential task of keeping comfortable on cold, wet rides, we’ll even resort to adding mudguards to an aero bike.

Just take a look at former Cyclist writer Charlotte’s Aeroad Custom Build, shown above, decked out with SKS Raceblades to keep her ride mates happier.

The best road bike mudguards reviewed

Portland Design Works Full Metal Fenders

£119.99 | Buy here

  • Among the quietest metal mudguards we’ve tested
  • Excellent spray protection, with pre-installed rubber mud flaps
  • Straightforward fitting, with adjustable stays

The Portland Design Works Full Metal Fenders are a premium aluminium option that combine generous coverage with impressively quiet running. Thoughtful details include pre-installed rubber mud flaps that extend close to the ground, helping keep both you and anyone riding behind you clear of road spray.

They’re also easier to fit than many traditional metal mudguards. Adjustable stays minimise the need for cutting, while anti-rattle stickers help keep unwanted noise to a minimum. The instructions could be clearer, but fitting is manageable at home without extensive mechanical experience.

PDW rates them for tyres up to 30mm, although clearance is on the tighter side with 28mm tyres. They’re best suited to 25-28mm widths, where they offer an excellent combination of coverage, durability and everyday usability.

At £119.99, they’re certainly not cheap, but if you’re after well-designed metal mudguards that are quiet, robust and relatively painless to live with, they’re a strong contender.

  • Read our full Portland Design Works Full Metal Fenders review 

Velo Orange Hammered 45mm mudguards 

£75 | Buy here

  • Beautiful hammered aluminium finish
  • Excellent full-length coverage for tyres up to 35mm
  • Solid, durable construction for long-term use

If aesthetics matter as much as practicality, the Velo Orange Hammered 45mm mudguards are a particularly handsome option. Their distinctive hammered aluminium finish gives them a lovely vintage look, making them especially well suited to steel touring, gravel and hybrid bikes.

They’re also impressively robust, with solid metal fittings and generous full-length coverage that does an excellent job of keeping road spray at bay. The 45mm profile accommodates tyres up to 35mm, making them a good choice for riders running wider rubber.

However, fitting is a fairly involved process. There’s plenty of fiddly hardware to assemble, the stays need cutting to length, and you’ll ideally want a workstand, hacksaw and a few workshop tools to get everything sitting properly. The supplied mounting hardware is also a little limited, so you may need additional bolts or spacers depending on your frame.

Once installed, though, they’re a sturdy, fit-and-forget option that should last for years. They’re not for anyone looking for a quick seasonal installation, but if you’re happy to put in the effort, the combination of excellent coverage, durability and classic looks makes them well worth considering.

  • Read our full Velo Orange Hammered 45mm mudguard review

SKS Chromoplastic

£49.99 | Buy here

  • Excellent full-length coverage and a neat, close-fitting profile
  • Plenty of adjustment options and widely available spare parts
  • Front safety quick-release helps prevent wheel lock-up

The SKS Chromoplastic P35s are a classic full-length mudguard option, combining a sturdy aluminium core with a plastic outer layer for a durable, practical design. They offer excellent protection against road spray and grime, while a generous selection of supplied bolts and spacers makes it easy to fine-tune their position for a neat fit around your wheels.

A particularly useful feature is the front safety quick-release, which allows the stays to detach if debris becomes trapped between the tyre and mudguard, helping to prevent the front wheel from locking up. They’re also widely stocked, so replacement stays, brackets and other spare parts are readily available.

Fitting is relatively straightforward, although you’ll need to cut the stainless steel stays to length and have a few basic tools to hand. More importantly, check your actual tyre width before buying. Although rated for tyres up to 28mm, real-world measurements can be wider, particularly on wider rims, and clearance is noticeably tighter than on some alternatives. The plastic seatstay bracket is also worth considering if you’re running traditional calliper brakes, as compression can affect brake alignment.

If your tyres fit comfortably within the available clearance, these are a reliable, well-made option for commuting and winter road riding, with excellent coverage and the reassurance of readily available replacement parts.

  • Read our full SKS Chromoplastic P35 mudguards review

SKS Raceblade Pro XL

£54.99 | Buy here

  • Extremely quick and easy to fit, with no mudguard mounts needed
  • Fully adjustable to suit different frame and brake setups
  • Easy to remove and transfer between compatible bikes

The SKS Raceblade Pro XLs are a convenient clip-on option for road bikes without traditional mudguard mounts, or for those who don’t want to commit to a permanent winter setup. Secured directly to the fork and seatstays using flexible rubber straps, they’re incredibly quick to install, taking as little as 30 seconds, with no specialist tools required.

Adjustable stays make it easy to position the mudguards around different frame shapes and brake setups, while supplied frame protectors help prevent damage to your paintwork. They’re also easy to remove and refit, making them particularly useful if you only want mudguards when the weather turns.

The compromise is coverage. Although they do a reasonable job of keeping spray off your back and protecting the frame, the short rear guard offers little protection for anyone riding behind you, while the front leaves some spray reaching your hands and face. They’re also prone to rattling on rough roads, thanks to their relatively minimal fixing points.

For solo riding in wet weather, they’re a practical and fuss-free solution. However, if you regularly ride in a group or want proper all-round protection for winter training, a full-length set would be a better choice.

  • Read our full SKS Raceblade Pro XL mudguards review

Kinesis Fend Off

£60 | Buy here

  • Robust aluminium and steel construction
  • Quiet running with excellent spray protection
  • Recyclable packaging doubles up as front and rear mud flaps

The Kinesis Fend Offs are a sturdy set of aluminium mudguards that offer excellent coverage and impressively quiet running. Their squared-off profile gives them a distinctive look, while the solid aluminium and steel construction feels reassuringly durable. They’re available in two widths, with the 40mm Standard version accommodating tyres up to 34mm and the 50mm Wide version taking tyres up to 45mm.

They’re relatively straightforward to install for traditional full-length metal mudguards, although you’ll need to cut the stays to length and have a few basic tools to hand. Once fitted, they’re impressively stable, with minimal rattling even over rough roads. A particularly neat touch is the recyclable, low-plastic packaging, which can be repurposed into additional front and rear mud flaps for improved spray protection.

There are a few compromises. Unlike some competitors, they don’t have a front safety quick-release mechanism, and clearance around calliper brakes can be tight. They’re also heavier than plastic alternatives, so aren’t the best choice if keeping weight down is a priority.

However, if you’re after a durable, fit-and-forget set of metal mudguards for year-round riding, the Fend Offs offer an excellent combination of coverage, quiet running and robust construction.

  • Read our full Kinesis Fend Off mudguards review

Crud Roadracer Mk3

£49.99 | Buy here

  • Excellent rear coverage, including protection for the drivetrain
  • Quiet running, even with tight tyre clearances
  • Adaptable design for bikes without mudguard mounts

The Crud Catcher Road Racer Mk3 mudguards offer an interesting solution for road bikes that lack traditional mudguard mounts or have limited clearance for conventional full-length mudguards. Their clever plastic design uses adhesive mounting points and adjustable sections to secure them to the frame and fork, with components that can be trimmed to suit different setups.

Coverage is particularly impressive at the rear, where an extended scoop-shaped section helps keep spray away from the drivetrain as well as the rider. They’re also surprisingly quiet in use, thanks to supplied anti-vibration pads and brush inserts that help keep everything centred, even with tight tyre clearances.

Fitting is more involved than you might expect, though. There are plenty of individual components to position, the adhesive mounting points need careful placement, and the initial installation takes patience. Clearance around the front brake can also be particularly tight with 28mm tyres and calliper brakes, so check your setup before buying. The adhesive fixings can occasionally come loose, too, although spare mounts are supplied.

They’re not the prettiest mudguards, but if your bike isn’t designed for conventional full-length mudguards, the Road Racer Mk3s offer an effective and relatively quiet alternative, with particularly good protection for your drivetrain.

  • Read our full Crud Catcher Road Racer Mk3 mudguards review

Zefal Shield R35

£40 | Buy here

  • Good rear coverage for clip-on mudguards
  • Extended flap helps protect the rear brake area
  • Affordable, lightweight option for bikes without mudguard mounts 

The Zefal Shield R35 mudguards are a budget-friendly option for road bikes without mudguard eyelets, offering a useful step up in protection from more minimalist clip-on designs. Made from lightweight thermoplastic, they’re secured using rubber mounting blocks and adjustable straps, with an extended rear flap available in three lengths to help catch spray around the rear brake.

Fitting takes a little patience, as getting the mounting blocks and straps correctly positioned can be fiddly, and adjustment is limited once everything is in place. The mounts can also shift slightly on rougher roads, while tight clearance around the front wheel may rule them out for some frames.

Once fitted, the rear guard provides surprisingly good protection for this style of mudguard, although the front offers less coverage and the drivetrain remains exposed. At £40, they’re a practical, removable option for occasional wet-weather riding, provided your frame has sufficient clearance and you don’t mind some setup faff.

  • Read our full Zefal Shield R35 mudguards review

Ass Savers Win Wing 2 Road

£24 | Buy here

  • Quick, tool-free fitting with no permanent mounting hardware
  • Lightweight, removable design for bikes without mudguard mounts
  • Adjustable blade lets you fine-tune the positioning to suit your frame 

The Ass Savers Win Wing 2 Road is a minimalist rear mudguard designed to keep the worst of the road spray off your back without the bulk or commitment of full-length mudguards. Weighing just 64g, it attaches to the seatstays using flexible rubber straps, takes only a couple of minutes to fit and is just as easy to remove. The adjustable blade can be positioned to suit your frame, while supplied protection stickers help prevent rubbing against the paintwork.

Despite its small size, it does a surprisingly good job of keeping your back dry, and is impressively quiet over rough roads. However, coverage is limited: the seat tube and drivetrain remain exposed, and the matching Speed Mullet front guard won’t keep your feet completely dry. They’re also not ideal for wet group rides, offering little protection to anyone following behind. A convenient, affordable option for occasional wet-weather riding, but not a substitute for full-length winter mudguards.

  • Read our full Ass Savers Win Wing 2 Road/Speed Mullet mudguards review

How do I choose the right bike mudguards?

Clearance and mounting points

The first thing you need to know is whether or not your bike’s frame has eyelets for attaching full-length mudguards, and if there’s enough clearance between the tyres, frame and fork to accommodate them. Check the manufacturer’s specifications if you’re unsure, and remember that the stated maximum tyre clearance doesn’t necessarily tell you how much room you’ll have left once mudguards are fitted.

If your bike lacks mounting points, clip-on mudguards are an obvious alternative. It’s also possible to fit traditional full-length mudguards using P-clips, which are available from DIY stores. Look for rubber-lined versions to help protect the frame’s finish.

Fortunately, more and more of the best road bikes, particularly endurance bikes, all-road bikes and gravel bikes, now come with mudguard mounts. These aren’t always immediately obvious, as some manufacturers use discreet or hidden eyelets, so it’s worth checking the frame carefully or consulting the bike’s manual.

Length and style

The type and length of mudguard you choose will have a significant impact on how much protection you get. Full-length mudguards offer the most comprehensive coverage, helping to keep spray and road grime off you, your bike and anyone riding behind. They also protect more of the frame and drivetrain, reducing the amount of cleaning and maintenance needed through winter. Don’t overlook the mudflaps, either. These small extensions at the ends of the mudguards can make a noticeable difference to how much spray gets through.

Shorter clip-on fenders are generally lighter, easier to fit and remove, and useful if you only need occasional protection or want to avoid permanent fittings. However, coverage is inevitably more limited. Some designs do a surprisingly good job of keeping spray off your back, but are less effective at protecting your feet, drivetrain or fellow cyclists. Minimalist under-saddle mudguards offer the least protection, primarily shielding your lower back from the worst of the rear-wheel spray.

Brakes and frame compatibility

Traditional full-length mudguards typically attach to the fork crown at the front and the brake bridge at the rear. Check that the necessary mounting points are available, particularly if your bike has disc brakes, as you’ll need a compatible fitting arrangement. Depending on the frame and brake setup, you may also need to work around brake callipers, which can make installation more complicated.

Clip-on designs avoid some of these issues by attaching to the seatstays, fork legs, downtube or seatpost instead. However, they’re not universally compatible either, and mounting straps and rubber blocks need to sit securely against the frame, and limited clearance can make positioning difficult.

If your bike has rim brakes, pay particular attention to the width of the mudguards and the space around the callipers. Mudguards that are too wide can interfere with the brakes or prevent the wheel from turning freely. Even when a manufacturer specifies a maximum tyre width, check the actual clearance on your bike before buying, as tyre dimensions can vary between brands and models.

Fitting and maintenance

It’s also worth considering how much effort you’re prepared to put into installation. Some full-length mudguards require stays to be cut to size, and may need additional spacers or hardware to achieve a secure fit. Others are designed for relatively straightforward installation, while clip-on options can often be fitted without specialist tools or permanent modifications.

Look for adjustable mounting systems if you’re fitting mudguards to an unusual frame shape, but bear in mind that some clip-on designs offer limited scope for repositioning once installed. Frame-protection tape can also be a sensible precaution wherever straps or mounting blocks contact the paintwork. Once fitted, check that all fixings are secure and that the mudguards don’t rub against the tyres, frame or brakes.

For more advice, take a look at our guide to how to winterproof your bike and keep riding comfortably through the colder months.

entry.title: Cyclist Magazine Podcast: The hardest Tour de France, with Gareth Cartman
entry.content:
Cyclist
Cyclist Magazine Podcast: The hardest Tour de France, with Gareth Cartman

This week on the Cyclist Magazine Podcast, James is joined by cycling historian and author, Gareth Cartman. Gareth’s life long love of cycling began watching Marco Pantani in the Tour de France on Channel 4 (remember when the Tour was on the tele?), and was cemented while living in Paris, witnessing, as he says, Lance Armstrong ‘not win the Tour seven times’.

Gareth’s latest book, We Rode All Night, tells the story of the longest, most gruelling Tour in history, the 1926 edition, in which just 41 riders finished, with several almost not making it back at all after the infamous Stage 10 – 326km and nearly 8,000m elevation, ridden through the night amid unprecedented storms.

In this chat Gareth brings to life cycling’s earliest days, from the iron-fisted rule of Tour founder Henri Desgrange, to the wacky-races cheating, near-death experiences, harrowing rider backstories, political and social unrest, Communist newspaper journalists, terrible roads, the mud, the blood, the countless soggy woollen jerseys and tear streaked faces… they don’t make ’em like they used to, so get the kettle on and pin back your lugholes.

Gareth’s previous books include We Rode All Day, retelling the story of the 1919 Tour de France through the voices of the riders; Walko, recounting Roger Walkowiak’s remarkable and unexpected victory in the 1956 Tour de France; and Koblet + Kubler, which explores the intertwined lives and careers of Switzerland’s two great cycling champions.

Check out We Rode All Night (Pitch Publishing) at pitchpublishing.co.uk

Chat begins at 11:40.

  • Listen to our chat with Gareth Cartman on the Cyclist magazine app or wherever you get your podcasts
  • Get the Cyclist iOS app / Get the Cyclist app on the Google Play store

This episode is brought to you by Rouvy, the indoor riding platform that makes indoor rides look and feel real, from smashing up the Sa Calobra to group rides around Vietnam. See Rouvy.com for more details, including how to sign up for a free month using the code KEEPITREALCYCLIST.
