entry.title: eBike Popemobile for Leo XIV, from Scott
entry.content:
We’ve watched cycling brands build custom bikes for Popes for more than a decade, yet Scott’s new papal edition of their Sub Tour 10 Wave city ebike looks like something Pope Leo XIV might actually want to ride.

Scott teamed up with the UCI to create this special papal edition urban ebike and a matching helmet to commemorate Pope Leo XIV’s “shared values of mobility, accessibility, and connection“. At the Vatican this week, Scott and the UCI presented the functional ebike to the Pope, citing bicycles’ role both as recreation, but also as a source of freedom to those who ride.

“Cycling can therefore be understood as a metaphor for that ‘life in abundance’ that is characteristic of every authentic sporting experience.”

– Pope Leo XIV

Scott’s ebike Popemobile: Sub Tour 10 Wave city commuter

Sure, a custom papal Pinarello for the previous Pope Francis was slick, as was getting a custom S-Works Venge and a rainbow jersey from World Champ Peter Sagan. But maybe more realistic were the classic Breezer Downtown townie or the Smart eBike from Daimler that he received earliest in his tenure, while already 76-years-old with just one lung.

But let’s be honest, Popes are rarely spring chickens. The Chicago-borne Pope Leo XIV is already 71-years-old, and just had part of his lung quickly removed after a recent lung cancer diagnosis. So, a step-through city ebike sounds like a much more appropriate gift for the holy septuagenarian.

Custom Papal edition graphics

Scott custom painted both the Sub Tour 10 Wave city ebike and a matching Sierra MIPS helmet to keep the papal head safe and sound zipping around town.

Seriously, this is maybe the most subdued papal paint job & graphics we’ve seen customize on a bike for the head of the Catholic Church. But that actually seems more fitting for the Pope, right?

What you get is just a silver monochromatic coat of arms Pope Leo XIV on a frame with a subtle white marble finish. Scott says the look was inspired by the 4-wheeled Popemobile – which currently is a pearl-white electric Mercedes G580, heavenly heavily customized itself, of course. So yes, now Pope Leo XIV has two custom electric rides to cruise around Vatican City.

Tech details

  • step-through alloy frame ebike
  • Bosch Performance Line CX motor: max 100Nm torque & 750W peak power
  • Bosch PowerTube 800Wh internal battery – removable
  • Shimano Nexus Inter 5e, 5-speed internal gear hub
  • Gates CDX belt drive
  • 100mm SR Suntour XCM34 BOOST AIR LO suspension fork
  • Shimano MT200 2-piston hydraulic brakes with 180/160mm rotors
  • adjustable height stem with integrated SP Connect phone mount
  • integrated Lezyne front and rear lights
  • Ursus U-mount kickstand
  • sadly, no dropper for the Pope though
  • 700x55mm Schwalbe Big Apple Performance tires
  • full-coverage fenders
  • Racktime rack with SnapIt 2.0 & Kid’nCarry mounting: max 30kg load rated
  • 29.7kg/65.5lb claimed complete weight

Scott ebike Popemobile – Pricing & availability

A papal Scott ebike is pretty much free and readily available. All you need to do is make it out of the next conclave.

Otherwise, you could get a regular-edition Sub Tour 10 ebike of your own for 4400€ with the same spec as Pope Leo XIV. Its standard colors are even named fit for the devout: Celestial silver or Paradise green. Perfect for getting around your own sovereign city-state, or just the regular town where you live. We don’t know what size the Pope rides, but it comes in four options (S-XL).

Scott-sports.com

entry.title: Scicon Sports Unveils New Aeronda Cycling Sunglasses With Patented Multispherical Lens
entry.content:
Scicon Sports, the official eyewear sponsor of UAE Team Emirates and Tadej Pogačar, just launched its latest cycling sunglasses, the Aeronda. The model name describes the lens and combines the words air and wave — onda means wave in Italian. These new performance shades are built around Scicon’s exclusive, patented MasterBlank lens, which combines a “multispherical” shape with outward-facing “flaps” across the top and bottom.

Additionally, the vented MasterBlank lens has a wraparound shape, temple attachments integrated into the lens, and Tactigrip temples/arms and FlexiFit 2.0 nose pad to optimize the fit. The Aeronda is currently offered in four multimirror lens colors, along with a low-light pink, and Scicon provides two options for prescription lenses.

Aeronda Development

Scicon says the Aeronda project started in April of 2026 when Tadej Pogačar raced Paris-Roubaix with a special lens fitted to his Aeroshade 2.0 Titanium glasses. This lens featured an outward-facing flap across the bottom, which was intended to help protect the face from dust, mud, debris, water, and generally harsh conditions experienced by riders racing the Hell of the North. 

MasterBlank

This experimental lens was the basis for what Scicon refers to as MasterBlank: “an oversize, multi-spherical Base 8 patent-pending lens that integrates to the temple attachments directly.” The brand states this new lens design is not a standard lens, and it is not available to other eyewear makers. Instead, it was designed and is owned by Scicon Sports and is exclusive to the brand.

If you’re into performance eyewear, then you’re probably familiar with the most common cylindrical and spherical lens shapes — and possibly toric too. So what the heck is a multispherical lens? According to Scicon, “It combines several spherical curves in a single continuous surface, and each zone has the right curve for its job: wrapping the face, protecting the eyes, working with the flow of air.”

The MasterBlank lens geometry, a base-8 monolens with a radius of curvature of 66mm, reportedly delivers uniform vision across the whole lens. Meanwhile, the wraparound curve follows the shape of the head, for a streamlined fit and unobstructed peripheral vision. Additionally, the temple attachments are integrated into the lens, a design intended to enhance structural integrity, stability, and security while riding. 

Lens “Flaps”

Beyond the multispherical shape of the lens, the “flaps” are arguably the most visually apparent feature of the new Aeronda sunglasses. These flaps, as Scicon calls them, are outward-flared portions of the lens, which help to give the glasses their distinctive look and “wave” profile. Scicon claims each flap, upper and lower, also serves a function.

According to Scicon, “The upper Aero Flap follows the brow line and deflects airflow toward the helmet: it is designed to reduce turbulence in the upper part of the field of view and to keep the eyewear stable at speed. The lower Safety Flap extends the lens downward to protect the face and reduce the risk of cuts in a crash. At the same time, it channels air cleanly around the lower part of the face.”

Ventilation

The upper and lower edges of the lens also include what Scison calls VortexFlow ventilation. These slim vents are designed to allow air to circulate and reduce fogging, of course, and the brand says they’ve been designed to not let any distracting sunlight in.

Adjustability

As mentioned above, the temple attachments are integrated into the lens design and make a sturdy fixing point for the temples/arms. Scicon says, “The diamond-pattern TactiGrip temples are made from high-quality flexible nylon, with TPE co-injected tips, and a metal core that adjusts to the millimeter.” Additionally, the FlexiFit 2.0 nose pad features the same TactiGrip thermopolymer with an adjustable design that can be adapted to varying nose bridges and face shapes quickly and easily.

Sizes

The Aeronda sunglasses come in two shapes/sizes, M1 and M3, which look nearly identical, but have very slight differences. The M1 lens is slightly taller at 66mm, has lower vents, and a more shapely upper and lower lens. The M3 lens is a touch shorter at 63mm, does not have lower vents, and has smoother lines to its upper and lower edges.

Lens Options

At launch, the Aeronda is available in a total of five different lens options. There are four multimirror colors: Silver, Red, Blue-Green, and Yellow, all of which offer Cat 3 protection and are designed for bright light conditions. Additionally, a Cat 1 Pink version is available as a low-light option. Scicon says that more color variants and a photochromic option are in the works. 

Prescription Lenses

For those who require corrective lenses, Scicon has two options for the Aeronda glasses. First, the SlideFit optical insert can be fitted over the nose piece. Second, the Prescription Insert Lens System (P.I.L.S.) integrates a prescription lens directly into the lens of the Aeronda sunglasses for a clean, single-piece solution. P.I.L.S. is an option in the Silver and Red lenses only.

Pricing and Availability

Scicon’s new Aeronda cycling sunglasses are priced at €170 / $195. They are available now at select retailers or directly from Scicon Sports.

sciconsports.com

entry.title: Preorders For The RatKing Frames Chull Cargo Bikes Now Open
entry.content:
The RatKing Chull is a compact steel cycle truck. This bike was originally designed for apartment living in town with its small footprint and grocery hauling capabilities. Now it’s been adapted for strolls into town, past neighbors’ cows, for post office deliveries.

The 20″ front wheel creates room for a low, frame-mounted cargo platform, while a full-size 26″ or 29″ rear wheel keeps the bike rolling easily. The rear wheel size is either/or; choose the 26″ for a shorter wheelbase or the 29″ for even better rollover. Or just go off vibes; the reverse penny farthing is a look.

The Chull uses a removable 20 × 16″ frame-mounted platform. The primary 14 × 16″ cargo area extends forward of the head tube, while another 6″ wraps rearward around it. By building the frame and platform separately, the platform is able to sit below the head tube, keeping cargo exceptionally low and stable.

The geometry is designed specifically around a loaded front platform, with a short overall wheelbase and steering intended to remain controlled and intuitive under load. (Geometry optimized for 2.25″ Tires)

The Chull is built for moderate loads (target load capacity of 75lbs). You could carry so many burritos on this thing.

The Chull’s cargo platform is not designed or intended to carry passengers, including children. The target load capacity applies to cargo only.

RatKing Chull Quick Hits

  • Price
    • Frameset (Frame, Fork, Platform, and Kickstand): $3200
    • Complete: $5800
  • Frameset Specs:
    • 20″ front wheel
    • 26″ or 29″ rear wheel
    • Clearance for up to 2.4″ Tires
  • FRAME & DRIVETRAIN:
    • 73 mm BSA bottom bracket
    • 52 mm chainline
    • 38T maximum chainring
    • 30.9 mm seatpost
    • Internal ST dropper-post routing
    • Two bottle positions on seat tube / down tube
  • AXLES & BRAKES:
    • 148 × 12 mm rear thru axle
    • 100 × 12 mm front thru axle
    • IS disc brake mounts front and rear
  • CARGO PLATFORM:
    • 20 × 16″ removable frame-mounted cargo platform (14″x16″ in front of Headtube / 6″ extension behind headtube)
    • Estimated frameset+platform weight: approximately 14 lb
    • Saddle height in reference diagrams: Small – 720mm / Big – 780mm / Bigger – 800mm
  • Tubing is a mix of straight gauge 4130 and Reynolds 631 chromoly steel tubing.
  • Timelines
    • Delivery for frames in or before Spring 2027
    • Delivery for full build Full Montys in spring 2027

Find out all the nitty-gritty details over at RatKing Frames!

entry.title: FIDLOCK’s Latest Bright Idea: The New PINCLIP Interchangeable Magnetic Light System
entry.content:
Always expanding its line of tool-free mounted accessories, FIDLOCK has now introduced lights to its magnetic-mechanically fastened ecosystem. Their new PINCLIP front and rear lights offer quick, easy-to-install illumination with mounts that can also accommodate other FIDLOCK accessories.

The PINCLIP front light is not a high-powered unit for night riding on MTB trails, but the set is ideal for commuting, evening road rides, or pedalling around town in the dark. When you’re not using the front light, the mount can carry a POV camera instead. The rear light can be swapped out for FIDLOCK’s PINCLIP saddle bag, or installed on your seat post.

PINCLIP Mounts:

FIDLOCK’S PINCLIP mounts provide a magnetic-mechanical fastening system. Magnets help guide the lights into the mounts, then the light securely snaps into position. The lights can be easily released from the mount with one hand. PINCLIP mounts offer a strong connection with no rattles, and can handle rough off-road terrain. Switching between accessories requires no tools.

If the front light is not needed, you can swap it for a POV camera and capture your ride. You’ll just need to add a PINCLIP Action Cam Mount (not included in the kit). The Action Cam Mount offers a GoPro-style interface for the camera itself, and it attaches your camera to the front light’s handlebar mount.

The rear light can be mounted directly to a seat tube. However, if you choose to use the saddle base to mount your rear light, you can also snap a PINCLIP seat bag into the mount when the light is not needed.

“At FIDLOCK, we’re always looking for ways to make everyday interactions with equipment simpler,” said Andreas Schulz, Marketing Director. “The PINCLIP Light System is more than just another set of bike lights. It’s about giving riders the flexibility to switch between lighting, an action camera, or a saddle bag quickly and securely, using the same mounting system.”

PINCLIP Front Light:

The new PINCLIP front light provides a 100 lumen/50 Lux output via a single OSRAM LED bulb, offering visibility up to 200m. The light is weatherproof and shock-resistant, and measures 43 x 52 x 108 mm.

The front light features High/Medium/Low settings. Run times are 5 hours (high), 12 hours (medium), or 22 hours (low). A battery level indicator on the light shows how much power you have left.

The front light is powered by a rechargeable Li-ion 2600 mAh battery, which charges via USB-C. A full charge takes five hours. The battery is also replaceable, due to incoming regulations in Europe.

The front light mount is secured to your handlebar with a ratchet strap and a dial to snug it up. The reversible PINCLIP interface gives you the option of running the light above or below your handlebar. This offers versatility for different handlebar setups, or bars already crowded with add-ons. The handlebar mount fits bars with diameters from 22.2-40 mm.

PINCLIP Rear Light:

FIDLOCK’s PINCLIP rear light uses three LEDs to output 4cd (candelas) in steady mode, but brightens to 16cd when it’s acting as a brake light. This light operates in a steady mode unless its acceleration sensor activates the brake light function. Dimensions for the rear light are 38x38x33mm, and it is both weatherproof and shock resistant.

The rear light includes a rechargeable 300 mAh battery, which provides five hours of run time. The battery charges in two hours via USB-C. The light has a battery level indicator, so you know when you’re getting low.  

This light either mounts directly to a seat tube or snaps into a PINCLIP saddle base. The seat tube mount is secured with a ratchet strap, which fits post diameters from 22-38.6mm. The PINCLIP saddle base bolts onto the rear part of your seat rails.

Pricing/Availability:

The PINCLIP Light System will initially be available as a complete set only, including the front light, rear light, mounting bases, a saddle base adapter, and a USB-C charging cable. MSRP for the kit is $99.99 (at the time of publication, the set is currently on sale for $79.99).

The system will be available in the USA around the end of November. FIDLOCK plans to offer the front and rear lights individually in the future.

fidlock.us

entry.title: How Primož Roglič Went From the Brink of Retirement to Signing With NSN in Days

entry.title: Best gravel bike tyres 2026 and how to choose the right ones
entry.content:
Cyclist
Best gravel bike tyres 2026 and how to choose the right ones

There’s a lot to consider when choosing the best gravel bike tyre for where you ride and we’re here to help to demystify the process. There’s no one gravel bike tyre that’s best for all surfaces and in all conditions though, so there’s a range of factors you need to weigh up when choosing a gravel bike tyre.

There’s a lot more detail about how to choose lower down the page, but key considerations are the surfaces on which you spend most of the time, the conditions and your level of experience and handling confidence. In general, gravel bikes come fitted with mixed condition tyres, but a dry condition tyre may roll faster, while a wet condition tyre will add extra grip on muddy trails.

You need to choose your tyre width, tread pattern and tyre pressure to match the conditions, along with deciding whether to set up tubeless. Your tyres also need to fit in your gravel bike’s frame, possibly with room for a layer of mud for winter riding.

Below is our choice of the best gravel bike tyres across a range of surface conditions, based on our experience of riding a large number of gravel bikes in a variety of conditions.

Our pick of the best gravel bike tyres

Dry condition gravel bike tyres

  • Pirelli Cinturato Gravel H: RRP £65
  • Continental Terra Speed: RRP £70
  • Challenge Gravel Grinder: RRP £50
  • Teravail Cannonball: RRP £70
  • Schwalbe G-One Allround: RRP £45

Mixed condition gravel bike tyres

  • WTB Riddler: RRP £60
  • Hutchinson Touareg: RRP £45
  • Maxxis Ravager: RRP £50
  • Vittoria Terreno T50: RRP £55

Wet condition gravel bike tyres

  • Teravail Rutland: RRP £70
  • Pirelli Cinturato Gravel M: RRP £65
  • WTB Resolute: RRP £60

Why trust Cyclist‘s advice?

Here at Cyclist, we’ve been reviewing the best gravel bikes right since their emergence over a decade ago. Over that time, there’s been an explosion in gravel bike options and we’ve witnessed the increased differentiation of gravel race bikes and gravel adventure bikes, with all-road bikes thrown in for good measure.

Gravel bike tyres too have seen a large increase in options available for all surfaces. We’ve ridden a huge range, both in the conditions for which each was designed and on surfaces that test their limits and reveal their vulnerabilities. We know our gravel bike tyres and can help you to choose the right tyre for the conditions you encounter too.

The best dry condition gravel bike tyres

Pirelli Cinturato Gravel H

£65 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 35mm, 40mm, 45mm, 50mm x 700c; 45mm, 50mm x 650b

The Pirelli Cinturato H’s centre knobs are low and closely spaced, leading to a fast rolling tyre that’s specced on some gravel race bikes and all-road bikes. Pirelli says that its SpeedGrip compound is engineered for grip though and, once it gets muddy, there are prominent side knobs to bite into the substratum.

Continental Terra Speed

£70 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 35mm, 40mm, 45mm x 700c; 35mm, 40mm x 650b

Widely spaced, low profile knobs help the Terra Speed maintain, well, speed on a mix of less demanding surfaces, while still offering decent grip and mud-shedding. You can choose between black, tan and cream sidewalls, depending on how much post-ride cleaning you like to do.

Challenge Gravel Grinder

£50 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 33mm, 36mm, 38mm, 40mm, 42mm, 46mm x 700c; 46mm x 650b

Challenge sells the Gravel Grinder in multiple spec levels: Pro and Race, as well as tubed and tubeless formats. Widths available vary with these, but all have the same central file tread for faster rolling, paired with get-you-out-of-trouble side knobs. In a long-distance test, Emma rode the tyres to Tunisia, proving their durability.

Teravail Cannonball Gen 2

£70 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 40mm, 45mm, 50mm, 55mm x 700c; 2.2 x 32″

Teravail bills the Cannonball Gen 2 as a gravel race tyre, increasing the dimensions considerably over the first generation tyres and discontinuing the 650b option. There’s a 2.2 x 32in tyre too.

Its close, directional central tread keeps rolling resistance down, but there’s the grip from the side lugs to handle fast cornering. There are plenty of size options and two casing choices: light and supple or durable.

Schwalbe G-One Allround

£45 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 35mm, 40mm, 45mm, 57mm x 700c, 35mm, 40mm, 57mm, 65mm x 650b

There’s a huge range of sizes available for the Schwalbe G-One Allround, going up to really wide MTB-style tyres, plus three different casing/compound options and four sidewalls, including two with reflective strips. 650b is particularly well represented. Schwalbe bills the Allround tread as a good option for tarmac and light off-road use, making it a prime option for an all-road bike.

The best mixed condition gravel bike tyres

WTB Riddler

£60 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 37mm, 45mm x 700c

WTB is one of the biggest names in gravel bike tyres, with a wide range of treads to suit different needs. The Riddler’s closely spaced small apex knobs deliver speed on hard surfaces, while the more prominent side knobs help keep you rubber side down when things get muddy. A great all-rounder, although with limited width options. For damper conditions, the Raddler has a similar tread, just more aggressive.

Hutchinson Touareg

£45 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 40mm, 45mm, 50mm x 700c, 47mm x 650b

The Touareg has slightly more aggressive central lugs than the WTB Riddler, while its side lugs are less pronounced and more closely spaced. It works well on slightly less even, less dry surfaces than the Riddler, but isn’t quite as adept once things get properly muddy

Maxxis Ravager

£50 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 40mm, 45mm, 50mm x 700c

The Ravager is available in three widths and with two different casings. Maxxis uses increasingly aggressive, spaced out lugs as you reach the sides, offering grip when things get messy, while the central tread is closely spaced enough to roll well on harder surfaces.

Vittoria Terreno T50

£55 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 40mm, 45mm, 50mm, 55mm x 700c

Vittoria places the Terreno T50 as its mixed condition gravel bike tyre, somewhat more capable on mixed terrain than its T30, which was formerly named the Terreno Dry. There are four other Terreno tyres for increasingly tough conditions, as well as the T10 semi-slick for hardpack. The T50 has a classic mix of smaller central knobs and more aggressive side grip for softer surfaces and uses Vittoria’s signature graphene-containing compound. It’s available in four widths up to 55mm that suit modern trends in gravel bike tyres.

The best wet condition gravel bike tyres

Teravail Rutland Gen 2

£70 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 40mm, 45mm, 50mm x 700c

Named for the surface conditions, not the UK county, the second generation Teravail Rutland is claimed to be designed for large and loose gravel. Everything’s well spaced, from the central tread through the transition lugs to the staggered side lugs, and designed to give you grip when things get coarse or muddy and there’s an updated casing for improved efficiency and fashionably wide options.

Pirelli Cinturato Gravel M

£65 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 35mm, 40mm, 45mm, 50mm x 700c; 45mm, 50mm x 650b

The Gravel M takes Pirelli’s SpeedGrip compound and applies it to a tread with large, well-spaced knobs at the sides and a close central tread for decent rolling resistance, although still with the depth for grip. There’s a wide range of sizes, to cover you whether you prefer a wider tyre that floats over damp surfaces or a narrow tyre to cut into them and maybe reach firmer ground below and to cater for non-UCI sanctioned cyclocross races.

WTB Resolute

£60 | Buy here

  • Sizes available: 42mm, 50mm x 700c

WTB bills its Resolute tyre as an all-season option that will roll well when it’s dry on the closer central tread but transition without fuss to messy conditions, thanks to the well-spaced side knobs. There are just two widths on offer, but they cater for the trend to wider gravel tyres thanks to the 50mm option.

How do I choose the right gravel bike tyres?

There is little doubt that choosing the right tyres for the terrain and conditions – and let’s not forget that all-important tyre pressure too (we’ll come back to that later), can make or break a ride.

With countless options available for gravel bikes, how do you choose which tyres are best for you?

You need to begin by asking yourself a few questions. Starting with: on what surfaces are you going to ride most of the time?

It’s worth pointing out from the get-go that there is no one gravel tyre that can be all things to all riders and for all conditions, and so when it comes to choosing the best gravel tyres there is almost always likely to be a level of compromise somewhere that must be expected and accepted.

The best advice, then, is to choose the gravel tyre best suited to where you spend the majority of your time on the bike. There’s no point dragging a set of hefty knobblies around if you barely venture off the beaten path, and when you do it’s only on well-established and hard-packed surfaces.

By the same virtue, expect a white-knuckle ride if you get a bit ambitious with your route finding and your tyres are not well-suited to the task.

Your level of off road competence/experience will inevitably play a part in your tyre choice too. Less experienced riders will probably feel more comfortable erring on the side of caution and opting for a tyre that will offer a more confident feel on loose or slippery, muddy terrain, and accept the impact on rolling speed on hard-packed, smoother trails or roads.

The two biggest decisions to make are width and tread pattern.

Tyre width

Tyre width directly influences a number of factors. Wider tyres have a larger air volume and so will potentially offer more cushioning (comfort) as that bigger pillow of air is more capable of isolating the rider from the bumps.

Crucial to understand here, though, is the relationship between air volume and pressure. Having a greater volume of air inside the tyre facilitates riding with a lower pressure without such high risk of damage to the tyre carcass or rim from impacts.

Another key consideration is how this influences the tyre’s ability to provide grip. A wider tyre has a larger surface contact patch in the first instance – putting more rubber in contact with the ground to aid grip. Riding at a lower pressure enables the tyre to deform around objects – tree roots, stones, rocks, etc, which also massively enhances its ability to provide grip.

So, with a number of significant benefits, why don’t we just use wider tyres all the time? Well, there are some downsides to consider. Increased weight is probably the most important, especially as tyres are a large rotating mass, which means their weight has a significant influence on bike handling (steering, braking and acceleration). There is also the fact that a wider tyre is more likely to increase drag (although not always!).

In the 700c wheel size the market seems to have settled on the range between 40-45mm as the most common for gravel tyres, although tyres of around 50mm to 55mm width are appearing, along with gravel bikes with the frame clearance to fit them. Mountain bike tyres (with widths measured in inches) also become an option with these wider clearances.

There are still many frames that do not have clearance for anything larger than 700x42mm. This is something that should also be considered. Make sure you check what your specific frame will accept prior to purchasing new treads.

Wheel size

Smaller 650b is an old French size that was popularised by touring cyclists, but was given a rebirth (as 27.5”) on mountain bikes. It flourished on gravel bikes a few years ago, but has largely gone out of fashion as tyre clearance for 700c wheels has increased.

Why use a smaller wheel size? The thinking is this: a 650b wheel (smaller diameter) can accommodate a larger tyre (e.g. 47-51mm) and still have an almost equal overall rolling circumference to, say, a 700x40mm.

This does depend a lot on the individual tyre brand and rim combinations but as a rough guide this will be the case. Therefore, importantly, the geometry of the bike will not be affected by switching between two wheel sizes, but the performance of the tyres will change dramatically, due to the reasons discussed above regarding volume, pressure and grip, and result in a very different riding experience.

The latest trend is to even larger wheels than 700c though, with 32-inch gravel bikes making inroads. The supersized wheels are claimed to increase rollover of trail obstacles and to help hold momentum, as well as offering a smoother ride.

Tyre tread pattern

Generally speaking, gravel tyres only have a very small amount of tread working to help us, so that means the tread pattern is really crucial to the ride characteristics. There is much more to consider for an off-road tyre versus a road-only tyre.

A common mistake is to assume big knobbly treads must be the most grippy tyres. Not so. A very knobbly tread pattern doesn’t automatically mean it will offer the best grip in all circumstances. For instance, if you ride on very rocky terrain, a tyre with large aggressive knobs will not be able to ‘bite’ into the surface and so will not be able to work and provide grip optimally.

In fact it may provide less grip compared to a less aggressive tread design, which will not flex as much, plus puts more rubber surface area in contact with the ground.

Knobbly treads will work best when the ground is soft, as only then can the tread get the necessary ‘purchase’ into the terrain.

Soft ground conditions also throw up another consideration, that of how well a tread can ‘clear’ itself. If mud simply packs into a tyre tread (basically reducing its effectiveness and adding a lot of weight) but does not clear, it can be a big disadvantage to its performance, so a well-spaced tread design is preferable if your trail conditions have a lot of thick, claggy mud (e.g clay).

More loamy or sandy soils are likely to clear much better, and so tyre clogging is much less of an issue.

Gravel tyre categories

It will help to narrow down the choices, if we group tyres into the following sub-categories:

Dry condition gravel tyres

Ideal for a mix of tarmac and predominantly smooth, well-made and hard-packed trails e.g. forest gravel roads, disused railways etc.

For many riders the ‘fast rolling’ element of a gravel tyre is still going to be very important as gravel riding is still about the sense of speed, just over more varied terrain, and definitely on tarmac at times too.

In this scenario a tread pattern with an almost continual patch of rubber created by a very closely spaced tread pattern will roll faster than a tyre with more spaced out knobs. It doesn’t have to be a solid strip, just closely spaced – almost connected – in the mid section.

A chevron pattern is quite effective as are file-treads to create fast rolling tyres and a stable feel for when the rider is splitting their time between road and off-road.

Some edge grip is useful for off-road excursions. That’s why many gravel tyres use a dense central portion but with low volume side knobs. It’s a good way to be able to do more with a single tyre choice.

Mixed condition gravel tyres

Mixed condition tyres are designed to offer a little more grip when it’s wet, without sacrificing speed too much in the dry and on tarmac. They tend to be the tyres that come fitted to gravel bikes when they are sold. Surfaces will be loose at times, but mostly hard ground e.g well-trodden paths, hard-packed sand and well-used forest trails during the summer months.

To better cope with a variety of off-road trail conditions it’s advisable to move to a more separated tread pattern, with individual blocks or knobs, which allows them to work independently and clear mud better.

By spacing the tread pattern it will sacrifice a little rolling speed as we move from riding ‘on’ the tyre towards being ‘in’ the tyre. The separated ‘blocks’ have room to flex and therefore achieve grip on a given surface.

The size and height of the block is what is most crucial in influencing how a tyre performs. Too tall and it will flex too much, causing an unstable feel and a lot of additional drag on harder surfaces. Too chunky and it may feel too rigid, and of course will add weight too.

Tyre design is so much about getting the balance right. Dual-compound tyres are one solution, whereby a firmer rubber durometer in the mid-section will help reduce rolling resistance whilst a softer rubber compound can be used on the shoulder/edges of the tread for improved cornering grip.

Wet condition gravel tyres

Designed for grip and tread clearance in soft terrain, e.g. mud, grass, wet condition tyres have the most aggressive tread. The softer the terrain the more a less-populated knobbly tread design will work in your favour, with pronounced knobbles, spaced to bite into the ground.

The knobs are essentially working alone. The spaced tread pattern will shed dirt much more easily, which is important in conditions where the soil is claggy and would otherwise clog up the tread. The tread cannot perform optimally if it is clogged, so a key thing on this kind of tyre design for manufacturers to figure out is the exit points for the dirt. Dirt and mud must be able to be pushed out if the tread is to stay clear.

Softer compound rubber is really useful in tyres designed for muddy/wet conditions as it adds flex and improves grip, but as always there’s a balance to be struck. If the knobs flex too much this can make the ride feel really squirmy on harder surfaces.

Often this type of tyre is best kept for muddy, wet off-road rides, as the nature of the tread patterns make them less ideal for more varied terrains, and hard/fast conditions.

One for all?

As already mentioned it’s unlikely there could ever be a ‘Holy Grail’ of tyres that can do everything well, but if you could only own one gravel tyre (one pair, obviously) my choice would be the WTB Resolute in 700 x 42: this tyre is a superb all-rounder, very capable and able to make a decent fist of practically any surface/trail conditions. It’s not so wide that it won’t fit in most gravel bike frames though, even on gravel bike wheels with wider rims.

It’s also worth considering a swap-out to a faster-rolling tyre for use on dry summer trails and a more aggressive tread if you often ride on muddy surfaces through the winter. A mullet set-up with a gripper front and faster rear tyre may also add extra speed.

Tyre pressure

Checking your tyre pressure might be about the simplest mechanical task on a bicycle but it’s also one of the most important. We simply can’t talk tyre choices without also talking PSI.

Here’s why…

Tyre pressure (PSI/Bar) affects grip, comfort and rolling speed, and all of these are intrinsically linked. In our experience almost all riders run too much pressure.

A tyre has to deform to perform. It sounds like a cliché but it really is true. But there’s clearly a balance to be struck. Too low and a tyre will feel mushy and rob you of speed, and also runs the risk of sidewall damage plus air burping (if using tubeless) or pinch flats (if using inner tubes).

Too firm and a tyre will bounce over objects as opposed to flexing and conforming to surface changes which is the best way to achieve grip, plus it will feel much less comfortable.

For most riders there’s often a bit of a light bulb moment when the realisation comes that tyre pressure is hugely influential to a tyre’s performance, and especially that you can use much lower pressures than you might think, especially if you use tubeless tyres.

Tyre pressure tips

Correct tyre pressure is not a one time deal. Trail conditions, body weight, riding style, plus the weight of anything you plan to ride with (luggage etc) must all be taken into account.

Don’t just rely on the pump’s pressure gauge. These are often less accurate versus a dedicated tyre pressure gauge.

An electric mini pump is small enough to take in a pocket or small bag and makes it possible to experiment with tyre pressures on the trail. Many include a digital gauge.

Tubeless tyres facilitate use of lower pressures without the risk of pinch flats and with reduced rolling resistance, while tubeless sealant will help to heal small holes and a tubeless repair kit should take care of the rest.

Rocky or very rough terrain generally requires more tyre pressure than soft terrain where the risk of impacts (and subsequent rim/tyre damage) is considerably less.

Narrower tyres generally require more pressure to avoid pinch flats, sidewall damage and potential rim damage.

Harder tyres do not make for faster-rolling tyres. Rolling resistance is a combination of many factors and in many cases a lower tyre pressure leads to improved performance overall versus an over-inflated tyre.

The post Best gravel bike tyres 2026 and how to choose the right ones appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: ENVO Announces Their First Full Suspension eMTB – The Affordable M50
entry.content:
ENVO is based in Vancouver, B.C., home to the world-famous North Shore trails where trail riding evolved into freeride with ladder bridges, big drops, and lots of gnarly terrain. Until now, ENVO has mostly produced commuter ebikes, but since many of their staff ride trails, a full-suspension eMTB has now joined ENVO’s lineup.

The M50 is an accessibly priced eMTB. It features the company’s own motor and battery, X-Fusion and DNM suspension, MX wheels, and a wide-range 9-speed drivetrain. The frame is available in two sizes. These specs won’t blow away anyone familiar with top-of-the-line eMTBs, but the M50’s price presents a reasonable option for those who are curious about stepping into assisted trail riding.

ENVO M50 – Key Specs:

The M50 is an all-mountain eMTB, featuring a hydroformed 6061-T6 aluminum frame. The frame offers 150mms of rear travel, and the bike comes with a 160mm X-Fusion fork. ENVO went with an MX wheelset for the M50, with no mention of full 29er compatibility.

It’s clear ENVO did their research on suspension linkages, as their first full-suspension eMTB is presented with leverage ratio, axle path, anti-squat, and anti-rise charts. That data reveals the M50’s four-bar linkage aims to deliver the same performance aspects as any of today’s high-end eMTBs.

ENVO says their linkage is designed for initial sensitivity, but gets progressive enough to resist hard impacts and bottom-outs. It also provides a slightly rearward axle path, which typically translates to very good absorption of sharper hits. Anti-squat was tuned to ensure maximized pedal efficiency when you’re in your lowest gears, but deeper in the travel it drops off to offer responsive suspension action. The M50’s anti-rise aims to keep your rear wheel planted under light or strong braking forces.  

The air-sprung rear shock is one component that reflects the M50’s price tag. It is made by a company I’m not familiar with called DNM. The shock features adjustable rebound and a two-position Open/Firm switch. It is tuned to provide plush sensitivity over small bumps and ample support against bigger impacts. The shock is a 210x55mm unit, so upgrading it is a possibility.

As for gearing, the M50 is equipped with a 9-speed Microshift drivetrain. The 9-speed cassette does offer a wide gear range (11-46t), but comparatively the ‘high-end standard’ 12-speed drivetrain provides lower gearing and finer increments. The M50 frame does use a Boost 148x12mm rear axle, so the bike could be upgraded to 12-speed (or even the supremely durable 11-speed Linkglide Shimano components).

One nice inclusion on the M50’s build is a 170mm travel dropper post. Something this frame lacks is a UDH-compatible dropout, instead using its own replaceable derailleur hanger. The frame also features a water bottle mount on the down tube, and the bike comes with an upper chain guide.

Drive System:

The M50 is assisted by an Ananda M230 Motor. This mid-drive motor uses both torque and cadence sensors to deliver pedal assist power up to 20mph.

The M230 motor provides 350W of power, which is not much compared to most full-powered eMTBs that crank out 750W… let alone many ‘lite’ or ‘SL’ class eMTBs that still offer more. Interestingly, the motor does produce 100Nm max torque, which is far more competitive with today’s high-end eMTBs.  

The motor is powered by ENVO’s 50 Series battery. It is a 48V, 15Ah lithium-ion battery offering 720Wh of capacity. The battery performs well in cold temperatures and has its own Battery Management System (BMS) to prevent overcharging or faults. This helps to ensure consistent performance and longevity. Fully charging the battery should take 6-8 hours. The bike’s max range is listed at a very optimistic 150 km, so it’s hard to say how that would translate to miles or elevation on MTB trails.  

The M50’s handlebar display unit has a color display and connects to the motor via Bluetooth. Since the M50’s electronics use CANBUS communication, the display can show you the status of your battery’s health and provide diagnostic info on top of the usual ride metrics. The battery and charger also communicate to ensure safe charging.

Geometry:

The M50 is available in two frame sizes – S/M and L/XL. ENVO says these options should fit riders from 5’2” to 6’4”. Given that most well-known eMTB brands would have three or four sizes covering that height range, I’d say ENVO is stretching a bit with only two.

Reach on the S/M is 440mm, and the L/XL grows considerably to 485mm. The M50’s 64° head angle is appropriate and up to date, and its 77° seat tube angle should offer a strong pedalling position. Rear ends for both frame sizes are 450mm. It might be nice to see two different rear ends, as 450mm is on the long side for the small frame and on the short side for the large. 

ENVO M50 Build Specs:

The M50 is an entry-level eMTB, so you won’t see many fancy brand names in the build spec. Components like rims, hubs, crank arms, grips, the dropper post and saddle, plus the display unit/controller are all from generic suppliers.

Some key components of the M50’s spec are an X-Fusion Trace 36 160mm fork and a DNM AO-38RC rear shock. The 1×9 drivetrain is comprised of Microshift’s Advent components.

Tektro handles stopping duties with a set of HD-M535 four-piston hydraulic disc brakes, on 203mm rotors front and rear. The rims are wrapped with WTB Trail Boss tires – 29×2.6” front and 27.5×2.4” rear. Up front, the M50 gets a 780mm-wide ZOOM handlebar with a 35mm clamp, and a pair of Wellgo flat pedals are included. For complete build specs, check out ENVO’s website.

MSRP for the ENVO M50 is $3,199 USD. Frame color options are maroon or aquatic.

envodrive.com

entry.title: Selle Royal Turns 70 with a See-Through Saddle and a Shrine to Failed Prototypes
entry.content:
Selle Royal just wrapped its “Nothing to hide” exhibition in London. It was a four-day pop-up that ran November 12-15 alongside Rouleur Live. It’s the centerpiece of the Italian saddle maker’s 70th anniversary. And yes, the theme is exactly what it sounds like: a brand airing its dirty laundry.

The star of the celebration is a limited-edition Lookin Evo with a transparent cover that lets you see the saddle’s inner structure and materials. It’s a collector’s piece, but Selle Royal says it’s meant for actual riding.

It’s also, let’s be honest, a saddle you can see right through, that lands somewhere between “engineering showcase” and “something you’d rather not discuss after a questionable gas-station burrito.” Or one of these tacos. Obviously, with the Stracciatella name, they’re going after the classic gelato flavor with shards of chocolate, but there’s something about that yellowish base that is odd, to say the least.

Selle Royal is selling it in limited quantities, exclusively on its own website, in special anniversary packaging.

The Exhibition

The exhibition took the “Nothing to hide” idea literally. Visitors got a look at failed prototypes and materials that didn’t behave the way engineers expected, which is a refreshing change from an industry that normally only shows you the one thing that worked.

Also on display were artworks from Università Iuav di Venezia design students made from leftover production materials, transparent Stracciatella saddles on custom steel structures, and armchairs made from Stracciatella foam. Yes, you could sit on the foam made from saddle scraps.

Stracciatella is Selle Royal’s tech for recovering production waste and turning it into new saddle padding. The Lookin Evo’s development also used life cycle assessment to guide design and material choices, which ties the whole thing to the brand’s environmental work.

70 Years Supporting Your Booty

The brand has been around for 70 years. Riccardo Bigolin founded Selle Royal in 1956 in the province of Vicenza. By 1960, most of its output was heading to European markets. Along the way came polyurethane foams, Royal Vacuum technology, and Royalgel in 1990. The mission today is still “Support Cyclists.”

Seventy years in the saddle business, and the big flex is “look at all the stuff that didn’t work.” Honestly, I respect that approach. I mean, most brands would rather bury the failures in a landfill than put them in a gallery with a DJ. Just don’t expect me to explain the see-through cover to my riding pals.

SelleRoyal.com

entry.title: Aero vs all-round race bike: Save on both with Ribble this Black Friday
entry.content:
Cyclist
Aero vs all-round race bike: Save on both with Ribble this Black Friday

These days shopping for a new bike can be tricky. With so many different options across more genres than ever, finding what’s right for your kind of riding isn’t easy.

If you’re craving speed on the road, whether that be in levelling up your current setup, taking part in sportives, doing actual races or simply riding faster day to day, the choice boils down to two types of road bike: an aero road bike or more of an all-rounder – lighter in weight but slightly less aerodynamic.

That goes some way to make the choice easier on paper, but do you actually know which of the two would make your ride faster? To answer that, let’s take a look at the pros and cons of aero and all-rounder bikes separately, and how they compare to bikes that attempt to balance the two.

Which is faster and where?

By breaking down the different kind of riding you might do – or want to do, if you’re preparing for a big challenge – you can then make an informed decision on what your next bike should be (and read on for specific suggestions on a pair of highly capable models).

One big change in the bike industry over the past few years is the sidelining of the outright ‘lightweight’ road category at the pro level. That’s largely down to brands now being able to find enough general weight savings to get all-round race bikes down to the UCI minimum weight limit of 6.8kg without the need for major aero sacrifices. Yes, you can still get lighter, but not while staying within the UCI rules, and the latest all-rounder bikes are as light as previous generations of outright ‘lightweight’ bikes anyway.

Conversely, while you might also see the top pros riding aero bikes on mountain stages, that’s because the speeds they’re hitting on the WorldTour’s toughest climbing tests are high enough for aerodynamics to still make a difference.

The consensus from extensive real-world testing is that aerodynamics generally starts to come into play at around 15kmh, meaning that from those speeds, the scales start to tip in the favour of aero bikes and kit over lighter weight equipment; and the faster the rider the more difference it makes. In terms of gradient, it’s generally on gradients of around 6% that weight starts to gain in importance – though that is still dependent on speed.

With all that in mind, for most regular riders a fully flat ride will be quicker on an aero bike than on a slightly lighter but slightly less aero all-round race bike.

From there, the hillier the ride the quicker the speed balance tilts in favour of the all-rounder. But where is the sweet spot?

If you’re doing big days in the mountains, the weight savings of an all-round race bike is what you need. Testing has shown that a 100km ride with a big climb – such as a Cyclist magazine Big Ride – is considerably faster with that kind of bike.

The same could be said for tough British sportives such as the Fred Whitton. but unless you’re seeking out all the hardest climbs in your area, most riders averaging 30kmh or more will gain more from an aero bike.

It’s important to note that spec plays a massive part in this too, and a bit of extra investment often goes a long way in saving weight or adding aero when it comes to wheels, groupset or handlebars.

Something else to consider is that part of the gains that many aero bikes provide come from putting the rider in a more aggressive riding position, reducing the area that has to cut through the wind. For many people this can become uncomfortable over long rides, so unless speed is your only concern, all-round race bikes generally – though not always – put the rider in a more sustainable position.

You should also factor rolling resistance into your equations, with tyre width playing a big role in how smoothly you roll over the tarmac. That again depends on where you actually ride, with poor road quality – something British riders will be all too familiar with – making a wider tyre a highly recommended spec choice. For smooth tarmac, 28-30mm is ideal, otherwise 32mm tyres set up tubeless allow you to run lower pressures without the risk of pinch flats, helping you roll over most lumps and bumps.

Which race bike is right for me?

Taking all of those considerations forward, each bike type still offers many options, but British brand Ribble seeks to make the choice easy.

If speed is what you need, its ULTRA-AERO and ULTRA-RACE models tick all the boxes that road riders could need.

The ULTRA-AERO SL R is Ribble’s all-out fastest bike, with the frame design and component choice heavily influenced by extensive wind-tunnel testing to make it the only choice for flat and fast riding. The super-aero component list is headlined by Ribble’s ULTRA-AERO handlebars and full bike weight ranges from 8.2kg to 9.3kg, depending on spec.

For hill-seekers, the Ribble ULTRA-RACE comes close to the lowest limits of the UCI’s rulebook for racing, with the lightest spec choices coming in at just 7kg in a medium size, and the frame itself comes in at just 775g.

The breadth of those two bikes’ ranges includes both pro-race level builds and more affordable options for those looking to level up their riding within a more restrictive budget.

Save up to £1,550 on Ribble’s aero and racing bikes this Black Friday

Rest assured, though: affordable doesn’t mean slow, and with Ribble’s Black Friday discounts, the ULTRA-RACE and ULTRA-AERO SL R are at more accessible prices than ever.

Until 11.59pm on Tuesday 1st December, you can get a black colourway ULTRA-RACE specced with Shimano 105 Di2 for just £2,799 – a saving of £650 – or with Ultegra Di2 for just £3,599 – a huge saving of £1,050. You’ll struggle to find that kind of value for a racing calibre bike equipped with electronic shifting anywhere else.

The Ribble ULTRA-AERO SL R has similarly mouth-watering prices, with the ULTRA-AERO SL R 105 Di2 reduced to £2,549 – a saving of £1,200 – and the Ultegra Di2 build a massive £1,550 cheaper at £3,199. Or you can opt for the range-topping ULTRA-AERO SL R Dura-Ace Di2 for £5,549, saving a phenomenal £1,900.

These prices are exclusive to Black Friday, so whether you’re a speed demon in the market for an upgrade or you’re eyeing up a dream Christmas present for a fast loved one, you’ll need to be quick with this one.

entry.title: Brooks Opens its Special Edition Saddle Vault with Unearthed Collection
entry.content:
In 2025, the team at Brooks Unearthed an assortment of leather saddle tops in its factory from a variety of manufacturing processes and periods. Rather than see them go to waste, the UK saddle makers made them into a small, vibrant, limited release batch of leather saddles.

Each Unearthed saddle is the result of a small discovery moment inside the brand’s Smethwick factory: leather tops produced over years and decades of saddle-making, each one bearing the character of the period and technique that shaped it. Rather than discard or recycle these unique pieces, Brooks’ craftspeople carefully built each one into a finished saddle, hand-finished to the same Brooks standards that define every model it makes.

Check it out at Brooks Unearthed.

entry.title: From the Coast to Ayacucho: Crossing the Spine of the Andes – Ryan Wilson
entry.content:
After a multi-year trip across Asia, Ryan Wilson returns to the Andes Mountains to link up new routes he’s had his sights set on for years.  Follow along as he climbs from Peru’s rugged desert coast to the high Andes and to Ayacucho…

If you’ve spent much time perusing The Radavist over the last decade, you know by now that I’m a huge fan of the riding in the Andes. At this point, it feels kind of like a home away from home. There are few places on earth that have this combination of dramatic landscapes mixed with quiet roads, fascinating culture, and incredible camping opportunities.

Every few years, I’ll find myself scrolling over near South America on the map toward some of the countless routes that I’ve mapped out here over the years, but have yet to ride, and my mind starts to formulate how I could link them up to form a new route.

After a few years in Asia, where it’s very rare that I can speak much of the local language of the country I’m in, it’s also a nice break from relying on Google Translate for everything, and it’s great to be able to strike up a conversation with just about anyone, even if my Español got a little rusty while I was away.

Starting from the Bottom

The zone from central Peru, down toward Northern Patagonia, is about as good as it gets for bike travel, as you can link up thousands of kilometers of quiet, scenic roads virtually the entire way. This would be the stretch of South America that I’d focus on for this trip, starting in a coastal city just south of Lima, Peru, called Chincha Alta.

I would forgo the classic Peru Divide on this trip and instead link up some of the bustling Spanish colonial cities that are tucked into the high Andes. But first, as any good Peru trip starts, I had to ascend all the way up from that desert coastline to well over 16,000ft in one big steady climb.

This could seem like some form of torture to start a trip with 3 days of nonstop uphill, but these are some of my favorite parts of Peru. You get to ride through many different zones, from the first barren folds of the Andes, as cacti and trees slowly fill the valleys, on the way to the more fertile zones up around 10,000ft, and then up into the frigid, windswept highlands where there are more llamas than people.

The Desert Coast

I left the chaotic streets of Chincha Alta on the day of the weekly street market, with my bags full of any supplies I might need for the next 2-3 days. There would be some settlements along the way, but I didn’t really have an idea about what I might find in local shops. Sometimes it’s as barren as Coke and some various cookies.

The area right near the coast is reasonably cool, but as you make your way into the lower Andes, that sea breeze disappears, and the equatorial sun begins to cook. I was thankful that some of the first settlements had small tiendas with big water bottles stuffed into frigid coolers, something of a rarity in Peru.

These parts of the country are also home to many petroglyphs, some of which are up to 4,000 years old, like at Petroglifos de Huancor, where around 200 engraved rocks can be found, only a short walk from the road.

The broken pavement road continued gradually up the valley until I spotted some trees down by the river shortly after sunset. It was just far enough away from the road that I decided to set up camp. At this altitude, it would be one of the only mild camping nights of my entire time in Peru. Oftentimes, you have to sprint into your sleeping bag and close up the tent right when the sun goes down in the Peruvian Andes, so I tried to savor this one.

The Temperate Zone

By the time I reached roughly 10,000 feet of altitude the next day, there were more farms and villages popping up across the hillsides. When asked where I was going, people were constantly confused as I said Ayacucho. They would insist that I’d gone the wrong way and should turn around, go all the way back to Chincha, and take another valley that was further to the south. I would reassure them that I took this road to avoid that traffic, but to them it made more sense for me to descend back 10,000 ft of elevation and re-climb all of that along a main road, I guess to avoid some dirt roads in the high mountains. “Me gustan las trochas” (I like the dirt roads), I’d say with a smile as they squeeze my tires.

I spent a day in a small accommodation in Villa de Arma to help with my acclimatization a bit. It wasn’t much, but it would have to get me through the next stretch, which would find me climbing well over 16,000 ft and camping at very high altitudes.

Into the Puna

For a (mostly) paved road, I was shocked by how little traffic there was. On the slow and steady climb up to the high puna, I don’t recall seeing more than a couple of vehicles. Most of the company I shared on my way up was in the form of alpacas, roaming around, chomping on vegetation, and looking on with skepticism as I rode by.

At one of the first high points on the route, a view to the north opened up, with my first sight of snow-covered mountains in the distance. Shortly after, I came across a flat spot tucked next to a small lake and a ridgeline at 4650m or 15,256ft and decided to set up camp. I knew it was going to be a long night at this altitude. The cold is one thing, but the main issue is trying to sleep properly without proper acclimatization, which makes it very challenging to fall asleep and stay asleep, despite being pretty well spent from the climb. I’d get used to the lack of air pretty soon, though, because the next few days would all be spent at these lofty heights.

Off the Beaten Track

The morning brought sweet relief from the cold, but the sun didn’t last long. By the time I was packed up, the clouds were already moving in. I had some ups and downs across the desolate landscape before I turned off the “main road”, if you want to call it that, and headed for a shortcut through a canyon.

Frigid rain began to trickle down as I descended into the canyon. Slowly, the road was looking less and less used as I passed through a small, seemingly deserted mining area. I came up to an open gate, with no one around, but I wasn’t going to wait for somebody to come along and tell me to turn around, so I kept heading downhill.

With every bend, I was becoming more skeptical that this road would even connect to where I was trying to go. It was heading down into some very rugged terrain, and I struggled to spot a recent-looking tire track on the road’s surface. But I was committed now, having descended far too much to consider turning back.

Thankfully, the track squeezed through the narrow canyon and came out the other side to a pristine dirt road. Just a couple of kilometers further, I came across a few shepherds who waved me down, telling me in a serious tone that this was a private mining access road, despite the lack of signage. They assumed I took a wrong turn, but when I told them the name of the village I was trying to get to, about 25km down the road, their concern level dropped, and they sent me on my way with some info about the route.

In the clear now, after going through the exit gate, I climbed up from the low point a bit and scrambled up a hillside toward a hidden-from-the-road flat spot and called it a night.

Over the Top

The first real village I’d seen in a couple of days was Santa Ana. Of course it was a Sunday, so the place was deserted, and the only restaurant in town was closed. But I was fortunate enough to meet a local man who must have felt bad when I nearly shed a tear as he told me about the restaurant, because he went to his home and tracked me down with some freshly boiled potatoes and an avocado, which really complemented the saltine crackers and cookies that I found at the small shop well.

There was one more climb left to tackle before I’d be on the biggest descent of the trip so far. But first, I’d have to make it to over 4960m / 16,273ft.

The road gradually twisted and turned its way up another mountain. Ominous clouds gathered nearby, with light painting the mountainsides. It was looking pretty iffy as I summited the pass, but thankfully I was heading the opposite direction with nearly 60 kilometers of descent in front of me before I’d reach the town of Lircay, the biggest I’d seen since leaving Chincha Alta.

It was the perfect spot to rest up for a couple of days and catch the local festivities where locals dress up in traditional costumes and whip each other with ropes.

The Road to the Big City

From Lircay, I had a shade over two days of riding to get to Ayacucho. I mapped a route over the most remote road I could find, and immediately found myself sheltering in a small village when a rare thunder-snowstorm hit. It started with lightning and hail, but gradually morphed into full-on snow as I hid under a small metal roof next to a house. A local man joined me who was riding up the road on a motorcycle.

I ended up waiting it out for around an hour and a half before getting back on the road just as the sun broke through the clouds for the last bit of light of the day. Needless to say, it was a very frosty night in the tent.

A roller coaster of ups and downs led me straight toward one of my favorite cities in Peru, Ayacucho. It happens to also be one of the very few places where you can reliably get one of my favorite meals in Peru, the Puca Picante. It’s a dish with a vibrant red sauce made primarily from blended beets and peanuts to go with the usual Andean staples of rice, potatoes, red onions, and crispy pork. It’s local to this region, so when I rolled into the city around lunchtime, I searched around all of the almuerzo spots to track one down. It was a perfect way to cap off my first couple of weeks back in the Andes.

﻿

Ryan is supported by:

See the Prospector frame he’s touring on at Tumbleweed Bikes, the bags he uses at Revelate Designs, and the CrossPeak 1 shelter he sleeps in at Hyperlite Mountain Gear.

The post From the Coast to Ayacucho: Crossing the Spine of the Andes appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Mazda Teams Up with NICA as the Youth Cycling Organization’s First Non-Endemic Partner
entry.content:
Automotive sponsors and partnerships are fairly common in professional cycling, with vehicle brands supporting teams and events around the world. Until just recently, that has not been the case for youth cycling, at least not in the U.S. Just a few months ago, NICA announced an exciting new partnership with Mazda North American Operations, naming Mazda as its Official Automotive and SUV Partner nationwide and the Presenting Sponsor of NICA’s Regional Events.

Until now, NICA has relied on the generous support from industry partners, including lead partners like SRAM/RockShox and Trek, and platinum partners, like Shimano and Specialized. In what many would consider a watershed moment for NICA, Mazda is the first non-endemic partner for the world’s largest — and growing — youth mountain biking association. And this multi-year agreement runs through the end of 2029.

“At NICA, everything we do is in service of youth development — building confidence, community, and a lifelong love of the sport in a positive, welcoming environment for every rider and family. Partners like Mazda, who invest at every level and for years to come, help us grow that community and reach even more young people who deserve a place to belong.“

-Amanda Carey, NICA President

This new partnership began in September, with Mazda signing on as both a lead partner and the presenting sponsor of NICA’s Regional Events. This fall, that included Eastern (Oct. 24-25), Central (Nov. 7-8), and the first Western Regionals (Nov. 14-15). As mentioned in my NICA article last week, I was invited to St. George, Utah, to attend the inaugural Western Regionals, which included road-tripping in a new Mazda CX-50 Meridian Edition (more on this later). I also had the opportunity to chat with folks from NICA and Mazda about their new multi-year agreement.

When I arrived at NICA Western Regionals two weekends ago, the Mazda presence was quite obvious. I was ushered through the parking lot up to a special Mazda owners parking area right up front. A nice perk, and certainly not the kind of treatment that I’m accustomed to. In the expo area, Mazda was set up between SRAM’s massive tractor-trailer rig and the Trek booth.

Mazda had an adventure-ready CX-50 on display for folks to check out and get inside. They were also drawing a crowd with a Trek SuperCaliber giveaway. Outside of the expo area, Mazda had two of its wrapped Trek-Unbroken team cars lining the racecourse.  

Mazda and Cycling

NICA is in the business of getting more kids on bikes, while Mazda is in the business of selling vehicles. To some, it might seem like an unlikely partnership, but Mazda has recently gotten more involved in the cycling world. In fact, Mazda entered into a multi-year partnership with Trek’s off-road race teams in August of this year. That includes the Trek-Unbroken XC and DH teams, the Trek Driftless gravel program, and various Trek events.

With the NICA partnership, Mazda is clearly expanding that involvement to youth cycling. I spoke with Matthew Rhoads, Mazda’s Programs Manager of Retail Digital Marketing, who explained the brand’s interest in youth mountain biking. He said, “As an organization, we identified the cycling community as one that our owners and fans are participating in. Mazda also has an ongoing commitment to youth sports. This partnership with NICA allows us to show up and support both communities.”

Shared Values

Rhoads was quick to point out that Mazda also knows it needs to show up intelligently and authentically. He said, “We want people to recognize that we share their values, like getting kids outdoors and promoting active lifestyles, and we want to lift the NICA organization because they share those values, too.” 

Kate Punderson, NICA’s VP of Development, shared a similar sentiment, saying, “We’re not going to just partner with anybody, especially a non-endemic; the values really need to align. So we did a lot of research around Mazda’s values and who they are as a company, and we found that we’re clearly aligned.”

The partnership is only in its early stages, but it’s already making quite an impression, and Mazda’s booth in the expo and presence out on the course definitely got people talking. NICA’s Kate Punderson told me that “people are so excited for NICA to have been able to develop this partnership; they see it as a whole new door opening. The kids think it’s so cool, too.” She went on to say, “I think there’s a lot of pride there, like the whole community feels proud to have been noticed. It’s validating.”

And while getting the Mazda brand and vehicles noticed is the point, Rhoads made it clear that there’s more to it than that. “If you have a brand come into your space with cool-looking wrapped cars, that’s going to make an impression,” said Rhoads, “but beyond that, we’re not just supporting a few athletes; instead we’re showing up in a way that provides support and actual value to the community.”

Mutual Benefit

Of course, any sponsorship or partnership needs to be mutually beneficial. Mazda is obviously in the business of selling cars, and partnering with NICA strikes me as a pretty smart business decision. It’s one thing to sponsor a professional team, but this partnership has broad reach along with the potential for meaningful impact. According to Rhoads, “Mazda has over 540 dealers and NICA has 33 leagues nationwide, which cover roughly 90 percent of our business. This gives us a platform for our dealers to be involved across the U.S. and provide value to their communities.” 

NICA, on the other hand, is in the business of getting more kids on bikes, and Mazda’s financial support directly supports that mission. Not only are they the presenting sponsor of all three Regional Events for the next three years, but they are joining Trek and SRAM as one of three top-tier lead partners. “Our vision is that every youth in America has access to a thriving cycling community,” said Punderson, “and I think that fits so well with the Mazda ethos, and their support helps us work towards that goal.”

“We use investments from partners like Mazda to ensure we can keep our membership fees as low as possible and keep those barriers to entry down,” said Punderson, “as well as to provide scholarships and support to leagues.” And as we all know, mountain biking isn’t exactly an inexpensive sport, and the support of a brand like Mazda will undoubtedly be very important as NICA continues to expand and provide opportunities for more student-athletes across the country.

My Takeaway

A brand like Mazda could do a lot of things with its marketing dollars, but I’m glad to see them choosing to support youth sports and mountain biking. I think this new partnership shows recognition of the growth and popularity of the NICA program, which has been impressive, to say the least. The numbers are frankly pretty staggering, with 26,000 student-athletes, 16,000+ volunteer coaches, 100+ teams, and 33 leagues and counting across the U.S.

Now, with a non-endemic sponsor like Mazda involved, NICA can continue pursuing its mission of getting more kids on bikes while insulating itself a bit from the volatility of the cycling industry and ensuring a stable future. And as I observed at Western Regionals in St. George, that future looks pretty bright thanks to NICA, its partners, and the growing community of all those involved.

nationalmtb.org

entry.title: Forget the Skis: UCI Snow Bike World Championships Return to France in 2027
entry.content:
There’s no off-season for rainbow stripes! The UCI has announced that the 2027 Snow Bike World Championships will return to Châtel, France, on January 23, 2027. This marks the fourth consecutive year the Portes du Soleil ski resort has hosted the event. Expect to see familiar discipline names, with riders competing for world titles in Super-G and dual slalom. However, the conditions and terrain will be very different.

Both men’s and women’s championships will take place on the same day. Giving riders two chances to leave Châtel with a rainbow jersey.

What Exactly Is Snow Bike Racing?

It’s not Fat Biking, so let me clear that up now. But if you’ve ever taken your mountain bike down a ski slope and wondered how fast you could go before things got out of hand, you already know the general idea.

The UCI’s snow bike discipline borrows heavily from alpine ski racing. But you’re trading dirt and rocks for snow, ice, and some particularly interesting traction management.

The Super-G is a single timed downhill run through a series of gates, same as on the dirt. It still rewards outright speed and precise cornering, but now throws in the need to find grip on snow.

The dual slalom is a little more familiar to mountain bike folks. Two riders race head-to-head on parallel courses through tightly spaced gates, advancing through elimination rounds until a winner is crowned.

As you might imagine, tire choice and setup matter a lot. Riders aim for enough grip to hold a fast line without sacrificing speed. It presents a slightly different set of problems than your typical downhill mountain bike race.

Can Anyone Beat Lisa Baumann?

Switzerland’s Lisa Baumann has been particularly dominant since the discipline received its own UCI World Championships in 2024.

Baumann won both titles in 2026. She became the first rider to successfully defend a Super-G World Championship title while taking her third consecutive dual slalom title.

On the men’s side, France’s Pierre Thévenard reclaimed the Super-G title he originally won in 2024. A fellow Frenchman, Vincent Tupin, took the dual slalom title.

France swept both men’s podiums in 2026, so the international field should have plenty of motivation heading into January.

So are you ready ot watch? Check out the schedule below!

2027 UCI Snow Bike World Championships Schedule

Saturday, January 23, 2027

  • 10:00 AM: Women’s and men’s Super-G
  • 12:00 PM: Super-G podium ceremonies
  • 5:00 PM: Women’s and men’s dual slalom
  • 7:00 PM: Dual slalom podium ceremonies

All times are local (CET).

The Super-G will take place on the L’Aity and Linga slopes. The evening dual slalom will be contested on the Linga slope.

It’s also a big year for non-snow cycling in Haute-Savoie. It will play host to the larger 2027 UCI Cycling World Championships later in the year.

Snow bike racing is still a relatively young UCI discipline. But four consecutive World Championships suggest it’s found a home in Châtel. It’ll be interesting to see whether more World Cup downhill regulars start working snow bike racing into their winter schedules. Because the call for a rainbow jersey is just as powerful in winter as in summer.

Either way, it’s considerably more entertaining than watching someone ride a smart trainer in January.
To learn more about Snow Biking and the discipline, check out all the details here
