entry.title: Tech Talk: One bike to do it all? I think I’ve found the answer
entry.content:
Cyclist
Tech Talk: One bike to do it all? I think I’ve found the answer

Thanks to more than ten years testing products for Cyclist, tech editor Sam has plenty to say when it comes to new bikes and gear. Tech Talk is Sam’s fortnightly newsletter, with a focus that hops between his thoughts on the latest kit to be featured by Cyclist and wider tech trends that people are talking about, or should be talking about. Click here to get Tech Talk directly to your inbox.

In recent years a bit of a paradox has developed in the bike market where all bikes are getting more capable and yet the categories they sit in are getting more specific. Where originally there were just road bikes, there’s now things like endurance road, all-road (though the differences between those two are semantics more than anything else), lightweight race, aero race… and then there’s gravel.

Initially itself an offshoot of a road bike, even gravel has diverged into at least two categories, which potentially a third now splitting the difference as well (don’t believe me? Just ask Factor about its Sarana). Obviously cyclocross bikes continue to float somewhere in between everything, but given their specific design quirks, they’re excused from this particular discussion.

I can’t say I like this category expansion because it has more than a little to do with brands just trying to sell more bikes. It also makes it harder for new cyclists to access our hobby by increasing the likelihood of decision paralysis. However, it’s not all bad: the diversification of gravel has given rise to a type of bike that I think, for a lot of riders, can effectively consolidate several categories.

That kind of bike is the gravel race bike. Over the last year or so I’ve ridden four that stick out – Factor’s Aluto, Open’s Upper 2.0, BMC’s new Kaius and now Giant’s latest Revolt – for their ability to make any type of riding fun. Quick road rides? They give next to nothing away to road bikes. Easy gravel? They positively glide along. Gnarly single track? OK, it’s a bit white knuckle, but it’s never in doubt that they’ll get you down to the bottom of the trail in one piece.

Their versatility is explained in some of their stats. Take the Revolt for example – it weighs 6.95kg. That’s lighter than most road bikes and it’s got 45mm knobblies on. Weights like this combined with stiff, carbon spoked wheelsets means their acceleration is lively, but compliance is baked in via compact frameset geometry and skinny tube shapes, so they’re comfortable too.

Their fit geometry tends towards the aggressive, but not so much that it can’t be mitigated with a few spacers under the stem, and the handling geometry is pretty forgiving on different surfaces and tyre/wheels setups as well. Admittedly, it gets a bit goofy with narrow road tyres, but any slicks in the 34mm+ region will make the bike steer fine on the road. Off-road, these bikes now have the clearance to go up to mountain bike tyres. There’s no other category that allows this kind of build variety and works so well with it all.

With the increasing dominance of Sram’s excellent XPLR drivetrain, even their gearing gives the ride plenty of bandwidth. A 44t chainring still creates a sub-1:1 bottom gear with the 10-46 cassette and I challenge you to spin out on the flat in the 44-10. Campagnolo has a similarly versatile 1×13 drivetrain options and rumour has it, Shimano’s GRX will have an update next year as well, so gravel race bike gearing is just as flexible as the frameset designs.

Understandably, there will always be those that favour master-of-one type bikes (generally those that can afford more than one machine) and there’s still plenty to be said for that. But as my 500-odd words above show, there’s more than ever to justify the jack-of-all alternative thanks to the rise of the gravel race bike.

The rumour mill

Tech tip-offs from your man in the know

As I mentioned above, there has been whispers that the current GRX generation might be due for an update next year. For many, that’s likely to be welcome – the various guises of the current generation was rolled out in staggered fashion over a couple of years and the most important version of it – 1×12 wireless Di2 – is one sprocket behind SRAM and Campagnolo. 2027 might be the year we see Shimano’s gravel offering get back up to speed. If that’s the case it’ll be a big year for the brand, as we know Dura-Ace will show its new face in 2027 as well.

Tech tidbits

A couple of small product launch highlights from the last week or two

Silca tyres complete the ecosystem

Since Josh Poertner took over the historic Italian parts and accessories brand in 2013, Silca’s range has expanded steadily to include sealant, valves, TPU tubes, rim tape and a tyre pressure calculator alongside its famous pumps.

‘There was one product missing to complete the ecosystem,’ says Poertner. ‘The tyre itself. With that in mind, we’ve launched our Protocol series – three gravel models and one road option, the RCR.’

The RCR comes in 29, 34 and 38mm sizes. It might look like an eclectic mix, but the range was deliberate.

‘We engineered them specifically for modern rim profiles,’ he says. ‘29mm is the narrowest tyres that can officially fit on a 25mm internal rim width, for example. Unlike standard manufacturers who scale up narrow tyres as rims and clearances get wider, we started with the 38 mm model, which we believe to be the marquee tire in the road line up, and scaled down to 34mm and 29mm.

‘This means that rather than treating wide road tires as a traditional endurance options by adding layers of thick rubber (that compromises suppleness and speed) the 120 TPI Race Casing and low-rolling-resistance Pulsar compound in RCR tyres enable lower inflation pressures and wider contact patches in a fast, supple, lightweight package.’

Poertner claims practicality along with performance as well, explaining that the tyres use carbon fibre beads instead of Kevlar, ‘to guarantee dimensional stability and tool-free installation’, custom ply casing angles for suppleness and protection.

‘We even have thought to use a mould-release agent that plays nice with sealant – some can prevent proper adhesion and cause premature coagulation,’ says Poertner.

Mechanical shifting ain’t dead

Founded in the Lake District in 2018 by a pair Cambridge engineering graduates, Ratio Technology got its start making mechanical drivetrain upgrade kits – the small parts necessary to make 11-speed shifters and derailleurs compatible with newer 12-speed cassettes and chains, for example. The release of its own Mech was an extension of this business.

‘We already had three years of our shifting upgrade kit sales to prove to us that there was an appetite for reliable, serviceable mechanical shifting,’ says Ratio’s director, Tom Simpson. ‘Through these kits we built a “shopping list” of all the features we wanted to see on our own derailleur and built it to perform as well as an electronic one.’

Items on that list and present in the Mech include stainless bearings for all rotating components (rather than bushings) and a specific spring type and location inside the derailleur’s parallelogram to control the pull through the derailleur’s travel down the cassette.

‘The result is much less friction, so a light lever action without sacrificing return force. It makes the shifting much less sensitive to cable friction, contamination or imperfect cable routing,’ says Simpson.

Cannily, Ratio has made the Mech to be modular, so it isn’t locked into a specific manufacturer’s drivetrain.

‘By changing the cable fin or the cage length, the Mech can adapt to the bike or components around it,’ says Simpson. ‘We also design and manufacture it ourselves in the UK. That gives us particularly close control over the entire process, and means we can develop individual parts without having to redesign or replace the whole derailleur.’

The post Tech Talk: One bike to do it all? I think I’ve found the answer appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Introducing The Cub House TroubleMakers Component Line Shakabsorber 26″ Fork
entry.content:
In a world of an increasingly precarious bike industry, the Cub House knows it’s time to take some matters into its own hands. You’ve heard of Problem Solvers; now meet TroubleMakers, The Cub House’s newest division. The first launch is the Shakabsorber — its first offering!

The Shakabsorber™️ is a suspension-corrected 26er fork handmade in San Diego. Threaded eyelets, dynamo ports, fender + rack mounts, and offered in TM Blue, Hi Vis Ooze, Rattlecan Raw, and Black™️ 🤙🤙🤙🤙

Why a Rigid 26er Fork?

Steezy 26ers are a huge part of the Cub House, so we thought, why not make our own fork! We also wanted to be different, as there are some really cool options made by our friends out there. With a sprinkling of BMX inspo, these are made here in California by our buddy Sal, who made all the original SE Landing gear forks. Who better to make a fork in this style?

The troublemakers at TroubleMakers thought long and hard about measurements and stuff, but eventually they just prototyped some different forks to test out, and these measurements are the ones that rode the best. They landed on a 1 1/8″ steerer, 1 ½” suspension-corrected, 420 mm axle-to-crown, with a mid and lower rack mount, and fit 26 x 2.5 and probably bigger with ease!

There is internal dynamo wire routing, so it looks super clean if you want to run a light. There are 4 color options: Black, ™ Blue, Hi Vis, and Rattle Can Raw.

The first 3 are powder-coat finished; Rattle Can Raw is really gonna be Benny the Big Cat rattle-canning clear coat on your fork in the back of the shop. It looks rad, lasts great, and will patina over time.

TroubleMakers Shakabsorber Quick Hits

  • $320-$350 depending on color
  • 1 1/8″ Steerer
  • 100×9 mm Quick Release
  • 300 mm Threadless Steerer
  • Axle To Crown 420 mm
  • M5 Rack Mounts (Mid mount and lower mount)
  • Routing for Dynamo Wires
  • Brake Studs Included
  • Weight: about 3 lbs 6 ounces (plenty strong)
  • Made in the USA!
  • If you are outside the USA and want one of these, shoot TroubleMakes an email, and they can sort out getting ya one

Dropping along with some TroubleMakers soft goods TODAY at 10 AM PST, exclusively on Cubhouse.cc

entry.title: COROS Vertix 4 In-Depth Review: Flashlight & Satellite Maps!
entry.content:
﻿

COROS has just announced the new COROS Vertix 4, which takes all of the hardware innovations that COROS has implemented in various watches over the last 18 months (e.g., new HR sensor, microphones, speaker, action button, etc.) and rolled them into a larger Vertix unit. But on top of that, the company has added an LED flashlight to the side, as well as the ability to download satellite imagery onto the watch (in addition to traditional topographic-style maps). Of course, there’s a bunch of other features as well that come with the newer hardware package. Oh, and yes, it’s now an AMOLED display.

I’ve been putting the COROS Vertix 4 through its paces over the last little bit, seeing where things work well…and where they fall short – just like usual.

With that, let’s dive straight into the newness.

Lastly, this is a media loaner from COROS. I’ll soon order my own unit for long-term usage/comparison/testing purposes. As always, I don’t accept advertising from any company I review, and no company sees my reviews before you do. So, if you found this review useful, consider becoming a DCR Supporter, which gets you an ad-free site, plus the behind-the-scenes video series between both me and my wife on everything that happens in the DCR Sports Tech Cave/universe.

What’s New:

It’s been 2.5 years since the last COROS Vertix series device was released (the Vertix 2S), but realistically we’re talking almost 5 years since a major update (the Vertix 2). The Vertix 2S was essentially just an update of the heart rate sensor and GPS antenna. And by ‘essentially just’, I mean that was literally it. They also decreased battery life at the time, and it became chubbier, as a result of those GPS/antenna changes.

Since then, though, COROS has released an incredible number of new watches, all of them lower tier but ultimately mostly more capable. This includes the COROS Pace 4, Pace 4 Pro, Nomad, and Apex 4 (in two sizes). And each of those watches layered in new hardware features, like a proper speaker, or a microphone, or an action button, or a depth gauge that doesn’t track depth, increased storage, and so on.

By the time the Vertix 4 has come along, its sole job in life is simply consolidating all these new things into a beefier Vertix-sized watch and calling it macaroni. And that’s aside from all the new software features the Vertix 2S mostly got along the way. So I’m gonna skip those things, since everyone already has them. Make sense?

– Switched from MIP display to 1.47” LTPO AMOLED display at 3,500 nits (466x466px)
– Maintained sapphire glass on display
– Added LED flashlight (white) on right side
– Moved the Digital Crown to the upper right (from center right)
– Upgraded to the latest COROS 4th gen optical HR sensor package
– Added Speaker (for voice calls & audio alerts)
– Added new ‘Action’ button (customizable extra button…sorta)
– Added dual-microphone with voice pins/notes feature
– Added ability to take phone calls (with phone nearby)
– Added voice control from watch
– Adding downloadable satellite maps onto watch (coming in 2027)
– Added new multi-data page field that can cram in 13 data fields
– Added street & trail names to the offline maps
– Added POI database to offline maps
– Added depth gauge sensor (very limited though)
– Upgraded internal processor
– Increased storage to 64GB (from 32GB)
– Increased battery claim from 43 hours to 48 hours (multiband, always-on display), but decreased all-systems GPS from 73 hours to 58 hours (always-on display)
– Unit weight is 60g (or 68g with Nylon strap)
– Switched from 26mm band to 24mm bands
– Case size is a 49mm case
– Decreased thickness by 14% to 13.8mm
– Final box includes two watch bands, Nylon and regular silicone band
– Increased price from $699 to $799

One interesting quirk, the new Vertix 4 doesn’t have the newer satellite ‘Auto’ modes that the Pace 4 Pro has. It just has the forced multi-band (Max), all systems (High), and GPS only modes (Standard). Speaking of which, here are those battery claims. More about reality later on…

Also, as noted earlier, the watch comes with two bands. For whatever reason, the media loaner units sent out to reviewers didn’t include two bands, just a single band.

Finally, the Vertix 4 announces today, but won’t be available to order until…checks notes…Black Friday (November 27th). Yes, for real, COROS is actually launching a new watch on Black Friday. I can’t make this stuff up. More about that later.

The Basics:

In this section, I’ll walk through all the daily usage/basics of the watch, from the buttons to the user interface, to activity tracking, to voice control, and more. Whereas in the next section I’ll get into the sports bits.

First up are the buttons: the Vertix 4 has shifted the Digital Crown to the upper right corner (from the right-center), to make room for the flashlight. Meanwhile, it’s gained an ‘Action’ button on the lower left side, like other recent COROS watches. This is still, in total, just three buttons (the Vertix 2S had three buttons on the right, including the Digital Crown):

As I’ve noted in past COROS reviews, while COROS might have had good intentions with the action button, in reality they never bothered to finish the code for it. So it does very little and isn’t really customized, especially in sports modes. More on that later.

One minor note is that they changed the strap release design on the Vertix 4. Aside from decreasing the band/strap from 26mm to 24mm, they also shifted to the industry-standard strap quick-release system. This has pros and cons. The previous design allowed for quickly removing straps and was more secure. The newer design allows for broad compatibility with anything on Amazon, but is less secure and a tiny bit fiddly.

Above are the two side by side, Vertix 2S on the left, and Vertix 4 on the right. Again, hardly a big deal to me, but I figured I’d mention the trade-offs.

In any event, back on the front is the watch face. COROS does have a good selection of watch faces, especially via their app, including plenty of creative ones tied to races, seasonal bits, etc. In this case, you can press the lower right corner on this stock watch face to iterate through a few different stats from the day.

Scrolling down from there, you’ll find the widgets. The first smaller bit of information lets you open it up to more detailed bits about that topic (such as steps, sleep, training history, weather, etc.). You can lightly customize the order and selection of widgets here, roughly on par with Suunto, maybe a smidge more.

One of them being sleep, of course. In looking at the sleep tracking here, things have aligned well with the other wearables I’ve been using during this time period – including an Apple Watch Ultra 4 on the other wrist, as well as a Whoop 5.0, Garmin Cirqa, and Fitbit Air on the biceps.

As always, for sleep tracking I’m specifically focused on the times it shows I went to sleep and woke up. I don’t find much value in trying to compare sleep phases/stages, because the so-called ‘gold standard’ technological options to do so simply aren’t that accurate (only in the mid-80% range). Thus, pretending to compare sleep stages/phases is nothing more than bro science at this point, unfortunately.

In any event, all these things are visible not only on the watch, but of course the COROS smartphone app as well. You can see your current day stats on the main dashboard, and then dive into other stats and historical data pretty easily.

The app is simple to use, which COROS has long said is their mantra. As always, there’s a balance between being simple to use and depth of data. The reality is that the more data you get/store/etc., the more complex the app will become. COROS records a relatively small amount of daily health data (or even fitness metrics) compared to some of their competitors; thus the app is relatively straightforward still.

Shifting topics to some smartwatch features, there’s the ability to see smart notifications on the watch. You can’t respond to them, but you can at least see them and clear them. Likewise, there are media controls for bits on your phone, though I find this kinda finicky where sometimes it doesn’t see your phone’s media and sometimes it does. Here’s a moment where it decided to be happy:

Further, one of the newer COROS features is the ability to do voice control. This requires holding the lower left button, and then speaking your request. At which point the watch goes off and tries to fulfill your wish. This works reasonably well when not moving, though like the COROS Dura 2, it falls apart at bicycle speeds. Still, most people on a watch will be doing this while standing still or walking, so that’s fine.

Though there are quirks, for example, you can’t ask it what time sunset is during a workout, since that falls into the ‘general use’ questions, and only ‘workout’ questions are permitted during workout time. I’m not kidding. Note that this is different than a full voice assistant that you might see on other smartwatches where it can answer tasks/questions off to the internet. Instead, this is specific to performing actions on the watch itself. That’s fine though, I rarely care to talk to my wrist anyway.

With that, let’s illuminate the new flashlight before getting into sports modes.

The Flashlight:

There’s no doubt the flashlight on the Vertix 4 will be controversial. Even COROS themselves acknowledge this during their media briefing, and then went on to spend half the presentation with an engineering dissertation about why they are right. Or rather, why their flashlight is on the right.

You see, up till now all smartwatch flashlights (including Inspector Gadget) were on the front of the watch (the 12 o’clock position). That had both benefits and drawbacks. The main benefit is that it worked for both left- and right-handed folks (regardless of the assumption that you tend to wear your watch on the opposite wrist to your dominant hand). The other benefit is that the back of your hand didn’t block the light being emitted.

The downside though, was that it meant depending on what you were doing, you weren’t actually facing the light towards the subject area your hands might be working with. For example, finding something in a bag, changing a diaper, or eating ice cream. COROS had been pondering this for a while. It was at least a year or so ago that they first approached me for my thoughts on the topic. Which, in case you’re wondering, were roughly “just follow everyone else; people are pretty happy with that”. The risk, as I saw it, was that you both alienated left-handed people (since the light was either facing the wrong way, or you had to flip the watch, so that button usability wasn’t really ideal), as well as potentially left yourself with a light that might work for one task, but not another.

Anyway, fast forward to the final decision and enough schematics to build a fighter jet:

And more:

I’m not done yet. Or rather, they aren’t. Here’s more:

So what about real life? I’d say it’s growing on me. I think it depends on the task. For hand-focused tasks as outlined above, the side position generally works better than the 12 o’clock position, for me as a right-handed person.

Whereas for area illumination tasks, it still feels a bit weird and forced – since you have to basically point your arm/wrist at where you want to go, forcing it out away from your body. But that could also be years of using flashlights the other way. Shrug.

For walking on a trail at night, that’s halfies. Neither Garmin’s nor COROS’s implementation is great orientation-wise, since your arm stroke essentially means both would be required to cover the ground.

As for running, just as with Garmin’s, neither light has enough throw to make it work well on uneven/technical trails. It works fine at lower speeds, or if you were on a ‘trusted’ path where random rocks weren’t going to be there. But for all smartwatch lights, once I get up to speed, I quickly ‘outrun’ the light. The camera here makes it seem quite bright, in reality it’s both a very small area relative to my running speed and not as bright as the camera makes it seem.

Now, when it comes to turning it on, you’ll quickly double-press the lower left button – just like with Garmin. You can adjust the brightness level on the watch using either the touchscreen or the digital crown. There are three white brightness levels. There is no red (or green) LED option here.

Then naturally, just like with Garmin, you’ll quickly double-press the same button again to turn it off. Oh, wait…you mean that actually now goes into emergency SOS mode at night in the bed? Or flashing mode. Hmm…never mind.

Instead, we now tap the upper right button to turn it off. Plus the back buttons to get yourself back to whatever you were doing (watch face, widgets, workout/etc.)

Point being, if you tap the lower left button, it iterates between solid on and SOS and flashing. While I get the idea of putting SOS/flashing here, this just seems weird. Nobody needs either on the daily during day-to-day actions, so having it be prominent just means accidentally flashing (or SOS’ing) your friends and family constantly. Or flashing yourself. And again, it means switching back and forth between buttons unnecessarily. It’s just a haphazard UI.

COROS says the flashlight can stay on for many hours without killing the battery. They also say it won’t turn off after a set time, since they noted that “if you turned it on, you probably wanted it on”. And that’s true to an extent. We’ve all seen someone in daytime with a flashlight accidentally turned on, so turning it off after a long time (like 30 minutes) does have some benefits (rightly or wrongly). Plus, as I’ll talk about in a second, I actually used the near-30-minute bit last night.

That said, there’s one big gap today – which is trying to turn on the flashlight during a workout. The regular button triggers don’t work here, and instead you have to first long-hold the lower right button, then rotate around a bunch until you find the flashlight, then turn it on. Then back out to the sports pages you were on. And then finally, do the whole thing in reverse to turn it off.

What’s baffling here is COROS literally has an ‘Action Button’ they added 18 months ago to the COROS NOMAD. But as I noted then, it was half-baked and could not actually be assigned any custom action. I’m not kidding. Here we are now, 1.5 years later, and the only action you can assign during a sport mode is whether to toggle to maps or compass.  In between then and now, they’ve rolled out the action button, which doesn’t do anything, to all their other watches, yet…still haven’t fixed the software underneath to actually make it useful. C’mon COROS, stop being lazy. It’s infuriating how bad this is. Assigning existing shortcut functions is literally the easiest code thing you should be able to do here. You should have a vast list of shortcuts, just like your competitors do.

Now, that said, on my ride just last night I started far later than I expected, and thus the last 30 minutes were solidly past sunset. I had a rear taillight/radar, but didn’t have a front light. So, I used the Vertix 4 flashlight. When holding on to the handlebars, it did a so-so job of lighting up the road in front of me at lower speeds (10-20KPH), though it was mostly useless at higher speeds (e.g. 30-40KPH). But it did one thing super well: Let cars know I was there.

The wrist, while holding on to the handlebars, ends up bending to block much of the light you’d need in front of you (as you can see above, there’s no car behind me), but it still lets oncoming vehicles easily spot the light. So that was a strong win.

Note that COROS doesn’t have any of the other modes that Garmin and Amazfit have around automatic after-sunset light enablement in running, or any of the cadence lock features while running, etc. In this case, cadence lock means the flashlight will ‘lock’ to your running cadence, blinking at the same rate. Plus a bunch of configurable flash modes. I don’t really consider those a dealbreaker or such, but they would be handy to have.

Overall, from a hardware/position standpoint, I’m pretty happy with the flashlight. While I think it’d be nice to have the secondary red light, I don’t miss it a ton either. I just feel the software needs some solid work.

Sports & Navigation:

There’s no question that if you’re getting a COROS watch, you’re probably doing sports with it. To access the sports menu, you’ll tap the upper-right button/Digital Crown, which opens up a list of sport modes.

Within that, you can iterate through the initial list, or open up a deeper list of sport modes. There are also some non-sport modes listed, for things like some Fitness Tests (Cycling FTP, Running Fitness, Running Form), as well as a shortcut to structured workouts.

Once you select a sport mode, such as running in this case, you’ve got a few options from the pending screen. At this point the watch is off connecting to GPS, firing up the HR sensor at a higher power (for better accuracy), and connecting to any external accessories/sensors you have. But from here you can apply/set a structured workout, add a course, tweak settings like automatic lap and voice alerts, and more.

One of those options is loading a course/route. To load a course/route you’ll need to get it to the COROS app first (e.g., by linking Strava, Komoot, or simply creating the route in the COROS app), and then you’ll tap to send it to the watch. Unfortunately, COROS doesn’t send favorited routes automatically (something I keep hoping they’ll do), so you’ll need to do so manually.

Once that’s done, you can see the route on the watch, as well as the elevation profile. I would like to see COROS expand this a bit more, specifically by showing climbs, or showing the map/satellite view behind it.

After selecting a route, you can specify if you want to reverse the course, turn off deviation alerts, as well as a few other minor options.

So with that, let’s get out running on the trails. Once you’ve started, you’ll see your data pages as you’ve confirmed them. You can configure these within the COROS app just like with past watches. Nothing new or crazy here, except the 13-data field option I mentioned up top. But even I don’t need that.

As for navigation, you’ll get a turn prompt as you approach a turn:

And if you go wild and head off-course, you’ll eventually get an off-course warning as well. In this case, I somehow missed the initial turn, and then figured it’d merge again. Spoiler: Not for a while. Obviously, instead of just staying the course like a logical person would, I ended up bushwhacking for a bit.

The COROS watch doesn’t have any form of re-routing, so if you go off-course, it’s up to you to get back on course. That’s usually straightforward enough (assuming you notice it soon), but just be aware of those nuances. You can also see your overall elevation profile as well:

For climbs, it’ll automatically detect the climb within a course and show your position on the climb. This too worked reasonably well for me on my running climbs:

The action button here merely allows you to toggle between the map view and regular view (and media view if you want). You can’t assign any other action to it unfortunately. Again, such a bit of a lost opportunity here to do…I don’t know, anything else. There are so many things it could do!

Once your workout is done, you’ll see all the stats on the watch, like normal:

And then these also sync over to the COROS smartphone app as well for even more viewing:

Further, if you’ve connected any platforms (e.g., Strava, Komoot, the DCR Analyzer), it’ll immediately sync into those as well. All of that worked just fine.

Lastly, from a sports standpoint, you do have a handful of training and recovery analysis bits. There’s your training load, which shows training volume. Note that this resets every Monday morning, which I’ll continue to point out is silly. The marathon you just completed on Sunday doesn’t magically evaporate that training load pain Monday morning. Training load should be rolling, not resetting (on the COROS app, it’s rolling, but on the watch it resets):

There’s also Training Status, which compares your recent training load to past training load. This is sorta like Garmin’s Productive/Unproductive/etc, but a wee bit more simplistic and is just comparing historical volumes, not training types (e.g., aerobic/etc).

After that there’s Recovery status, looking at how many hours till your next hard workout:

And then there’s your estimated VO2Max and Race Predictions. I find COROS continues to underestimate me, both in measured VO2Max and actual run times. But most runners have known that COROS’s predictions tend to be pretty rough, especially because they only meaningfully update when fed a diet of totally flat-ground runs, not hilly ones.

In any case, setting that all aside, let’s get into the satellite maps pieces.

Satellite Maps:

Next up is the new addition of free satellite maps on the watch. Garmin has had this for years, but it required an annual subscription to their Outdoor Maps+ (and named other things prior to that). To be fair, the Outdoor Maps+ included a gazillion other map types as well, so satellite maps were just one part of it.

Still, despite me paying for Outdoor Maps+ all these years ($49/year or $4.99/month), I never found it terribly useful in terms of satellite maps. Not because the maps were bad, but because in real life out on the trails, having topographic maps was generally more useful than satellite maps, which, when zoomed in, tended to just show an endless sea of green trees.

So, would COROS be useful here, especially if free?

Well, the first thing to know is that it’s not going to ship at launch. COROS has delayed the launch of the satellite maps to the public until sometime in “early 2027”. That said, they have given beta access to reviewers. In their media briefing, it sounded like the reason it was beta was less because of the watch experience, and more because getting it onto the watch was flaky right now. And having done that, I can confirm: It’s flaky. Not horrific or anything, but very much beta. Still, it’s pretty simple, and in the end, some time later, it worked out.

You’ll go into the Map Manager for the device via the COROS App, and select the area that you want to download. You can see the size at the bottom, which grows super fast. So this isn’t really great for downloading large areas, merely because it’ll take a long time to download.

Once you’ve done that, the app will actually connect via WiFi directly to the watch (not to your WiFi network). This is basically like how a GoPro or other action camera would connect to your camera. This is different than how it downloads the regular maps, where the watch connects to your WiFi network and then to the COROS platform/cloud. I’m gonna guess at some point they’ll leverage that way instead for satellite maps too, because frankly it’s just more logical and removes the device fiddly factor. In any case, that WiFi connection piece is the piece that’s clearly pretty beta from my testing.

But once downloaded, you’re good to go!

To use the maps, you’ll need to toggle that map layer on from the settings. You can’t have both map layers on at the same time. Switching back and forth between regular maps and satellite maps can be quickly accessed from the upper-right button. Nice and clean.

Once you’ve done that, you can see the two side-by-side:

The above is actually probably the best example of where satellite imagery works well. I was in an old abandoned military base, and I had come to a junction in the trail with like 5-7 real-world ‘path’ options. Figuring out the correct way from regular maps was kinda tricky, because there were so many options. But seeing the building clearly on the satellite maps made it easy.

Inversely, for other areas in heavier tree/forest/whatever coverage, satellite maps tend to be kinda useless. For example, here it’s so-so, but in other areas I didn’t think to take photos of, it’s just a blanket of trees/shrubs.

And that’s sorta where I was with the Garmin Birdseye Satellite maps back in the day, not rebranded Outdoor Maps+. There were select cases where they were useful, but more often than not, it was shrug at best over regular maps.

Still, it’s awesome that COROS is delivering this feature for free. While Garmin’s Outdoor Maps+ includes 18 other layers, the reality is that most people just want the satellite map layer. The other layers are awesome for selected use cases, but not super useful for the majority of people.

Thus, I’m looking forward to COROS getting this focused satellite piece shipped to production and out the door!

Accuracy (Heart Rate, GPS, Elevation):

In this section, I’ll look at the accuracy of the GPS, heart rate, and elevation data.

From a GPS accuracy standpoint, I used the default settings, which is “High”, and not dual frequency. Somewhat oddly, COROS hasn’t implemented any smart switching into dual frequency like they have on other recent units (the recently announced Pace 4 Pro has ‘Auto’, but the Vertix 4 doesn’t). This implies a different GPS chipset (for better or worse), or perhaps they’re having problems with Auto mode. Whereas Suunto forces always multiband in default, and Garmin by default uses an automatic algorithm to switch back and forth (called SatIQ), to switch mid-workout dynamically based on satellite needs. In any case….

We’ll start with the new optical HR sensor, which is the same as seen on other recent COROS watches. But definitely newer than the one from the Vertix 2S.

First up, let’s look at an easy 5KM warm-up run. Just to shake things out and make sure nothing is dorked up. Here we can see a slight bit of latency from the Vertix 4 at the beginning (and the Fitbit Air on the bicep), but then within about 2 minutes all of them combine together fairly nicely. One brief moment about 7 minutes in when I did a slight increase in pace and it didn’t quite catch what the chest strap did for those few seconds, but otherwise all good.

After that, we’ve got a trail run I did. This has plenty of ups/downs, technical terrain, and then some fun faster slightly downhill bits. It’s a good mix of things. On the whole, it’s not bad, but equally so, there are still some solid errors here. It loses HR entirely around the 6-minute marker as I ascend a short steep climb. Then again later on, at the top of another climb, briefly. In fact, a few times at higher-intensity stuff, it stumbles briefly.

Next up, for a slate of high-intensity intervals, I pitted it against the Garmin Fenix E, which uses Garmin’s older Gen4 optical HR sensor, but is otherwise the same as a Fenix 9 in terms of software features. It’s also down to $399. In this case, you can see both the Vertix 4 & Fenix E struggled during my warm-up briefly (about 60-90 seconds), before locking in. During the main set of 6×400 intervals, they were both perfectly fine (save one mistake from the Vertix 4 on the 2nd interval). But during the shorter 30-second even faster intervals at the end, the Fenix E struggled for the first two, and the fourth. I don’t entirely know why – usually the Gen4 optical HR sensor can handle this, but apparently not today.

Next up we’ve got a fairly straightforward one, an indoor trainer interval workout. Here we can see the COROS Vertix 4 against the Garmin Fenix E, as well as the chest strap. Also, there’s an Apple Watch Ultra 4 on a bicep band of sorts. Not really optimal placement, but I didn’t want to lose my rings. :)

There’s absolutely nothing of concern up there in that workout; it’s spot-on. But of course, indoor cycling is the easiest thing for optical HR sensors, since there are no road vibrations like outdoor cycling, or massive ‘thunks’ of your footsteps like running.

Then, going outside to a nearly 2-hour-long ride into the mountains (road bike), we can see it’s…rough. On the first half, where I’m ascending, it’s fine as long as I’m steady-state with intensity. But anytime I surged, it immediately lost the plot. The Vertix 2S would also lose the plot a fair bit as well, but actually the Vertix 4 overall did worse here (notably worse).

Switching over to GPS, I didn’t really see anything major of concern here across all my data sets, including others not included here. There are some minor issues, but nothing that’s a dealbreaker. So, just quickly running through these. Here’s an hour-long trail run I did with cliff overhangs, trees, etc… As you can see below, at a high level, no issues:

Zooming into one area of overhangs (where I’m basically in a cave), all the units struggled a tiny bit here. I’d say that the exact correct track is somewhere between the Garmin Fenix 9 & Apple Watch Ultra 4. Along the shoreline the Vertix was more correct, but then it veers off above the cliffs somewhere, losing the points/momentum it gained. None of them failed this though.

And the same in some tree areas: it’s very close between the units, but pretty consistently the Vertix 4 tends to just slightly overshoot some corners. It’s barely different, but when you’re talking flagship units, those differences do exist.

Another example here:

So, moving along to another run of many loops doing those 400m repeats, I want to zoom in on the loop specifically, to see just how perfect each repeat was. This is always a fun test of GPS, doing the same circuit over and over and over again, and in my case, almost precisely on the same part of the deserted roads as well:

So, while these look good at a high level, none of them really absolutely nailed it. I was basically in the middle of the road, except for the corners (again, this place is deserted this time of year). Now, GPS maps don’t always perfectly line up, so if we were to shift very slightly over (north a touch), then things line up better. Which, perhaps given all units were basically atop each other, then maybe it’s fine. Who knows, but at least they get an A for consistency.

Next, we’ve got an outdoor road cycling ride up into the mountains. Here at a high level, all things are good:

And on this first set of switchbacks, you can see how much better it does than the Vertix 2S, despite the Vertix 2S being in multi-frequency and the Vertix 4 being in the lesser ‘All Systems’ mode.

Again, same story here – the Vertix 4 does very well:

From an elevation standpoint on that ride, I do see a bit more variation than I’d prefer at the beginning from the COROS Vertix 4. I had kinda seen the same to a lesser extent in one of my runs, but here, with going straight to the mountains, you can see it’s lagging a bit (though the COROS Vertix 2S had no issues).

Looking back at a 5KM run I did just last night to test the slight offsets theory a bit more, I can see again that in certain orientations it loses accuracy compared to the Vertix 2S and Fenix 9:

It would depend on which way I was running/going.

Finally, we’ve got an openwater swim. I’ll be honest – I’m actually impressed with both the swim buoy watch and the COROS Vertix 4 here. I was trying a new swim buoy, and it promptly flipped over and stayed over, so the watch (COROS Pace 4 Pro) was actually upside-down facing the water the entire time (though with the backside against the airbag of the swim buoy), and it recorded a really darn good reference track:

In any case, the Vertix 4 was very close here, though it did cut some corners (specifically going into some of the coves there (in the upper left and very bottom), it just sorta shorted it). But overall, it was one of the best performances from a COROS watch recently (which has historically really struggled with open-water swims).

Overall, across all GPS & heart rate things look reasonably good, yet at the same time there’s a lot of small errors on GPS during running (but not cycling), and some notable cycling heart rate issues. Yet for running, the heart rate was mostly pretty good. For me, I got better performance from the COROS Pace 4 Pro overall than I have from the COROS Vertix 4. It’s not that the Vertix 4 is bad, but it’s definitely far from industry-leading right now.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Wrap-Up:

On the whole, the COROS Vertix 4 is a good watch. I mostly like the flashlight’s hardware implementation, even if it has some drawbacks (and needs some software fixing). But in terms of the 3-o’clock flashlight? No biggie to me either way. Likewise, I really like the beginnings of the satellite map pieces. They’re handy to have, especially since COROS streamlines the downloads a bit and just makes it simple to download the area around you. Heck, it’d be even handier if anytime you go to charge it, it just downloads a 25-50km area around you (similar to what Apple does automatically behind the scenes for their maps). That’d be super cool.

Likewise, for the display – it’s awesome, just like it was on the Pace 4 Pro, and the overall build quality feels good too. And including two straps? Amazing – I hope that’s a trend. Of course, software finish continues to be COROS’s challenge lately, and bobbles I see in both HR and GPS accuracy are slightly concerning, especially since other reviewers are seeing things too. But that’s not the biggest problem here.

The elephant in the room is that COROS arguably picked the worst day ever to launch a watch (Black Friday is when you can first buy the watch). This is a baffling business decision. By doing so, COROS is pitting themselves directly up against a Garmin Fenix 8 (with the new Fenix 9 features) at $749 (with titanium and sapphire glass), which has a better flashlight with more modes and colors, more accurate GPS (and certain longer GPS modes), much better heart rate sensor, certified dive support to 40m, medically certified ECG by the FDA/EU/etc, better/deeper voice & speaker support, full offline music services like Spotify, far better navigation/maps, 3rd party apps, and a gazillion more polished features. Yes, COROS wins by a couple hours of GPS cases when compared to the 51mm unit, or by about 25% more when compared to the 47mm unit; COROS has a brighter display that’s slightly bigger, and COROS earns points for including two straps. Of course, that $50 savings buys a lot of Amazon watch straps.

But here’s the longer-term problem: That Fenix 8 pricing isn’t going away next week. That *will* undoubtedly become the new norm for the Garmin Fenix 8 after the holidays. History tells us that. Over and over and over, every single year this pattern plays out. By pricing the COROS Vertix 4 at $799, COROS is making the same mistakes they made with the Vertix 2S pricing. Heck, remove Garmin – you’ve got Suunto with the Suunto Vertical 2 (which also has a flashlight) that sits at $599 ($200 less than the Vertix 4) – and it’s not even on sale yet. The Suunto Vertical 2 has the same-sized display, but isn’t as bright as the COROS Vertix 4. But it beats COROS on battery life (both on spec, and very much real world in my testing), maps are a wash as is HR accuracy. Point is, it’s $200 cheaper. And we don’t even want to rope in Amazfit’s prices here too.

To be clear, the COROS Vertix 4 isn’t a bad watch. I’d argue it’s probably one of the best watches COROS has made to date (though I might give the COROS Pace 4 Pro the edge here based on GPS/HR accuracy right now). Still, it’s certainly the best COROS Vertix series unit, though. And yes, I can see why COROS felt like it should cost $100 more than the Vertix 2S. But that’s living in a vacuum, ignoring the competitive landscape. Simply put: They should have either priced it lower, or launched it months ago.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: The Wizard Works Zambini is its First Rack Bag
entry.content:
Wizard Works, the London-based bag makers known for their colorful and high-quality London-made bike bags, released the Zambini Rack Bag (£175), a top-opening rack bag that prioritizes stability and easy access to your gear…

First previewed in our Brother in the Wild coverage, the bag is now ready to order…

Sitting at around 12 liters, Zambini rolls closed, giving ample and flexible storage; a wide top opening means it couldn’t be easier to rummage for snacks. Folded tight, the seam-taped liner keeps the main compartment fully waterproof for peace of mind on adventures.

Zambini attaches with removable, adjustable hitch straps that fit a huge range of racks and allow you to snap the bag on and off in seconds. The straps clip together when the bag is not in use to keep everything tidy and tangle-free. A grippy Hypalon base combined with the camlock compression strap means Zambini is super stable and off-road ready, and the tapered shape makes it dropper-compatible.

Front and rear mesh pockets take layers or more snacks, while one internal drop pocket keeps small bits findable without emptying the bag. Proudly manufactured in-house at Wizard Works’ London workshop. The Zambini Rack Bag is available now from Wizard Works direct and selected dealers, globally.

Zambini Quick Hits

  • Price: Core: £175, Custom: from £200
  • 12 Litres
  • Waterproof main compartment
  • Roll top closure for flexible storage
  • Top opening for easy gear access
  • Tapered shape for dropper post compatibility
  • Front and rear mesh pockets with replaceable elastic cord
  • One internal drop pocket
  • Grippy Hypalon base and camlock compression strap for improved stability
  • Easy on and off with removable and adjustable hitch straps
  • Hitch straps clip together when bag not in use
  • Available as part of the WW Core Range (ready to ship) in Black, Olive, Splatter, and Tan. Or Custom (made to order) in any fabric from Wizard Works’ extensive range
  • Made in London
  • Weight: 570g

See more at Wizard Works.

The post The Wizard Works Zambini is its First Rack Bag appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Salsa Fargo 32 Steel Review: 32 Coming Through – Sean T. Randolph & Spencer Harding
entry.content:
“32 Coming through!” Sean yelled at his friends as he passed them, going downhill on Harshaw Road. Why is he passing his friends all of a sudden? Is it bigger wheels? Is 32” faster? Or is he just boasting because he’s riding the new monster truck of drop bar MTB’s, the Salsa Fargo 32? Read on to see what’s going on with the new steel Fargo 32” and if it does indeed go far, then how far does it go…

For a very long time, my favorite bicycle was a 2008 Salsa Ala Carte in Goldrush Brown. You can see a picture of the bike in Salsa’s archive if you look up 2010 Salsa Ala Carte. This 26” MTB went everywhere with me and withstood many upgrades and Iterations: rim brake to disc, tubes to tubeless, 8 to 9 to 10 speed, and so on. The model was one of the few that held over from the original Ross Schafer days. If you don’t know about Ross, I recommend checking him out.

This bike was very important to me for many reasons, but it established how a quality bike should feel. It had True Temper Ox platinum tubing, which made the frame hella flexy, but oh so comfortable. The 26” wheels were stiff and nimble, and I was used to them, so I held out from getting a 29er way past when it was acceptable. You know those stickers that say “26 ain’t dead yet,” well, that was my mantra.

I have since moved on but hold a little bit of that “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” attitude. Naturally, my entry into the 32” world was laced with a healthy dose of skepticism, and at the same time riding the Steel Fargo 32” gave me feelings of riding my own Salsa relic.

Salsa Fargo 32 Steel Frameset Quick Hits

  • Small, Medium, Large, X-Large sizing
  • Pearl Orchid paint
  • Standard boost spacing
  • Internal dropper routing
  • Internal dynamo wire routing on carbon fork
  • Front and rear rack mounting options, as well as anything cage mounts on the frame and fork
  • Triple-butted chromoly tubeset
  • Alternator 1.0 flat-mount dropouts with UDH accommodate Transmission drivetrains and belt drive systems
  • Alternator dropouts are available for flat or post-mount brakes
  • Fork is post-mount and will need a Wolftooth post-flat adaptor for drop bar groups
  • Multi-fit geometry that accommodates both flat and drop bar setups
  • Steel Frameset is listed for $1799 USD (frame, fork, headset, thru axles, and seat collar)
  • Also available in Ti for $3499

The Steel Fargo 32” is currently only offered as a frameset and comes in one striking color: Pearl Orchid. I love flashy bikes. Pearly paint jobs and metallic glitter, yes please! Take me back to the days of Schwinn Homegrown bass boat paint and the pink 2 Hip Pork. The Fargo’s paint morphs between lilac purple and sage green depending on the light. It also has a shimmery metallic flake. If you have read any of my other reviews, you know that I’m big on subtle logos and branding. The Salsa logos on the downtube are bold, but match the green sheen of the paint nicely, so they get an aesthetic pass. But how does it ride, you ask? Well, I’d argue that a good part of what makes a bike ride well is how you feel on the bike. When I buy a skateboard, I do care about the artwork. It’s true that I’m going to scrape the bottom paint off on my first boardslide, but it has to feel right. Same with the Salsa frame, it’s gonna get covered in dirt (and it did; we got stuck in a monsoon) and bags, but you want the frame to look good underneath it all. We often forget this, but I’d like to remind you that the way things look matters. And this bike does look good. The build we reviewed came with silver wheels, tan wall tires, and black components. Very classy.

Does The Fargo 32 Shred?

But Sean, does the bike shred? The short answer is, yes, it does shred. If I were to make an even more complete review of this bike, I would have a size run and try every size with every size rider, but I do not have this luxury, so we’ll have to settle for someone 6 feet tall (me) and someone else 6 feet 1 inch (Spencer) riding an XL frame. The XL frame fit me well, but was on the big side. I think I’d prefer the Large for my own bike. Salsa equipped the bike with a 70mm -25 degree stem that the bike was designed around. This accommodates the 80mm suspension-corrected fork and 32” wheel. It looks a little funny at first, but I can assure you that it doesn’t handle funny. The bike is stable and slack, but responsive at speed. The stem drop made me think someone much taller than me could ride the bike with a positive-rise stem and have a very happy back.

My question is then, why doesn’t the bike come in an XXL? This seems like an instance where bigger wheels mean the bike should follow suit. This is not an original idea, but it seems like something we might see in the land of 32” as a design choice to accommodate taller riders. Salsa responded with two reasons: firstly, the economics of producing a niche size. Second, their multi-fit geo should accommodate much larger riders with a longer stem.

One of my main concerns about the bike was that the larger wheels would mean excess flex. To be clear, I am a fan of flex, but too much can lead to a sloppy ride. The bike came with silver i9 hubs laced to silver Velocity Blunt SS rims. Out of the box, the wheels didn’t feel too tankish, and on the bike they felt smooth as buttah’. While standing out of the saddle, they were peppy and maintained a good line downhill. The best way to describe the ride feel of a 32” wheel with a 2.4 tire is “comfortable.” I know that’s not the most exciting word to describe a bike, but outside of how a bike looks, comfort is king. On a bike like this, comfort means you can ride longer, harder, and stronger. This had a lot to do with the Fargo platform: slack touring geo, robust tubeset, and wider tires.

If my old Salsa ala Carte gets a “cotta” on the pasta cook scale, I’d say the Fargo 32” falls somewhere in between “al chiodo” and “al dente.” It feels stiff enough to carry weight without getting loopy but still more compliant than a Surly. Check out the Flex Capacitor for more info on the noodle scale.

Mechanical Concerns

From a mechanic’s point of view, there is something about the angle of the spokes and size of the cassette that makes for a very tight margin for adjusting the low limit without the cage of the derailleur hitting the spokes. I’ve had this happen on some 29er derailleur setups as well; the spoke’s attack angle is such that setting the low limit perfectly is imperative to keep the derailleur from ticking the spokes in the 52-tooth cog. This left me wondering if component manufacturers will have to be paying closer attention to how 32” wheels affect the setup of their drivetrain and brake systems. I was also curious if the bike would fit on my bike rack, and it did not. This is not a deal breaker for me, as my rack, the Kuat NV 2.0, probably wouldn’t fit a 20” wheeled bike either. This could be a concern if you use the bike for commuting and need one of the SportWerks-style racks to supplement your commute. Also, bigger wheels mean bigger boxes. So if you are traveling with this bike, you may need to be more careful when choosing a box or travel bag. Folks at Salsa have had success so far with Evoc bags traveling with their prototypes. These are small details to evaluate when adopting a new standard.

On The Necessity of 32″

Do we really need a new wheel size? Isn’t 29 inches plenty of inches? Honestly, I’m not totally sure. What I am sure of is that the Salsa Fargo Steel 32” is super comfy and looks great. And it harkens back to a Salsa that I know from the past. A Salsa that proclaims “If it ain’t moto, it’s worthless.” And that’s enough to sell me on it. I loved how it handled on the chunkiest of dirt roads, and I think that if you have the opportunity to try a 32”, you should, especially the Fargo. At the same time, I feel a bit like Carrie Bradshaw in reflecting on my experience of this bicycle. I have the desire to make a pun that will make you roll your eyes and shed a tear simultaneously. Maybe that’s because sometimes trends and new standards in cycling feel more like fashion than innovation.

Pros

  • Can’t beat the color; it’s beautiful
  • Frame is robust without feeling heavy
  • Plenty of mounting points to attach all the bags and racks
  • Better for taller riders
  • Insanely comfortable
  • You’ll make your friends wish they had the cool new thing

Cons

  • Maybe purple is not your thing (then you can just get the Ti one)
  • Might not fit in your car’s bike rack
  • You’ll need a bigger box to bring it on the plane
  • Somewhat less nimble in techy situations
  • Fewer options exist for tires and rims at this time

Spencer’s Take On The Fargo 32 Steel

While this is Sean’s review, we live in the same town, and I got to take the bike out for a few rides, so I wanted to add my thoughts and some details Joe Meiser of Salsa shared with me.

On the whole, I am excited by the prospect of a 32″ platform for us taller riders. Though the bike was sent with a negative rise stem, and since I’m dying on the “stack height is too low” hill, I swapped it out. In our moment of glory and comfort, the bike designers see fit to snatch victory from our hands with insane negative rise stems and short head tubes. Don’t let this become permissible.

I took the Fargo 32 out on some AZT singletrack as well as rough gravel roads that are quintessentially southern Arizona. At speed, the 32″ wheels do an impressive job of mediating chatter and holding tempo. On singletrack, I never found the bike overly unwieldy, even on tight switchbacks, though I wished it had flat bars more than once. At slow speeds, the large contact patch can feel sluggish, but I’m telling you, point this thing straight and it goooooes.

I found the overall silhouette of the new Fargo easier on the eyes, looking more akin to a gravel bike with its 80mm of suspension correction over the longer 100mm travel of the 29er Fargo. Despite the boost MTB spaced hubs, 73mm bottom bracket, and 2.4″ tires, the Fargo 32 always felt like a gravel bike to me. One could attribute this to my general lack of desire to ride drop bars on singletrack and my love for mountain bike-sized tires on my gravel bikes.

That new silhouette is due to the updated geometry of the Fargo, bringing the Fargo 32 in line with what I would expect from a modern mountain bike: longer TT, steeper seat tube angle, and slacker head tube angle. It may not surprise you that this project started out as an update to the 29er Fargo, but the engineers (even one who rides a small frame) decided they enjoyed the 32″ wheels more and ran with the idea. The geometry comes close to the geometry of the Tributary that I was so fond of a few years ago and wished would be offered on a non-e-bike.

I can’t decide if it is frustrating to see brands reuse many year-old 29er suspension-corrected forks on their 32″ bike or if that fact is just efficient and fine. The fork on the Fargo 32 is the now-discontinued Whisky No9 Boost LT fork. Joe from Salsa illuminated the fact that the fork allowed for ~80mm of suspension correction, which is the travel a few manufacturers have teased for 32″ forks. I was initially turned off by the mix of post mount and flat mount on either part of the bike, but Joe talked some sense into me. He mentioned that the post-mount fork is easily adaptable to flat mount, and I remembered most bikes need some kind of adapter for the brakes. The flat mount rear alternator dropout can also be swapped to post mount, if someone wanted to do a full post mount setup for flat bars, since this is a frameset after all. Bike manufacturers might not need to fully reinvent the wheel for new 32″ bikes, but I look forward to seeing where the numbers all land for the new forks, rigid and suspension.

I also inquired about the redesign for the Fargo 32, asking if a new tubeset had been selected for the bike. Joe told me that in addition to a specific new tubeset, the Fargo 32 Steel would be produced by the same premium factory as their Titanium offering.

Check out both the Ti and steel versions of the Fargo 32 over at Salsa Cycles.

The post Salsa Fargo 32 Steel Review: 32 Coming Through appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Team Dream Chubby Bob’s Bar Tape Review: More Cushion, More Pushin’ – Travis Engel
entry.content:
Team Dream is a bastion of Los Angeles cycling culture, and it just dropped some fresh and functional merch. Chubby Bob’s Bar Tape is grippy, girthy, and ready to go nationwide. Travis was the first to wrap his mitts around them.

Bar tape used to be boring. Everything was about 2.5 mm thick and 30 mm wide. And besides a few freaky leather and canvas outliers, everything had the semi-soft texture of imitation cork. But now there are countless combinations of shapes, thicknesses, and surfaces.

These are great times for those of us who are touchy about our touchpoints. My preference for large-diameter mountain bike grips inspired me to hoard a few rolls of the thick, tacky fi’zi:k Bondcush. But I bailed on it the moment I tried SQlab’s rubbery Gravel Tape 714. And I’m ready to bail on that if something better comes along. So, when I heard that legendary LA tastemaker, Team Dream, was developing its own take on tape, I was eager to see what was on the spool.

Chubby Bob’s Bar Tape Quick Hits

  • Available in three sizes:
    • XL: 30mm X 3mm X 2100 mm
    • XXL: 30mm X 5mm X 2100 mm
    • XXXL: 40mm X 5mm X 1800 mm
  • Lightly textured foam
  • Kingsford BBQ Black Charcoal available at launch, with 15 more colors coming soon
  • $45 (pre-order discount for the first 24 hours after publishing)
  • Shipping in early January
  • Will be available at participating retailers by early spring, a first for Team Dream products.

Chubby Bob’s Bar Tape takes a modern approach to classic foam. There’s no veneer of fake leather or real rubber. But the surface has a slightly rougher texture than the velvety faux cork of the ‘90s. The folks at Team Dream didn’t just order this stuff unaltered off a manufacturer’s shelf and brand it with their logo. They were pretty hands-on with the Chubby Bob’s design. It feels a tad firmer than the old-school foam I had on hand for comparison, which I think makes sense for an oversized tape. That prevents it from feeling mushy or vague, but maintains its generous surface area to help distribute pressure. All three sizes are on the thicker side, as detailed above. That includes the 40mm “XXXL” version, which I installed first.

All Chubby Bob tapes feature a non-adhesive silicone strip running along the inner surface. I can’t overstate how helpful that is. No matter how many bars I’ve wrapped, every new tape is a new experience. I never know exactly how much tension I want, or how much excess I’ll have. This non-stick surface eliminates any consequences if I ever need to backtrack. And I did need to backtrack. The XXL Chubby Bob was the first 40mm tape I’d ever wrapped, and I wasn’t totally sure how to line it up. I started with my default 50% overlap, and I realized once I got to the brake hood that I was going to come up just a tad short. So I started over, without fear of peeling away chunks in the process.

I ended up with slightly more “ribbed” structure than I’d get with a 30mm tape. My best attempts at measuring on a standard, round, 23.8 mm bar got meabout  35 mm at the thickest bits and 33 mm in the valleys between. That doesn’t sound (or look) like it’d be noticeable, but the contoured shape did offer a more locked-in feeling in the drops.

To make another flat-bar comparison, those ribs are like gradual versions of the dimples in a waffle-print grip. They give your fingers a little more to grab on to. That was aided by the slightly rougher surface I mentioned. I haven’t put enough miles on the Chubby Bob tape to know if this might soften with age, but there’s almost (almost) a cat’s-tongue thing going on. It offers some of the traction that I appreciate in rubber-coated tape, but with the familiar warmth of semiporous foam.

The 30mm-wide version shares that sensation. It’s just as firm and almost as thick, with a mostly consistent diameter of about 33 mm once wrapped with 50% overlap. It looks normal from a distance, but it’s pretty dramatic when you lay your hands on it. If you’re not used to 5mm-thick tape, it’s a bit disorienting at first. Like, you almost wonder if your fingers are getting enough wrap to be secure. And if you’ve got smaller hands, or you know from experience that you don’t like thick tape, Team Dream’s 3mm x 30mm XL tape may be a safer bet. I only tried the XXL and XXL, though. And to my surprise, I liked the 5mm x 30mm XXL the best.

Personally, I didn’t get significant benefit from the novel contours of the 40mm tape. I actually preferred the 30mm tape’s flatter surface when casually gripping behind the hoods. Then, when I was in the drops, its thickness offered plenty of comfort and its material offered plenty of control. But I did my testing on bikes with front suspension and 55mm tires, which offer a lot of comfort and control on their own. I know that makes me a bit of an outlier. The 40mm XXXL version probably is an optimal choice for rigid bikes that spend any time on rough terrain. In fact, Team Dream gave the XXXL tape the nickname, “Front Suspension.”

All the new Team Dream Chubby Bob tapes come packaged in a lightweight but durable mini drawstring bag. I’ve already repurposed two of mine as travel organizers. It’s a clever approach to product presentation that will also happen to look pretty cool on a store shelf. That is worth highlighting. While the Team Dream brand’s headquarters is at The Cub House bike and plant shop just outside LA, Chubby Bob’s Bar tape is the first product they’ll be able to distribute at wholesale. That means shops around the country can get a piece of the action. It’s a big step for a small movement like Team Dream. And it’s helping ensure bar tape will never be boring again.

Pros:

  • Offers three unique approaches to the oversized tape concept
  • Non-stick silicone band keeps the tape secure and allows for hassle-free mid-wrap adjustments
  • Feels more robust than most all-foam grips
  • Available at a shop near you

Cons:

  • Not as “high-tech” feeling as some multi-material tapes
  • You’ll have to wait until January to buy it

Dropping today at 10 AM PST on Team Dream’s website.

The post Team Dream Chubby Bob’s Bar Tape Review: More Cushion, More Pushin’ appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Heads Up: All Garmin Fenix 9 Models $100 Off!
entry.content:
﻿

While Black Friday sales on Garmin Fenix series units are common, it’s virtually unheard of for Garmin to list a sale on a brand-new Fenix unit. I went back through the last few years of Fenix August announcements, and there has not been a Garmin-initiated sale of any just-announced Fenix units during that time. Sure, Uncle Amazon occasionally threw us a brief but appreciated bone, and discounted for a few hours or such, but nothing Garmin-sanctioned.

But here we are, with the first Garmin-approved sale of the Garmin Fenix 9 series, exactly 88 days after the product was announced. I’ll dive into some thoughts on why down below. But, given this rarity, I figured I’d call it out. Of course, the reality is that plenty of other companies discount their products by $100, but equally, the reality is that, around these parts, there’s a ton of interest in the Fenix 9 among DCR readers. Thus, here we are with a quick overview.

(Why this matters/backstory: In the US, companies like Garmin, GoPro, etc., all ‘sanction’ sales, or make allowances under so-called Minimum Advertised Price policies. If you advertise below the MAP price, you’ll get whacked with various penalties, usually including a product turn-off, restricting your ability to refill stock. In the rest of the world, this concept is highly illegal…but hey, it is what it is in the US.)

In any case, here’s what’s on sale, which is basically everything, and what the prices end up at:

Garmin Fenix 9 Base (AMOLED) now $899

Garmin Fenix 9 Pro (AMOLED) now $999

Garmin Fenix 9 Pro (AMOLED) inReach now $1,099

Garmin Fenix 9 Pro Solar (MIP) now $999

Garmin Fenix 9 Pro inReach Solar (MIP) now $1,099

Notably/oddly, the Enduro 4 isn’t seeing a discount here, despite being kinda part of the same family. That said, it only came out last month, so perhaps for Garmin that was a step too far.

In terms of the differences between the models, here’s the gist of it from my review (I’ve got a much longer section detailing them all side-by-side). With the first step, the differences between Base & Pro (non-inReach) are about material finishes/updates (and a bigger storage size that you may or may not care about):

– Pro adds brighter 3,000 nit display (over 2,000 nit on Fenix 9 base)
– Pro adds faster internal processor
– Pro adds full titanium case (vs just the bezel)
– Pro offers a MIP/Solar display option
– Pro adds green flashlight
– Pro gets slightly longer battery life in most categories (due to the processor upgrade)
– Pro 51mm adds 1.5″ screen vs 51mm model is a 1.4″ screen on base

Then the next step up to Pro inReach gets you all the above, plus the below satellite communications & LTE pieces:

– LTE Live two-way voice calls
– LTE LiveTrack (30-second sampling rate)
– LTE Voice Messaging
– LTE Text Messaging
– LTE Weather
– LTE & Satellite Emergency SOS
– LTE Location Check-Ins
– LTE Incident Detection & Assistance
– Satellite Messaging (basic texting)
– Satellite position/location check-ins
– Satellite Emergency SOS (via Garmin Response)
– Satellite updating of weather (new in the Fenix 9 Pro)

What’s my recommendation? Honestly, it just depends on what you want. If you’re gonna leverage the inReach pieces for either LTE or satellite messaging, that makes sense. Of course, keep in mind there’s a subscription fee for that. In terms of base vs Pro, you’re essentially paying for newer/brighter display tech and a new processor. In my review video I show base vs Pro side-by-side in terms of that map-rendering speed. It’s faster, but I wouldn’t call it a dealbreaker. Happy to answer questions down below.

One could speculate why Garmin is putting forth a sale on its flagship wearable. They already had both the Fenix 8 & Fenix 8 Pro on sale, per usual ‘last gen’ sale mantra they usually do. Garmin’s Outdoor segment, which had language in previous quarters, actually turned things around in Q3 (which posted Oct 28th, 2026). I could talk all day about what they probably were thinking when they decided to do this, but according to Garmin’s own earnings statement, they listed new adventure watches as a key reason for the higher revenue (read: the new Fenix 9).

On top of that, we’ve seen a bunch of pricing changes from Garmin in the last 4-6 months that indicate it’s becoming a bit smarter about pricing products at the point where people will still buy them. The Fenix 9 didn’t increase in price over the Fenix 8 Pro, and having an early sale will drive more sales during a period when Garmin is probably seeing a greater slowdown due to the economy.

Of course, there’s also the fact that just a few hours ago COROS teased their Vertix 4 watch, which clearly shows a flashlight on the watch. Many times these companies get their intel from retailers who are briefed on things, and then share it bidirectionally. It wouldn’t at all surprise me if Garmin is aiming to be a spoiler here on price.

Or there’s always the simplest explanation: Garmin is simply (finally) joining everyone else like Apple, Google, GoPro, etc., in putting their newly released devices on sale. Revenue is revenue.

With that – thanks for reading!

Found This Post Useful? Support The Site!

Hopefully you found this review/post useful. At the end of the day, I’m an athlete just like you looking for the most detail possible on a new purchase – so my review is written from the standpoint of how I used the device. The reviews generally take a lot of hours to put together, so it’s a fair bit of work (and labor of love). As you probably noticed by looking below, I also take time to answer all the questions posted in the comments – and there’s quite a bit of detail in there as well.

entry.title: Neuhaus Rolls Out the Hummingbird Titanium Core 32er (and 29er)
entry.content:
Neuhaus Metalworks just launched two options for its Hummingbird Core line of titanium frames ($2,999). Made in Taiwan, the nimble and snappy Hummingbird comes in a ready-to-order package in either 29er or 32er with an X-Fusion fork…

29er Hummingbird Ti, left, 32er, right

When Neuhaus first started experimenting with 32in wheels – remember the article Daniel Yang wrote for us? – the two-person bike team were shocked by how much ground they could cover. Nick Neuhaus and Daniel Yang dreamed up a titanium version: lighter and a little stiffer, it would be a rocket ship.

That said, 32ers ain’t for everyone, especially if it doesn’t fit you. Plenty of riders also want an intuitive, familiar feel, which is why the (29) Hummingbird is so popular in the first place. Fit is the very first thing we focus on when Neuhaus designs a bike, so the team split the size range by wheel size, with an overlap at ML. If you’re XL, you should really try the 32er.

Hummingbird Ti29 is the bike that likes to be pushed: a 120 mm fork, 29in wheels, a 66° head angle and 430 mm chainstays. Those are the same numbers that made the steel Hummingbird what it is.

Hummingbird Ti32 is for big days out and covering a lot of ground. Some people call that XC; reasonable people call it “riding our bikes.” It has a 100–110 mm fork, 32er wheels, a 66.5° head angle, and 445 mm chainstays. The big wheels roll over everything and hold their momentum. You could race XC on it, but Neuhaus drew it for exploring.

Check out an informative post on the Neuhaus blog about why they made it and who built these frames, as well as some demystification of the material itself. As for inventory, Neuhaus has frames in stock and shipping today. No pre-orders, no lengthy wait times. Shipping today.

Want to know more about the Hummingbird? Check out Hailey’s review. Want to see inside Neuhaus Metalworks? Read John’s shop visit. Looking for a racier bike at a premium price? Miguel reviewed the Hummingbird HBSL. Want more travel and a more affordable frameset price? Check out John’s review of the Solstice. Want to work with your local shop on a Neuhaus build? They do that too!

entry.title: French Makers: Avalanche Titanium Cages + Copra Panniers
entry.content:
Avalanche is launching a new artisan partnership with Timothée from Copra Bags, whose workshop is a few kilometers from theirs. If you recall, Marie displayed Timothée’s gravel bike at Bespoked Dresden this year. From that collaboration and others over the years, the two Parisian brands joined forces to offer up a titanium cargo cage and pannier set (€285)…

Copra Bags designed a set of side bags specifically for use with titanium cages, manufactured by the Avalanche team in its workshop. Each bag offers a maximum volume of 4.5 liters and is spacious enough to easily store camping gear, food, or spare clothing thanks to its rigid back and rear attachment system. Each bag has its own small, independent pocket, allowing for optimal organization, even in a compact package. Each bag is equipped with a durable and robust Fidlock magnetic buckle that opens and closes easily with one hand.

Avalanche titanium fork cages attach to fork eyelets at three points. They are entirely designed and manufactured in France at the Avalanche workshop.

Check it all out at Avalanche Cycles.
