entry.title: Suunto Run 2 In-Depth Review: Worth The Premium?
entry.content:
I’ve now been wearing the Suunto Run 2 for exactly one month straight, 24×7, for every workout from run to swim to ride to strength, and everything else in between. The Suunto Run 2 takes the existing Suunto Run 1 and elevates it a fair bit with offline mapping, a new brighter display, and a much improved optical heart rate sensor. They also increased GPS battery claims by about 30%, though smartwatch battery claims went down slightly.

Suunto seemed laser-focused on improving the things people rightfully complained about in the Run 1 and addressing those in the Run 2. Albeit, it now costs $100 more (and nobody complained about the price being too low last time). I suppose you can’t win them all.

The thing to understand about the Suunto Run series is that it’s hardly focused on just runners. In the same way that Garmin’s Forerunner series is hardly for just runners. Both these watches can just as easily be used for triathletes and any other sports that you can throw at it. And I’ve done just that.

With that, let’s get right into it.

What’s New:

The Suunto Run 2 takes the existing Suunto Run 1 from last year and turns it into something that’s more akin to a Suunto Race 2S. Except it’s still called the Suunto Run series, despite being just as capable a multisport watch as a running watch. While last year Suunto pitched the first Suunto Run as an inexpensive running watch, this second-generation model shouldn’t be viewed through that restricted lens.

Here’s what’s changed since the Suunto Run 1:

– Increased display brightness up to 2,000 nits (previous panel was ~1,000 nits)
– Same 1.32” display size as before
– Updated GPS chipset, though still multi-band/dual-frequency
– Notably new optical HR sensor that’s substantially better than before
– Increased GPS battery claims from 20hrs to 30hrs+ (depending on modes)
– Decreased daily smartwatch usage claim from 12 days to 10 days.
– Added offline map capability (download maps)
– Added EnergySense feature for run pacing
– Added HeatStrain Score
– Roughly the same weight as before (35g vs 36g on previous unit)
– Base price increased from $249 to $349USD (or from 249EUR to 349EUR
– Now offered in either 4GB or 64GB models ($349/$399)

In any case, keeping in mind the Suunto Run series still operates on a different operating system than the rest of Suunto’s watches, there remain some restrictions there (such as not supporting any apps in the Suunto App Store, and not supporting structured workouts from 3rd-party platforms). Further, it has fewer sport modes (~35) than the 95+ sport modes on the rest of the Suunto watches. But otherwise, it’s largely the same, minus a few little software quirks here and there that I discuss below.

The unit comes in three color options: Black, green, or white.

In The Box:

The design of the Suunto Run 2 box isn’t much different than other Suunto boxes from the last few years, but I’ve gotta say – every time I open one of the Suunto boxes, it’s one of the cleanest and best-done variants in the industry today. Of course, they took inspiration from Apple Watch boxes years ago, but the little touches on design/photography are well done.

In any case, once you extract all the pieces, here’s what you’ve got:

It’s really pretty straightforward:

– The watch pod
– The band/strap
– The charging cable
– A book you won’t read
– Some other pamphlets you also probably won’t read
– A few stickers you might use

And here’s a closer look at things:

As always, the unboxing section isn’t complicated, so let’s get right into using the watch.

The Basics:

For this first bit, I’m going to dive into all the basic features of the watch, things like activity tracking, daily usage, sleep tracking, and so on. Plus some bits from the Suunto App in those categories. In the next section I’ll cover all the sport-related aspects (including navigation).

The Suunto Run 2 mirrors the also-recent Suunto Race 3S in terms of the Suunto 3-button layout. This means there are two main buttons on the right side, plus a Digital Crown (that also acts as a button). The upper right button goes straight to accessing the most recent sport profile, the middle accesses your ‘Today’s Plan’ and the rest of the sport modes, and the bottom button acts as an escape. The Digital Crown also allows you to access the widgets. On top of that, you’ve got the touchscreen display.

If you’re familiar with other Suunto watches, the Suunto Run 2 might cause you to stumble a little bit with the user interface. While it is similar to other Suunto watches, the Suunto Run 1 & Run 2 run a slightly different operating system than all other Suunto watches. The differences are minor, but enough that muscle-memory tasks (like tapping the upper-right button to select a different sport mode) will cause some stumbles until you re-map that to the middle button instead. It’s no biggie if coming from any other brand watch, and after nearly a month of wearing it, I’ve mostly gotten used to it.

In any case, as for the display, the Suunto Run 2 uses a 2,000-nit display. It’s been perfectly fine in all my outside testing here in the Mediterranean over the last month, even on the sunniest of days. That said, as I noted in my Suunto Race 3S review, launching with a 2,000-nit display in 2026 at this price point is a bit dicey. Companies like Amazfit are putting in 3,000-nit displays in the Balance 3 at the same price point. Again, the display is perfectly fine, but if Suunto is pitching this as a premium budget watch (as weird as that sounds), then it should contain premium parts.

In any case, scrolling down from the watch face, you’ve got the widgets, which include things like steps, training volume/metrics, the weather, and more. It’s funny to see again the differences here from the other Suunto watches, for things like a lack of a specific HRV widget for example (which is on the Suunto Race 3S and other watches), and instead rolling that into the “Recovery” widget.

Nonetheless, all the things are still there, just the deck chairs in slightly different places. And as you’d expect, you can tap into any of these items to see an expanded view of them, such as steps, weather, sleep, etc.

In terms of things like sleep tracking, I haven’t had any accuracy issues here. It’s been basically spot-on with all my other wearables in this realm, and of course, the actual times I went to sleep and woke up. Note that I don’t compare sleep phases/stages, because doing so is peak faux-science. The best-case reference devices you can use to do so are only about 80% accurate, which isn’t all that great (and again, that’s a best-case scenario in perfect lab conditions). Thus, we’d never compare a heart rate sensor to a chest strap that was wrong 20% of the time. Therefore, I’m not gonna do it here either.

Of course, all of this data is mostly driven by looking at your heart rate and other movement sensor data. The Run 2 features a new heart rate sensor on the back (same as the also-new Suunto Race 3S). This sensor is a big step up from the previous Suunto sensors, which didn’t have a history of being super awesome.

In terms of a few other odds and ends, the unit is sold in two variants in terms of storage. One option is at 4GB, and the other at 64GB. This allows for more maps, but most notably also offline music that you’re never going to put on the unit. Sure, it can technically support putting MP3 files via USB cable. But there’s no support for streaming services (e.g., Spotify/etc), because those walled gardens went up years ago, and Suunto was left out in the cold (and that’s not gonna change anytime soon). Still, the option technically exists to stick MP3 files and use Bluetooth headphones to play back the music.

For everyone else, you’ll just use the Media Controls option, which controls music/podcasts/etc on your phone from the watch. Though, I often find that quite finicky. As of this very moment, I’m playing music on my phone, and the watch doesn’t show anything in Media Controls.

Sigh. But when it does, here’s what it looks like (in this case, a few seconds later it decided to enumerate for its photo shoot):

As for smartphone notifications, that too can be finicky as to whether or not they show up. But when they do, here’s what they look like:

Note that there is no flashlight built into this watch. I’m not sure if Suunto got spooked with their current lawsuit fiasco (TLDR: They picked a fight with Garmin, and Garmin fought back against Suunto’s Vertical 2 flashlight). Either way, there isn’t a physical LED flashlight here, but there is a display-based one. I’ve used it a few times for some random under-the-bed type tasks, and it’s OK enough, but it’s no real flashlight either.

When it comes to daily battery life, I’ve been using the always-on mode this entire time. And with roughly 1-3 hours of GPS time per day, I’m getting roughly 4-5 days of battery life between charges. I’m OK with that, though, as I’ll cover in the GPS battery section, that battery life seems to be falling notably short of expectations.

In terms of charging, it uses the same charger as the rest of the recent Suunto watches, which is a magnetic charger that works perfectly fine. It even has a nice braided cable, something that Garmin only offers on their $3,000+ MARQ watches.

Finally, I do want to mention briefly that I’m not in love with the strap/band. Specifically, the tiny little doohickey at the end that keeps the band from flapping around. This doohickey portion that goes through the band is simply not big enough, perhaps 1mm too small (maybe 0.5mm too small), and thus it’s constantly popping off.

I know this sounds trivial, and sure I could go buy another band, but equally, it’s just as if nobody actually wore this thing.

In fact, one day while out gravel riding, I paused for a second to grab some stuff out of my hydration pack, and when I did so, it caught the strap of my watch and actually removed the whole thing and flung it out into the bushes (because it undoes so easily). Not a huge deal, as I was able to go find it, but frankly, I’ve never had that happen in my life before. Let alone the strap unhinging on a multiple-times-a-day basis.

Ok, with that, let’s get into the sports bits.

Sports & Navigation:

The Suunto Run 2 is definitely not just a watch for runners. It’s a true and fully capable multisport watch that can be used for running, cycling, swimming, and a gazillion other sports (including triathlon). And in fact, I pretty evenly spread my time out among those sports and more during my testing.

To start a workout, you’ll tap the middle left button. This then shows anything in our ‘Today’s Plan’ section, which can be structured workouts you’ve saved. Below that are your sport modes:

The Suunto Run 2 has 35 sport profiles on it, which are as follows:

Running, Indoor Cycling, Cycling, Trail Running, Pool Swimming, Openwater Swimming, Track Running, marathon, Treadmill, Vertical Running, Walking, Hiking, Trekking, Mountaineering, Climbing, Triathlon, Orienteering, Cross Training, Mountain Biking, Jump Rope, Indoor Rowing, Crosstrainer, Aerobics, Weight Training, Circuit Training, Stretching, Boxing, Yoga/Pilates, Cross-country Skiing, Alpine Skiing, Snowboarding, Tennis, Badminton, Outdoor Training, Indoor Training

Once you choose a given sport profile, you can then select to enable different features for it, such as following a structured workout, navigating a route/point of interest/bearing, as well as enabling certain targets, like a distance/calorie/pace/duration target.

It’ll also show you how much battery is remaining for that particular battery mode/configuration. Meaning if you get ready to start a workout and you realize you only have 2 hours of battery remaining, but need 4 hours, you can change to other battery modes, including performance, endurance, and power saving. These toggle various features on/off to eke out a bit more battery. I’ve generally found that the Suunto Run 2 overestimates how much battery it has. More on that in a second.

Anyway, in my case, I’ll pick a course for today: This straightforward trail run I did the other day that goes up a mountain and comes back down again:

I do wish I could see more details about the route before (or even after) I select it, such as rendering the actual map below it, rendering the elevation profile, etc. I create routes all the time for trail runs, and while I usually just know it’s the most recent one, it’d be handy to see exactly where this is – rather than just on an empty black screen.

In any case, we’ll head out and start running. You’ll see your normal data on the screen as you’ve configured in the settings.

You’ll also see your navigation and map fields as well. In my case you can see the upcoming route shown on the map, as well as distance remaining.

Then, you’ll also see an elevation profile of the route and where you stand in that situation:

If you go off-route, you’ll get a buzz that you’re off-route, and you can check the map page to see how you managed to screw up. There’s no automatic re-routing; you’ll just want to get yourself back to the course/route itself.

There’s also the new Energy Sense feature, which tells you how much juice it thinks you have left in the tank at that given intensity level, in distance. Suunto bills it to be used in a race-like situation, though there’s no need to do that. You could use it in everyday training as well.

In many ways, it’s got similarities to Garmin’s Stamina feature that’s been around for a number of years (and recently expanded to include both pace and heart rate stamina zones). Now, to be clear, I don’t really ever consult Garmin’s Stamina feature, as I don’t find it super useful.

That said, once you start using a Suunto and a Garmin side-by-side, you quickly realize the fatal flaw in Suunto’s implementation: It has nothing to do with energy (per the name EnergySense), but instead, Pace. It should be renamed “PaceSense”. That’s because the Suunto watch only looks at your pace, not your heart rate.

The easiest way to see this is to simply go down a hill (like above, showing a reduced 55%, when seconds before it was in the 90s). This isn’t because my heart rate is high (it’s not, it’s just 152bpm). But instead, because I’m going faster down a hill (4:06/km, or about 6:50/mi). Yet, when I’m going up a hill at a harder intensity like below (161bpm at 5:18/km or 8:32/mi), now I have somehow more Endurance (88%).

Again, I don’t really understand the point of calling this EnergySense, when it doesn’t look at energy at all (e.g., heart rate, or even calories). Instead, it’s purely looking at pacing, and even if you have a perfectly flat course, when looking at a longer event, like a marathon, how you pace energy-wise is just as much a function of heart rate as it is of pace. And further, to that extent, your ‘Endurance’ isn’t going to be a result of your pace, but of how hard your body is working to maintain that pace. I’m honestly baffled that this is as shortsighted as it is, even being marketed as a beta feature. Did nobody run with this anywhere with hills?

In any case, speaking of the data fields you’ve set up, these are configurable in the Suunto App, and you can customize them on a per-sport profile basis. I still wish I could just tweak existing core sport profiles, rather than having to create duplicates – but that’s just the way Suunto’s been for years.

Oh, speaking of things in the app, this is where you can download maps to the Suunto Run 2. As noted earlier, there is a 4GB and a 64GB model. The thing is, Suunto’s maps are divided up into very small regions, so you can pretty easily get away with just the 4GB model. Especially if you don’t do a ton of traveling. Realistically, I think Suunto could have just gotten away with a single 8GB or 16GB model and called it done. For example, while all of France would be 7GB, the region around Paris would only be 200MB (0.2GB).

In any event, once your workout is completed, you’ll see the details on the watch or in the Suunto App. For example, here on the Suunto App:

Beyond singular workouts, Suunto is also tracking your overall training load and recovery stats. Starting with training load, it’ll track that a few different ways, the first being TSS (Training Stress Score), in a widget you can see on the watch and the app.

It’ll show a bit of a breakdown of your sports:

Next, there’s CTL (Chronic Training Load), showing how this compares to recent history:

Within that, you’ll see your estimated VO2Max, as well as estimated 5K/10K/etc times. These all seemed a bit low to me (as in, both VO2Max was estimated low, and my current 5KM time seems about 1-2 mins slower than reality).

Then there’s TSB (Training Stress Balance), and it’s recommendation for me and my recent training load:

And then finally, there’s Recovery Time, looking at how you’re recovering from recent workouts. I do find the contrast between my TSB noted above and my recovery state noted below…well…notable. In theory, I should see some correlation here.

Meanwhile, within the Recovery area is where you’ll see your HRV values:

And all of this is also visible within the Suunto App as well:

Lastly, let’s quickly chat about battery during workouts. In my experience, this is falling short of my expectations. And seemingly, short of Suunto’s claims. Or more specifically, the watch’s own ability to predict battery life. In every case where I was under 20-25% battery, and the watch claimed one thing (e.g., 5-7 hours of battery remaining), the watch would run out of battery mid-activity, well below/before its own estimates.

Here’s the actual battery claims from Suunto’s site:

Here’s a simple battery example during a ride:

Start: 86%
End: 70%
Duration: 3 hours
Estimate: 5.45%/hour or 18.35hrs capacity
No navigation or external sensors enabled, multiband configuration AOD.

In this configuration, it got the 18 hours it’s rated for, but equally, every single time the estimates on the watch itself would be incorrect for what it actually burned. Meaning, I quickly came to not trust those estimates. If it said 5 hours remaining, you had at best 2-3 hours remaining.

But at least it did hit the estimates on their site. They just need to tweak whatever logic they’re using in the watch to correctly figure out battery burn.

Accuracy (GPS & Heart Rate):

In this section I’ll look at the accuracy of the new optical heart rate sensor, the upgraded GPS/GNSS chipset, as well as an occasional glance at the elevation profile, especially for mountain runs. These are compared to both a chest strap and other watch/band optical HR sensors.

First up we’ve got this mostly steady-state run, including an initial downhill portion for a few kilometers. Zero issues here, it looks good:

Next, we’ve got an interval run. This one got off to a rough start for whatever reason. But after that warm-up, things simmered down and it nailed all the intervals without issue.

Next, a trail run up/down a mountain. This had some variability in it, running with others (meaning, sometimes a bit lower HR’s). Still, overall this is pretty good. At some walking intensities, it was slightly mixed, but when actually running, it was mostly good enough.

Next, an indoor trainer ride. Here we can see it’s a bit wobbly in the first few minutes, but it gets the general trend right. After that it’s perfectly fine.

Whereas heading outside, looking at one of (many) outdoor rides, this one with lots of up and downs into the mountains, things are…shall we say, rough. Sure, it’s right for a good chunk at a time, but it’s wrong an awful lot – especially when I’m descending or at slightly lower intensities.

Switching over to the GPS side of things, starting off with a relatively straightforward run. Some occasional buildings and such, but nothing too complicated to begin:

Still, when I zoomed in, the Suunto was consistently the ‘odd duck,’ being just slightly offset from the others, even in basically open sky conditions:

Or here, where both COROS and Suunto are off in the road, playing in traffic. The Fenix 9 Pro has me properly on the sidewalk:

Next, a trail run into the mountains. Pretty straightforward up and down, but with lots of switchbacks:

Most of the trails were pretty good. Occasionally, a few quirks from different units being off a couple of meters, but nothing I was super concerned about.

Looking at the elevation profile, some slight disagreement there on the offset, but they all largely trended together. I don’t know the precise elevation of the ‘summit’ here since it’s sorta a forest service style road that just meanders along the mountains. Note: this was at/through sunset (over the course of two hours), so temps were shifting.

Next, looking at an outdoor road ride up into the mountains, from a GPS standpoint, things look perfectly fine at a high level:

And when I zoom in during some of the climbs, things are good here too:

That said, as I descend for some of these switchbacks at higher speeds, it’s a bit more Mario Kart than I’d like. I don’t tend to see this amount of variability here (into the bushes, wrong side of road, etc.), as I am from the Suunto Run 2.

Meanwhile, the elevation profile here is all good. No problems at all:

Finally, I’ve got GPS tracks from an openwater swim. Suffice to say, this was going well…till it wasn’t. No idea why it decided to slam through the side of a mountain when I didn’t. But maybe it just wanted some pool time instead. As for the swim buoy track, well…the watch fell into the water (flipped over on the strap). But you can pretty clearly see when it was above water and when it was under. Either way, the Suunto Run 2 was a hot mess here. MARQ was spot on.

Overall, I’d say that the GPS is probably perfectly acceptable for most land-based activities, but if you’re a bit nitpicky, you might not love some of the imperfections that I didn’t see on the higher-end Suunto Race 3S, or other competitive watches.

Meanwhile, for heart rate, this is a massive step up from the Suunto Run 1. While this sensor appears to struggle with outdoor cycling, for all other scenarios it’s been perfectly fine.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Wrap-Up:

The Suunto Run 2 brings with it a lot of improvements that make it a compelling upgrade over the original Suunto Run 1. While that original watch was aimed at the budget end of the spectrum, with the jump to $349, Suunto is focusing a bit more on the premium end of that budget running watch realm. For those that want a much better display, offline maps, and a better optical heart rate sensor, it’ll probably be worth that $100 jump in price.

Where Suunto gets themselves into a little bit of a pickle is they’re essentially giving up the budget end of the spectrum to COROS (with the Pace 4 and Pace Pro) and Amazfit (and even Garmin with the Forerunner 70/Vivoactive 6, sans-maps). While I think Suunto can largely justify the $349 price point with premium materials/looks, I worry that, long term, not having any current-gen Suunto watch model below this price point takes Suunto out of the running for a portion of the population. Time will tell, though; I feel like time and history already told us how this ends about 4-5 years ago, the last time Suunto tried this pricing shift and had to retreat. Adding to the complication is that the Suunto Run 2 doesn’t run the same operating system as the rest of Suunto’s watches, making it less likely to get as many new feature updates (again, as history clearly told us with the Run 1).

Nonetheless, if you view the Suunto Run 2 through the lens of what it has today, especially around the looks/materials, it’s a good option that gets the job done. Said differently, if what you see in this review, feature-wise, makes you happy…go forth!

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 2 // Cairngorm Traverse
entry.content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON

TRACK 2:  Cairngorm Traverse

Thomas and I wake to the pitter-patter of rain against the metal roof of the Ben Nevis luxury inn. We are happy to get a good night's rest and sleep inside, but the rain outside challenges our mood and stokes. I like to prescribe to coffee and then take on the day. No use formulating outcomes or stressors on the day till you're fully awake and alert. We are treated downstairs to a classic Scottish breakfast fare and some striking characters. Thomas and I don’t say much to each other this morning. Our crown jewel for this project — Tower Ridge on Ben Nevis stands mysteriously in the clouds, and the rain is picking up.

In these moments, I always wonder what good it does to check in with the weather. It is what it is, right? On this day, the weather gods were against us. Torrential rain, 40- 50 mph winds, and sub-freezing temps. I think we were both wondering if heading up into the cirque was even possible on a day like this, not to mention all the riding we needed to do. Thomas was also starting to show some signs of the previous wet and cold days, developing a minor cold. Still, we don’t speak about the obvious objective and weather challenge.

Dressed and ready for the day, we head down to the hotel's bike storage and start assembling and tinkering with our rigs for the day. There is a door to the outside there that is slightly cracked. I can hear the rain smashing against the door in waves, and gusts of wind occasionally breach this door and rush in. It’s at this point that we start to look at a more detailed forecast. Grim. At this point, it just seems a bit foolish and dumb to force this technical ridge in these conditions. Could we hike up the standard hikers route and summit Ben Nevis? Yes, for sure. That being said, our inspiration lacked for this alternative. So as the rain continued to fall, we biked away from Fort William with no peak.

On trips like this, the timeline doesn’t allow for you to wait on good weather or hunker down. The rest of the mixtape was waiting. I have a love-hate relationship with cruxes on a trip like this. You need to make a decision and get on with it. No point in sulking or being bummed about your current state. I told Thomas we would be back for it someday, and I’m sure he was grateful to focus on the bike for today and his body preservation. Certainly, going up into the Ben with those temperatures and winds would have only sent his body plummeting (and start my downfall too!). Which is totally fair; we have to compromise and make the best of our current situation. As you will find out in the coming paragraphs, we had a wonderful day as we started our traverse of the Cairngorms.

Leaving Fort William on Day 4, the rain only continues. This helps validate our decision. As every day prior, we are quickly into the rough stuff and off-piste trails. As we leave the highlands and start heading East, we assume that maybe today's riding will be slightly less vert-intensive. Only time will tell. An hour into the ride, the skies really open up. The torrential rain meets us a mile or so outside of the tiny village of Spean Bridge. The type of rain you can’t really ride in. Feels proper sketchy. Your first reaction under these conditions is to find shelter. We spot the first cafe and pull in. The sound of rush-hour traffic plowing through pooled-up water on the road keeps us alert. Inside the cafe, we see fellow cyclists and motorists looking soggy and dreary. This is all just part of the unexpected adventure. Going with the twists and turns of the day is what makes an outing rich and rewarding. We both order a big stack of pancakes and tea. Calories usually help keep the good vibes going. Plus, Thomas and I keep a healthy banter going that usually keeps the good times flowing.

Leaving Spean Bridge, we were treated to a brief moment of truly blue skies and sunshine, a first of the trip. As we transitioned from the Highlands and started riding East, we began to ride favorable winds, and the terrain started to shift. As we traversed many a farm field, we began to get a taste of the sneaky gnarly tracks that lie in the rolling hills between the big mountains. The riding here was lush and interesting. We chased sheep around corners and swooped down into grassy fields. To me, this style of riding is quintessential Scotland. Some low country, hard-to-read and faint tracks that really keep you guessing where you are going. We rode by some ancient ruins and crossed a few technical creeks. The riding here is playful and slow. Our bikes are filthy and covered in muck, yet Thomas and I forget about our morning sorrow and worries. We climb beautiful singletrack through a purple haze of heather and twist our way into new zones.

The rain and swirling clouds pick up as we climb towards Lochan na h-Earba. The exposure and grandeur of this place set in. The clouds shift to a darker tone, and Thomas and I space out. We are sandwiched between some peaks, but the atmosphere feels desolate and isolated. No trees or anything for shelter. The rain worsens. I start smashing pedals in hopes of crossing the few miles of this loch to a set of woods on the other side. The double-track here is lined with unavoidable mud and puddles. Franz Ferdinand jamming in my ears, the pedals turn over, and the legs feel good. I look back behind me for the flash of Thomas’s sinewave beacon, letting me know he is on his way. We both reach the safety of the woods in a bit of a blur. The cold has really set in, and Thomas and I comment on how things are getting quite serious. Both soaked to the bone, we know this isn’t a place we can really hang out.

After the wave of storms rolled through, we were rewarded with tailwinds and sunshine. Crossing castles and more lochs, our sights were set on the village of Kingussie. It felt good to stomp out some tarmac and make decent time to our final stop for the day. My classic memory of this day is rolling up on a pair of Highland coos. I will never forget their eyes slowly closing and their hair blowing in the wind. Symbolic of the day we had. Thomas and I were ready for our usual fish n chips entree and then sleep.

Day 5, our routine is starting to find its Scottish rhythm. Having ridden here in 2022, I can confidently say that the riding around Cairngorm National Park is world-class. The network of trails and gravel roads between the River Spey and CNP is amazing. You could spend a couple of weeks exploring and setting a home base in Kingussie or Aviemore. Definitely something I would consider doing sometime in the future. Diving bombing single track and pine needle tracks through quaint neighborhoods had Thomas and me stoked for this new shift in terrain and topography. Skies also looked calm and mostly favorable all day, a real Scottish treat! We stopped to admire ancient castles and babbling brooks. Our chatter flowing and bike cranks spinning.

Rolling into Glenmore National Nature Preserve at the bottom of Cairngorm National Park feels distinctly different than the Highlands. This side of the country feels more arid and dry. There are clusters of woods and trees that make this area feel more like Colorado. We can see the peaks forming above us, their alpine tundra looking distinctly beige and purple. On this day, we were going to be meeting up with a local friend and professional photographer, Johnny Cook. Thomas and I met Johnny at the Kendal Mountain film festival in 2021. We instantly hit it off with Johnny, and we both had just made a friend for life. It was extra special to reunite with him on this trip and have him show us our second ridge of the trip: Fiacaill Ridge.

From Glenmore, it was a roughly 1,000ft climb up to the Cairngorm Mountain and ski hill, our staging zone to start running. I reveled in the 1k tarmac climb, reminiscent of an alpine switchbacked road that we are both familiar with back home. The sun was shining brightly; I took my shirt off for the first time all trip. With the energy from the sun and our excitement to start running, we smashed our way up this climb. The juxtaposition of going from more isolated terrain to a more touristy spot is always a shock, but I have grown used to this dynamic over the many trips in my career. I just embrace the adventure and enjoy the side banter with random folks. We are on our own quest, and it's best not to get overwhelmed by much and stay rock steady.

As Thomas and I were transitioning from cycling shoes to running shoes, our friend Johnny appeared. Our morale was great, but when you see a friend after a long hiatus, our mood and vibe totally skyrocketed. Thomas and I were eager to catch up with Johnny and have him show us one of his local alpine romps. As we started to run, the wind said hello. Okay, maybe it was more of a raging hello! The wind couldn’t dampen our spirits as we started to travel cross-country towards Fiacaill ridge. From far away, this ridge looked unassuming and chill. Up close, the ridge became uniquely geometric and blocky. The granite scrambling here was super unique, and the positioning above the corries (bowl- or amphitheater-shaped hollows carved into the side of mountains by glacial erosion during past ice ages) was dramatic and exposed. The wind tried to blow us off the ridge, but it just added an alpine feeling to it all. Fall colors were beginning to show in the tundra, and the views were panoramic and otherworldly. Johnny does a lot of skiing and works in the ski industry, and he was pointing out all the couloirs and interesting lines. As we ran back down into the corrie, we spotted climbers on more vertical terrain. A subtle reminder for me to come back and do more exploring here. It's always inspiring to get out with a local and really absorb the flavor of a zone.

Back on the bikes, it was another transition and then a mach speed rip back down Cairngorm mountain road to Glenmore. On our way down, we could see the devastation from wildfires that have consumed and burned a lot of the hills surrounding where we were running. From my research online, “The blaze burned approximately 25 square kilometres (around 3,500 football pitches or 2,500 hectares) of rare Caledonian forest, Scots pine, and moorland on July 24th, 2026, prompting the evacuation of over 700 people from areas including Glenmore and Nethy Bridge. Over 500 firefighters, helicopters, and partner agencies fought the blaze.” From what I recall, the embers seep deep into the soil and burn for a while, making it super hard to control and mitigate. Seeing the burned hillsides is sobering and also reminds us of the very similar fire reality we live with back home. Okay, time to keep rolling.

Back down in Glenmore, Thomas and I are ready for some calories. Johnny meets us at the Pine Martin, a ski après-style bar for our post-run hang. We sat there and chatted for a while, eating some delicious curry, enjoying a pint of something light and refreshing. Thomas and I didn’t look at the clock or feel rushed. This was part of our adventure, and our agenda was being created in real time. Soaking up the good times together, not knowing when our paths would cross with Johnny again. When it was time to part ways, Johnny gave us a celebratory sip of a really nice whiskey. As we wet our palates with something way too nice and expensive for Thomas and I ever to own, the sweetness of orchard fruits, baking spices, and smoke dance on our tongues. We say farewell to our Scottish friend and hop back onto the bikes.

Due to the fires I mentioned above, our original plan to go up and over Ryvoan Pass is thwarted by wildfire closures. Moments like this always happen on bikepacking trips, so it's best to just stay calm and not stress about a potential detour or going a new way. In all honesty, I was excited to ride something new; I had done Ryvoan Pass before in 2022. It's really, really cool, but what we ended up doing was equally cool and unique. It was getting to be late afternoon, and Thomas and I were strategizing how far we could make it that evening. As we shredded down some loamy forested tracks, we set our sights on the village of Nethy Bridge; from there we would make our dinner plans and riding goal for the rest of the evening. I always really enjoy getting back on the bike after running. Feels like you end up covering so much ground when using multiple modes of transportation.

In Nethy Bridge, we were coming up on 5 pm. We dashed into a quaint convenience store in an otherwise tiny and quiet town. Inside, it was the usual grab for something salty and sweet. A sip of sugar and chips... oh wait, they call these things crisps. After the pitstop, we got back on track, linking our tracks to the fire detour. The afternoon and early evening were unfolding in good fortune, and hopping between villages kept us psyched and spontaneous. As the purple sky began to meet the purple heather-lined two-track, our stopping point for the evening came into focus: Tomintoul. The segment from Nethy to Tomintoul was a wonderful all-terrain delight. Premier Cairngorm cycling, a bit of an adventure navigating a twisting river, and a dash of hiking. An hour of sunset spinning brought us to a tarmac climb up to our final destination of the day.

Tomintoul felt a bit mysterious and quaint. Less than 800 people call this place home, and only a few spots of sustenance are available. The one place with lights on was the local hotel and Indian food joint. Well, I know what we are having for dinner. What seemed maybe slightly suspect ended up turning into a fine evening of calories. Maybe slightly chaotic for our tired bodies, but it was our only option. After dinner, it was a few-minute spin towards the park above town to find a spot to camp. Thomas and I set up our tarp, donned the midge nets, flicked our red lights on, and tucked into our bivy. A solid day out traversing one of Scotland’s wonderful landscapes!

Stay tuned for Track 3: the Pictish Trail.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots, Tailfin, & Skratch Labs

entry.title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 1
entry.content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON


Exploring a place by bicycle works its way deep into your soul. Once you’ve traveled this way, it becomes your beacon and north star for how you want to explore the world. Taking in the landscape pedal stroke by pedal stroke, you start to learn the fabric of a place. Feeling the weather and terrain isn’t just one aspect of the outing; it becomes your identity and sole purpose for moving. The reward for moving your body all day through a place is knowledge and wisdom, things you can apply towards future trips and life in general.

Scotland is world-renowned for its rugged and beautiful landscape. Its people are hardened by the weather, but their desire for exploration and adventure in the hills is very much alive. There is a deep mystery about this place that is intriguing to me. The craggy tracks and alpine roads cutting through magnificent mountains planted a seed of curiosity. What would it be like to travel through this place simply? On bike and on foot, carving our way through this ancient country. Thus the Scottish Mixtape was born — a fully self-supported mission to link up 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks. From Scotland’s capital, Edinburgh, we traveled over the famous highlands, traversed the Cairngorms, and then down the Pictish trail, creating a big, diverse loop.

For the purposes of organization and to showcase this route, I will break the mixtape into 3 separate tracks, each corresponding to the 3 cycling routes we explored.

Filmmaker and photographer Thomas Woodson was alongside me for this Scottish adventure. This wouldn’t be a bike blog without digging into the bikes, and I will touch on setups a bit throughout. Thomas was riding his Moots MXC, and I was on the new Moots Womble, both bikes equipped with front forks and dropper posts for maximum shredding and efficiency. As always, feel free to drop a comment or email if you have more specific questions about setups, and I will include full bike check photos at the bottom. Sit back, grab a tea or a pint, and listen to the play-by-play from the Scottish Mixtape.

   

Track 1: Into the Highlands

Our bodies are stiﬀ and creaky. It’s really 3 am Colorado time as we depart our flight into Scotland's capital, Edinburgh. I think the biggest stressor for a trip like this surrounds traveling with a bike. This topic alone deserves its own blog and write-up. Needless to say, our bikes made it, and soon enough we were building our extremely capable mountain rigs in the crowded airport arrival terminal. Thomas must have snuck some coﬀee in somewhere, because by the time I was getting organized, he was ready to roll. Dang, time to get with it! I was distracted by the bright lights and stream of people passing by.

Handlebars, wheels — straighten it up - wait, tinker again, fix. Okay, is this right? Thomas! “I need help!” Good thing we make a great team. I have been adventuring with Thomas for a decade now. We have traveled to many countries together and mesh super well. Finding a partner that complements you and brings out your best self is a wonderful thing. Outside of being strong in the mountains and competent on technical terrain, Thomas is a logistical wizard and has an everlasting attitude to get things done no matter the circumstances. These are instrumental attributes on a trip with so much uncertainty and the unknown. We have a tight timeline. We need to be back in Edinburgh in 8 days to then catch our flight back to Colorado the following day. Okay, enough of this, time to hit the road!

Moots all built up at Edinburgh International Airport

In classic Scottish style, as we roll away from the hustle and bustle of the airport, the skies open up. The wind picks up in a fury, and we put on our rain gear. This would be the first of a long trip- a long process of navigating and handling the weather. Under my hood and amidst the rain, I crack a smile and let out a giddy laugh. This is why we are here. To experience the full spectrum of conditions and emotions of traveling through a new place. Our first day of riding would almost exclusively be on canal and bike paths; what a treat! One of my goals for this trip was to get oﬀ the main roads and into the magic of a place. And by magic, I mean all the sneaky little roads that take you to the heart of place rather than around it. As we worked our way towards Callander, we got to experience the canal boats and farm lifestyle that make up this part of the country. Riding through tunnels and lush forest, we sneak glances at quaint villages and ancient cobblestone paths. At one point during another wave of rain, we pass by a school. It was clearly lunch break, and all the teens were out walking towards their favorite hangouts. In the pouring rain, we noticed that no one was wearing raincoats. Huh. Are we doing this wrong? Rain and being wet is a way of life in Scotland; not much fuss about the weather. Go do your thing and get on with it!

By this point in the day, we had linked into the famous GBDURO (Great Britain Divide), a cycling route that covers the entire length of Great Britain. We would use this route to help carry us North. We traversed our first fields of Scottish livestock and enjoyed varied riding on all types of surfaces. Our bodies still on Colorado time, we visualized and dreamed about our first proper. Bopping and weaving around more farms, we could see our first stopping point of the night in Callander. A beautiful little village right on the edge of the highlands. We had booked a night at the Crown Inn, knowing that a real night's sleep in a bed would help set us up for a successful trip. Thomas and I love to play games, but when it comes to bikepacking, we generally adhere to a few basic rules and let the rest go with the flow. We see what the land and weather give us. This trip wasn’t about how hard and brutal can we make things; it's about the full-body and mind immersion into a landscape. We have our notepads out and want to learn and grow from this place. Students of the world traveling by bike.

One of the beautiful things about Scotland is how popular and welcoming the people are to bikes. People tour here on bikes, and it's not a new thing. You won’t get any strange or random looks. You will get chirps of encouragement and curiosity. The hotel staﬀ and BnB hosts will welcome your dirty bikes and bike shoes and have a safe place to store that stuﬀ, either in your room or a dedicated indoor bike shelter. I think this way of life helps cut the tension and edge that one can have while traveling in a new place, especially when your body is depleted after a hard day of pedaling. After sorting ourselves in our lodging, we slipped on our running shoes and headed out to the streets of Callander for some fish and chips. Thomas and I exchanged stories from the day as the native language and tongue echoed through the dining hall. Mates bantered about golf and what pint to drink next; we quietly observed our surroundings as our new reality for the next week set in. With our bellies full, we enjoyed some sunset light while strolling down the River Teith. It was a hectic and full-on first day in Scotland. Time to dry out our clothes and get some rest.

Moots arriving in Callander Day 1


Alarms chirping at 5:45 am, the hot water kettle starts bubbling, and we tear open our instant craft coﬀee from Idle Hands Roasting. The little morning treat that brought us energy and psyche every day. Thanks to Peter Jones for the full trip supply! Skies were grey and overcast, with mild temps. After hunting down some classic Scottish pastries and goodies down the street, it was time to set oﬀ. Our day would start oﬀ following the GBDURO to the small town of Killin, before branching oﬀ towards the mega-classic West Highland Way — (Scotland’s premier long-distance walking route, stretching 96 miles (154 km) from Milngavie (just north of Glasgow) to Fort William in the Scottish Highlands).

A misty collection of clouds started to form as we made our way north along bike paths, contouring lochs and villages. It felt special and unique to be on such fantastic bike infrastructure, tucked away in the woods. After a couple of hours of spinning, we reached a tiny pass, and the skies started to open up. As we stopped, we came to our first interaction with the famous Scottish midges. Tiny microscopic flies, coordinating in unison and buzzing towards their next victim. I could feel their wrath as we stopped to put on our rain jackets and pants. Maybe it's better if it's raining? At least then the midges subside. More to come on that later. As we buzzed down to the town of Killin, we had our first proper feeling of being completely saturated with water. My giddy smile and laugh from the day before started to flatten.

Thomas Woodson on film above Loch Lyon


In the town of Killin, we rushed towards the first cafe in sight. Was this a storm that would pass, or something that was hugging the mountains and would be around all day? Only time would tell. No use looking a weather app or forecast, it was unreliable and inaccurate. In classic Scottish style, we ordered a few breakfast teas and some toasties (basically a grilled cheese with a sweet chutney). Thomas and I slipped out of our wet cycling shoes and air-dried our feet discreetly under our table. As we were eating, a pair of cyclists showed up in similar fashion. Good reminder that this is totally normal and what we were doing wasn’t anything extraordinary. They were from Poland on a similar grand adventure (albeit on gravel bikes) out taking in the wonderful countryside.

For us, it is always encouraging and enjoyable to chat with folks along the way and feed oﬀ the energy of a place. Our new Polish cyclist friends seemed to have a determined edge, and we ended up sharing a similar route for a few miles. As we hit some steep grades, I think they started to grow jealous of our mountain bikes and gearing. As we soft-pedaled up our first real mountain pass, I was grateful for our setups and the terrain we were about to encounter. While never truly quitting, the rain turned more into a soft mist, which is far more favorable than a straight downpour. Our views were limited at the top of this pass, but I could tell we were on the cusp of getting into the good stuﬀ. Remote, wild, and properly in the highlands.

As we traveled around the south side of Loch Lyon, we rode premier double track. The kind of tracks I dreamed about, my inspiration for putting this whole trip together. Riding the right bikes, with the right person, everything was falling into place. Steep grassy hillsides, sheep, Highland Coos, countless river crossings- this section really had it all. Quintessential Scottish riding. Beams of sun would occasionally pop out and highlight a magnificent hillside. My giddy smile and laugh returned. Thomas was on the same page, and we hooted and hollered around each bend. Finally able to let loose and ride our mountain rigs with some flair. Being out in the wild, tucked in the mountains, felt like being home in Colorado. This is where Thomas and I thrive. At the end of this double track segment, we started a long downhill towards Kinglass Cottage and the West Highland Way. It was pretty obvious once we were on the WHW, as we immediately started passing thru-hikers. As we traversed the hillside, we set our sights on our next pitstop: Bridge of Orchy.

In classic logistical Thomas style, he had found a semi-secret stop for dinner, just a ways past Bridge of Orchy. He had made a call during lunch to set up a dinner reservation. We planned to stop in Orchy, grab a pint, then roll down the road for dinner plans. After dinner, we would continue on the WHW and find camp somewhere. I think trips like this require you to act fast and think on your toes. No one decision is ever that hyper critical, but make a decision and then go with it. I think having a good partner helps this process. Sometimes it's easy to get lured into a resupply or waste time. Finding the balance between riding the flow and making calculated decisions is the game. On this Day 2, we played our cards right and were rewarded with a fantastic day of quality and diverse riding. At dinner, we enjoyed one of our best meals. Sometimes best on a trip like this equals quantity, but at this fine establishment, we were treated with massive portions and delicious food. We even had a first tasting of some local whiskey. Felt rude not to sample!

Throughout the day, we had heard rumbles of evening and overnight torrential rain. Let me skip to the chase. Yup, that happened. We ended up riding maybe 3 miles to one of the few clusters of dense trees in the area. All of the Highlands is barren due to centuries of deforestation. Which means finding a good bivy site that is protected is tough. I think most locals would have laughed at our sleep setup, but I think I still stand behind it. Between us, we shared a flat tarp and ground sheet. Individually, we each had sleeping pads, bags, and bug nets. It appeared most people camped out in the open with proper enclosed tents. Hmmm. So we were oﬀ into the dense woods and mossy floor for a tucked-away bivy. I like feeling cozy even if it has its downsides. An exposed tent out in the open just feels wrong, especially on a night forecasting torrential rain and high winds.

Sleep was on and oﬀ. Out of the whole trip, this was one of the harder moments. The rain was persistent and loud against the Dyneema tarp. I also don’t want to gloss over the fact that just a couple of hours earlier, I was being eaten alive by midges. It was the Scottish gods (and maybe Thomas) seeking sweet revenge on my trip and idea. Making sure you never walk away unscathed, gathering a few lessons to learn along the way. In some aspects, the heavy rain eased my tension and pain. As we would come to find out later on Day 3, which proved to be one of the grandest and hardest day yet. Despite the rough night, we still had the energy and stoke to keep pushing. Waking up in the mist, Thomas and I remarked back and forth how intense that was.

morning wakeup ritual with Idle Hands Instant coﬀee


Moots on the West Highland Way


Awake and caﬀeinated by morning cold brew in a running soft flask, a few bites of something go into the body (not to mention the bites I was nursing on my body). We pack our wet bikes and gear inside fully waterproof Tailfin bike bags, proving their weight in gold. For me, I think it was seeing the sun that morning. It provided me the internal stoke and confidence to complete this trip. The light and scenery were otherworldly and magical. Entering the Glencoe valley was what dreams are made of. Giant peaks and ridges in all directions. We stopped for breakfast at one of the few ski resorts in Scotland, the famous Glencoe Hill. Full Scottish breakfast and coﬀee for me, please. The midge welts on my face and arms burned and itched. This felt like a warm trap to stay here all day, and I’m glad we were both motivated and stoked to keep the pace up.

Back on the bikes, feeling small. Coming around the corner, seeing Buachaille Etive Mòr (Stob Dearg) is a top 3 moment of the trip for me. This perfect pyramid, erupting out of the earth, was visually too perfect. How could something like this even exist? It was full steam ahead to our next objective, our first scramble of the trip, Curved Ridge. I first heard about this route when I saw an iconic photo of Kilian Jornet Burgada scrambling up Curved Ridge during his 2017 win at Glen Coe Skyline. Ever since then, it’s been on my tick list. One of the anchors of this project was to link 3 technically interesting running and scrambling routes in Scotland. Curved Ridge proved to be indeed a mega classic. As Thomas and I approached this massive pyramid of a peak, we could see a series of twisting ridges jutting up towards the summit. Clouds were swirling and rays of sun stabbed through the sky. It was now or never. As we approached the trailhead, the scale of this mountain started to introduce itself. We stashed our bikes against a climbing school hut, switched into our running kit, and set oﬀ. I’m always full of stoke and excitement when switching to running oﬀ the bike. The legs feel wonderful with a new motion, fresh to carry us up the peak.

Starting up the iconic Curved Ridge


Curved Ridge was everything you could ask for. Exposed, steep, airy, with wonderfully solid rock. As we ascended higher and higher into the clouds, the moves got more interesting. Culminating in a steep crux with plentiful holds and jams, Thomas and I motored our way up this aesthetic feature as a light mist set in. The view of the valley floor as we climbed up seemed mystically low and far away. As we reached the summit, the perspective we were rewarded with was hard to describe. That sweet satisfaction after biking for 2.5 days and lots of hills; the trip and vision were all coming together. After a few summit photos, the clouds swallowed us up, and the wind said hello. Okay, time to get oﬀ this thing! Running back down was a techy treat, practicing some quick footwork to navigate many a slippery rock and chunky talus. When it was all said and done, despite feeling like a full day's adventure, we were back at the bikes in 2 hours. Plenty more time for adventure and progression in the day.

Back into bike shoes, we grabbed our rigs and crossed the road. Next up was the most infamous section of the West Highland Way: Devils Staircase. From the summit of Stob Dearg, we could see the Staircase. Coming from Colorado, Thomas and I are accustomed to hike-a-bike (HAB). Some of our favorite local rides include HAB. I’m on record saying multiple times that all good adventure rides need to have some HAB. Despite the hype, Devils Staircase made us feel at home. No big deal really, maybe 30 minutes of pushing at the most? Come on! That is light work for us, even after a 2-hour run. The thing that challenged us really in this section was the weather. It was raining pretty hard for the rest of our day. Towards the bottom of the Staircase, Thomas had a rear tire slash while riding over one of the many water bars that line this climb. If my memory is correct, this was the only bike mechanical issue we encountered all trip. One of the benefits of doing a trip like this with a partner is that bike mechanicals and problems are so much easier to solve as a team, especially when the weather is bad. Couple plugs, add some air, back on the trail!

We made fun work of that climb, hiking with our heavy rigs past many thru-hikers. Showing them who is boss. At the top of the pass, we then proceeded to encounter our gnarliest true MTB terrain of the whole trip. Rowdy riding and chunky terrain. It was a brake-squealing, arm-pumping descent down to Kinlochleven. We were reminded once again that our bike choice was 10/10. I was thinking to myself that if I had been on my fully rigid ESC, I would have walked that entire descent. The trip would have been nearly impossible and stupid on that bike. Hardtail mountain bikes for the win!

In Kinlochleven, Thomas and I hit the local grocery store for some orange soda and a bag of chips. Something on the lighter side to fuel us over the next pass to Fort William. In some ways, I think we both thought our day was close to ending; little did we know we had some brutal climbing and weather to contest with. Oh, and some really rough and muddy tracks. The day was starting to add up. Waking up in our wet bivy spot just some hours earlier felt like a lifetime ago. Eventually we made our way up a steep mixed-surface climb and started a long gradual service road to a small pass that gave way towards Fort William. The riding here was tough and tedious. Our progress slowed, and our motivation waned. As we battled into a headwind, we eventually hit our last steep climb before ripping down to Fort William. Town was a bit of a blur for both of us. I remember stopping at a bike shop, and Thomas pleaded for a hose. Our bikes were filthy and covered in all types of mud and manure. The rain started and stopped. Thomas had booked us luxurious accommodations down the road that included a full sauna/steam situation. Felt like we had earned that, and with how the weather was acting and our current location, sleeping inside felt like a no-brainer. When I think back to planning and dreaming up this trip, it was a day like this that really lit the spark. Interesting riding, run/scramble up an incredible peak, get back on the bike and do it all again. It was only the night of Day 3; Thomas and I were getting our full value experience I was grateful for how it was panning out.

Stay tuned for Track 2: Cairngorm Traverse

Moots Womble (Kyle)


Moots MXC (Thomas)

entry.title: More Wild Horses Than Cars
entry.content:
Thirty riders, eighty-eight miles, and the quiet fall backcountry of Routt County. Rapha x Moots Brevet, a fall gravel ride out of Steamboat Springs, Colorado.

Words by Richard Jara · Photos by Keegan Ashton, Nate Bradley


Friday

The factory is winding down on a Friday evening. The welding torches are off, and tubing sits racked along the walls in the miter shop. Evening light shines through settling into the corners. On the Friday before the Brevet, the shop floor filled with riders who had driven in, most of them from Boulder and the Front Range. We started the night with a tour, a look into the process behind a handbuilt titanium gravel bike, and a look back at Moots' history as we celebrate our 45th anniversary. Then we shared food and drinks to fuel up for Saturday's ride.

A brevet isn't a race. No clock, no podium, no free socks. There's the route, the people on it with you, and the experience shared after a hard day.

This day asked a lot.

Saturday morning. Thirty riders gather outside the Moots factory for the start.


The Climb

Wolf Mountain to Sand Mountain. The loop strings together some of our favorite roads and surfaces, from champagne gravel to rocky, rooted two-track over the divide.

The Route · 87.6 mi · 8,416 ft of climbing

Ride it yourself: Wolf Mountain x Sand Mountain on Ride with GPS →

The loop leaves the valley quickly, turning onto dirt county roads and winding through Mystic to the base of Wolf Mountain. If you weren't committed to the full route this was your chance to cut the route shorter. Long fence lines, grazing cows, and the quiet chill of morning. Golden, sunburnt hills in every direction, with dark pines along the high ridges, and off to the north sits the watershed divide we'd be crossing hours later. Recent rains had packed the dirt firm. We couldn't have asked for a better window.

More wild horses than cars. Somewhere in California Park, Routt National Forest

The climbing doesn't let up. It builds steadily through the first half, mile after mile, until the high point near mile fifty. By then the group had strung out across the route.

Nate Bradley putting the new Routt through its paces. Meet the new Routt →


Sand Mountain

The descent off Sand Mountain was, in Torin Lackmann's words, "chonky" loose, rocky, and a little above everyone's comfort zone. At the bottom, a pop-up aid station was waiting. Huge thanks to Gina, Keegan, and Indy for being there with food, water, and good spirits for a lot of tired souls.

Food, water, and good spirits at the bottom of Sand Mountain.


Home

From there, thirty miles and about 2,000 feet of climbing stood between us and the finish, most of it trending downhill. After Sand Mountain, the final stretch felt well earned, smooth champagne gravel over long, rolling hills, with the valley and Steamboat slowly coming back into view.

"The absolute fall ride of my dreams. Has to be my favorite single day out of the year. So pretty. So fun. So flowy. All. Time."

— Torin Lackmann, Rapha Boulder

Thirty riders rolled out that morning. They rolled back in dusty, cooked, and grinning. Post-ride beers waiting.

"Although there were a couple of hard, dark moments, everyone seemed to have an amazing ride. One rider told us back at the shop that afternoon it was the best gravel ride he'd ever done, hands down. We're truly lucky to have terrain like this right outside our front door. It validates why we make the bikes we do."

— Nate Bradley, Moots

We build bikes like the new Routt for days like this. Long days, rough roads, and every side of the map to explore.

Thanks to Rapha Boulder for making the trip to our corner of Colorado and making the roads we know by heart feel new again, and to all thirty of you for riding them with us.

Want to ride it yourself? Here's the route.

See you out there.

entry.title: One of One: The Vamoots CRD × Mavic x Campagnolo
entry.content:
Every so often a build comes along that only happens once. This is one of those.

When we were deciding what special project to bring to MADE 2026 in Portland, we kept landing on the same answer. Road. So that is what we built: a one-of-one Vamoots CRD, painted for this collaboration, built with Mavic and Campagnolo. It debuted at the show, and it is the only one we will make.

Handcrafted in Steamboat Springs, the way we have always done it since 1981.

The story

We have been welding titanium by hand in Steamboat for decades. Mavic has been building wheels for over a century. Campagnolo has been shaping road groupsets in Italy for generations. This bike puts all three on one frame, shaping the purest expression of the craft. Road.

The finish is where this one lives. A soft sea-foam green over the front triangle fades to white, with pinstripe detailing running through it. Get the light on it right and the paint stops behaving like paint. Fine flake sits suspended in the clear coat, and for a second, the right light catches it like the surface is still wet. The matching Moots seat post leaves a band of raw titanium exposed, and the Enve one-piece cockpit and fork are painted to match. Chris King's Jade finish on the headset, hubs, and lockrings ties it all together. The Jade Chris King surface is matte, but the color isn't flat, it shifts slightly depending on the light and the angle you're looking from. No two glances land the same. We designed the finish in-house for this frame, one of one.

The build

The Vamoots CRD sits at the top of our road line. It starts with our double-butted RSL titanium tubeset and runs a fully integrated cockpit, so the lines stay clean and the cables stay out of sight.

  • Frame: Vamoots CRD, 54cm, RSL double-butted titanium tubeset
  • Wheels: Mavic Comete 55/65
  • Groupset: Campagnolo Super Record 13, 2x13, 55/39T, 11-36
  • Finish: one-off MADE 2026 custom paint
  • Highlights: 3D-printed dropouts, Fully integrated, T47 bottom bracket, 32c tire clearance

See the full spec

The only one

Give us a blank canvas and one bike to make, and this is the result. Our best road platform, the best parts our partners build, and a finish that exists exactly once. An ode to the road, from a shop that has always loved it. Made to last.

There is only one, and this is it. The bike you have been looking at is the one for sale. See the full build and make it yours.

More from MADE 2026

The Vamoots CRD wasn't the only thing we brought to Portland. If you missed the show, here's the rest of what was on the floor:

  • The limited-edition "Phase" finish on the new Womble — the etched-and-anodized fade that ended up stealing the show. The Radavist has the finish story and a full gallery.
  • The new Routt — our reworked gravel platform, built around bigger rubber and a 3D-printed yoke, shown as a prototype. More to come soon. BIKEPACKING walked through it.
  • The new all road - one bike for smooth road, broken pavement, and the gravel shortcut, with clearance up to 42c. Shown a a prototype, more to come.
  • The 32" prototypes — two big-wheel hardtails we're still testing, including the Scrambler 32. Also in BIKEPACKING's builder rundown.

The conversations, the rides, the stoke, that's why we do this. Events like MADE are never just about the bikes, they're about the people who show up for them. Thank you for being a part of it.

We'll be back on the road later this year. Find us at Bespoked Japan in Osaka, October 23 to 25, and Rouleur Live in London this November.

Until next time.

Suggested links:

  • Womble → https://theradavist.com/2026-made-bike-show-06
  • Routt → https://bikepacking.com/bikes/bikes-and-builders-of-made-2026-part-5/
  • 32" prototypes / Scrambler 32 → https://bikepacking.com/bikes/bikes-and-builders-of-made-2026-part-5/ (same piece), or the video: https://bikepacking.com/plog/made-2026-video-part-4/

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: KELSEY HUTCHINSON
entry.content:
From Fashion to Frames

Kelsey’s path to Moots began far from a welding bench. After stepping away from a career in fashion journalism in New York City, she returned to her hometown of Omaha, Nebraska, looking for something more hands-on. A job at a local bike and coffee shop sparked a growing interest in cycling, but everything changed after visiting Co-Motion Cycles in Oregon. Watching a frame being welded made the direction clear. Two days later, she quit her classes and enrolled in welding school with one goal in mind: to build bicycle frames.

Betting on the Craft

Welding school in the Midwest focused on structural welding, not bikes. The idea of becoming a framebuilder earned skeptical looks and advice about taking a long, traditional path. Moots saw her focus and commitment and hired her before she even graduated.

“I went to welding school with the sole purpose of building bicycle frames.”

The Reality of Building a Moots

While Moots bikes travel the world, Kelsey works within an intentionally small team of makers behind the scenes. Every frame is built by hand, with pride taken in each step of the process and the details that define a Moots.

Challenges and Wins

Most bike welds are smooth curves, which makes the occasional straight-line weld surprisingly difficult. For Kelsey, welding binders onto steerer blanks can be the most challenging. The most satisfying moments come when everything lines up, especially nailing the drive-side front triangle welds.

No Compromises

Kelsey credits much of her growth to the people around her. Teammates who have been welding for years continue to push her to refine her craft and show up striving for that extra one percent. For her, “No Compromises” means honoring the trust riders place in Moots by delivering nothing short of perfect.

Forever Bikes

Bikes are memory makers. Even if a bike eventually changes hands, the rides, adventures, and everyday moments tied to it stay with the rider. Knowing she had a hand in creating something that meaningful is what keeps Kelsey invested in every weld.

Why Titanium

Steel is fine. Aluminum is less forgiving. Titanium is different. Smooth, precise, and endlessly satisfying to weld, it’s the material that keeps her inspired at the bench.

Life Beyond the Bench

Kelsey rides a Routt 45, RCS, Womble, and a Routt CRD. Outside the shop, she stays active year-round with workouts, dance classes, boot packing with her dogs in the winter, and riding or gardening when the snow melts. Her go-to coffee is a light roast with a splash of cream, unless she’s feeling sassy, then it’s a cortado. While others tune into music, she listens to true crime podcasts.

 

The People

Ask Kelsey her favorite part of Moots, and the answer is simple: the people. The factory feels like family, and that sense of trust runs deep. Being asked by a coworker to weld their frame is still one of the highest honors.

Dream Ride

If she could take any Moots anywhere, she knows exactly where she’d go. Spain, on two wheels, is high on the list.

entry.title: San Francisco Bay Area Loop by Thomas Woodson
entry.content:
The San Francisco Bay Area, despite its massive population, holds an equally massive amount of protected land: networks of multi-use trails and campgrounds stitched throughout. You trade remoteness for convenience, but this kind of variety is something I love to fold into my bikepacking goals. Plentiful food, quality sleep, hard-charging downhills—elements worth remembering the next time you’re really out there and feeling a bit thrashed.

My introduction to the area was the SF Peninsula Traverse, a route I used to start a weeklong ride from San Francisco Airport to Los Angeles Airport in 2019. In 2024, Adam Sklar showed me around some of the Marin and Fairfax classics. I’ve been fascinated by the sheer number of options ever since, to the point that my Gaia GPS maps are now borderline too cluttered to navigate.

Looking for ways to combine the SF Peninsula Traverse with the Bay Area Triple Crossover led us to Bikepack the Bay—a 265-mile, +27,000ft route that we trimmed slightly to fit more comfortably into a three-day window with limited December daylight.

Day 1 covered 64 miles and +5,600ft from Sklar’s shop in the Mission District, following the SF Peninsula Traverse through Half Moon Bay, climbing into the redwoods (at night), and dropping into a Palo Alto hotel. The route starts urban, slowly dissolving into crumbling abandoned roads through the hills, coastline bike paths, and finally a lush, pine-needle climb that’s absolutely grueling. From Skyline Road, the Kings Mountain Road descent—ridden in the dark—was the best road descent of my life. Dynamo-illuminated reflectors twisted through the redwoods like the ultimate video game.

Day 2 began with a long bridge and shoreline crossing, then followed nearly the entire skyline from Fremont to Richmond along the Bay Area Ridge Trail (decently signed).  77 miles and +7,700ft. Spending the entire day on bike paths, wide dirt roads, and ripping singletrack was hard to believe given the proximity to millions of people. Fifty-two-tooth cassettes and the absence of camping gear were especially welcome for just how steep every climb was on this stretch.

Day 3 opened with another bridge traverse and 67 miles of +7,300ft along ridge top fire roads to Lagunitas—the only resupply point—before a final push along Bolinas Ridge, around Tam, and across the Golden Gate back into San Francisco. Once again, a full day without really touching a road. We skipped the Headlands trails as sunset approached, but there are plenty of options to explore there.

The varied, ever-changing terrain kept us engaged. The urban offered a reprieve from the steeps; the steeps, a reprieve from the urban. Staying in cheap hotels felt like a luxury—less luggage, more riding. Kyle is typically the route master when we’re out together, but I believe I showed him some things to change his perspectives this time around. The Bay Area is about to be one of our winter classics.

Tips
– Navigation is constant. A head unit is essential, and having the tracks on your phone as backup is smart. Trail closures around the Baylands in Palo Alto before the bridge crossing added a few miles of backtracking
– The Richmond Bridge closes the bike lane during the week but offers a free shuttle bus in its place. If you want to ride it, check schedules and plan a weekend crossing
– Keeping a variety of Bay Area routes saved allows for easy on-the-fly modifications or side quests
– SFO Airport offers luggage storage and a bike stand if you want to start and finish the loop there

Incredible resources:
SF Peninsula Traverse – https://bikepacking.com/routes/sf-peninsula-traverse/
Bay Area Triple Crossover – https://bikepacking.com/routes/bay-area-triple-crossover/
Bay Area Ridge Trail – https://ridgetrail.org/
Bikepack the Bay – https://www.bikepackthebay.com/

--- 

Thomas Woodson is a Colorado-based photographer and Moots ambassador known for capturing long days, quiet moments, and the kind of riding that rewards curiosity over convenience. He currently rides a dropbar MXC in our Groundswell finish, a setup well suited to the mixed terrain and exploratory routes that shape his work.

entry.title: Winter Desert Miles
entry.content:
When the temperatures drop and the mountains start to get capped with snow, many of us in the mountains start looking south. As winter settles into the high country and riding up high fades, the desert opens up. Cooler days, fewer crowds, and long stretches of quiet make late fall and early winter the right time to ride White Rim. It’s not about speed or numbers—it’s about choosing the season, committing to the miles, and finding space before winter fully takes hold. Richard takes us on his adventure on the White Rim outside of the famed Moab, Utah. 

I just got back from eight days in the desert.

Already checking the weather for the next warm window, planning how I’m going to keep riding through winter, something I’ve always abandoned for skiing. Living in the mountains, you share an unspoken bond with winter. It’s a fortunate place with easy access to snow and the outdoors. I’ve skied resort and earned my uphill turns for the last nine years, but lately the chairlift scene feels played out. So when opening weekend and the first storm of the year rolled through, I did the opposite and headed west, away from the noise. Offseason in Moab.

Bike choice: Routt CRD. 34mm road slicks mounted. 44mm Mezcals in the truck for when dirt was good

One bike. Keep it simple. 

Day one: blue sky above the red rock canyons, fresh snow on the La Sals. No wind, just stillness in the cold desert air. Cold start that never really warmed up, but I was out there riding, and that was the plan. River Road to Castle Valley, then out and back to Arches National Park. One hundred scenic miles, and 7k. Easily one of the best road rides in the country. Had to bail into the truck near the end, blast the heaters, and warm up. Then back outside to finish it. Glad I did. 

I fell into a rhythm for the next three days. Wake up, coffee, pick a direction, go ride, try not to freeze. Hit all the Moab road classics: 313 out to Island in the Sky, Potash Road, the Canyon Path, Arches, Upper Colorado River Scenic Byway to Dewey Bridge. Missed the window for La Sal Mountain Loop Road, but that was okay. 

The views in the Moab desert are magnificent, whether you're on pavement or deep in the desert. I was chasing another route. By the end of the week, after the cold front cleared, it became clear that conditions in Canyonlands would be dry enough. Saturday would be the day. Forecast in the 50s. White Rim.

White Rim is a one-hundred-mile route through the Island in the Sky district of Canyonlands National Park. First rode it in December 2019, but I keep coming back to check in. It's become a benchmark. A testing ground. An escape. Just hard enough. Just remote enough. But this wasn't about PRs or pushing numbers. This was about chasing desert miles and the low winter sun. About being out there and just riding.

Texted Andrew on Friday. “White Rim tomorrow?”

“Yeah, I'm in.”

Quick logistics: 8am start, Mineral Bottom/313 intersection, counter-clockwise. Day permits sorted. Self-supported, everything we needed on the bikes. Keep it simple.  Andrew runs a custom bikepacking gear company with his wife Katie, out of an off-grid workshop at the foot of the La Sal Mountains. We first connected on the Colorado Trail back in 2019. It's always good to reconnect with racing friends, and to ride with someone who gets the appeal of long days, minimal setups, and backcountry routes. I’ve taken a lot of inspiration from the way Andrew approaches cycling and racing. Most of the ride was a conversation about gear, bikes, and what’s next on the list. By then, we had already approached the final climb up Schafer Trail, the sun had gone down, and we rolled the final 8ish miles by headlamp. A full day on the pedals, no major mechanical issues, and good conditions. Hard to ask for more.  

On the way back to the mountains, I stopped and camped on 18rd in Fruita, spun the legs out once more around the Colorado National Monument, another Colorado classic. Back to winter, for now. 

https://www.strava.com/athletes/6042499

 - Richard

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: ERIC HINDES
entry.content:
25 Years of Craft, Curiosity, and Getting It Right

Some people find their way to bike building through formal paths. Others through obsession. For Eric Hindes, it started at home and it stuck.

Eric has been part of the Moots team for 25 years. Today, he programs and runs multiple CNC machines, helps shape how we manufacture frames and components in-house, and carries decades of institutional knowledge across the production floor. But like many great bike builders, his story starts long before his first day at Moots.

A Family Affair and a Pile of Magazines

Eric’s entry into bikes came courtesy of his dad. Mountain biking was new, exciting, and everywhere in the pages of Fat Tire Flyer, Mountain Bike, Dirt Rag, and Bike. Those magazines introduced Eric (and his family) to the early pioneers of the sport: Charlie Cunningham, Joe Breeze, Kent Eriksen and sparked something deeper than riding.
